parts.title: Adding a little easy-to-digest food for bacteria keeps nitrogen removal strong and reliable in an anammox tank treating city wastewater
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Wastewater carries nitrogen, which has to be removed before the water returns to rivers and lakes. One promising approach relies on special microbes called anammox bacteria. They combine two nitrogen compounds, ammonium and nitrite, into harmless nitrogen gas. We ran a tank of these bacteria, an anammox reactor, on weak wastewater that held only 25–35 mg/L of ammonium plus nitrite.

We ran the tank in two phases. In phase I, the wastewater contained no easy-to-digest organic matter. In phase II, we added some. By "easy-to-digest organic matter" we mean carbon-based food that bacteria can break down quickly. Engineers call it readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand, or rbCOD.

In phase I, the reactor removed nitrogen well at first. After a long run of 75 days, though, a third nitrogen compound, nitrate, built up in the water leaving the tank. The share of nitrogen the reactor removed fell to 30%. When we looked at the microbes, anammox bacteria had dropped from 2.15% to 1.78% of the community. Meanwhile, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) had risen from 0.14% to 0.56%. These are unwanted microbes that turn nitrite into nitrate.

In phase II, we added the easy-to-digest food as acetate, a simple compound related to the acid in vinegar. We added it at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 0.9. Within 2 days, nitrate in the outgoing water fell. From then on, the reactor removed nitrogen very thoroughly. On average, the treated water held only 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen.

Even with the added food, the anammox route still did most of the nitrogen removal. Large-scale genetic sequencing of the microbes showed a high share of anammox bacteria (2.48%), which further supports their leading role.

We credit the improvement to three things. First, the unwanted NOB were held back more strongly. Second, leftover nitrate was cleaned up at the same time through partial denitrification working together with anammox: other bacteria turned nitrate back into nitrite, which the anammox bacteria then used. Third, the sludge (the mass of microbes in the tank) clumped more readily into small grains called granules.

Overall, adding small amounts of easy-to-digest organic matter is a practical way to make nitrogen removal reliable and efficient in anammox reactors that treat the main flow of city wastewater.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, main flow of city wastewater, nitrogen removal, easy-to-digest organic matter
parts.introduction_first:
Over the past ten years, one way of removing nitrogen from city wastewater has drawn a lot of attention. It is called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A), and it could let a wastewater treatment plant run without using more energy than it produces (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017).

PN/A works in two steps. First, in partial nitritation, bacteria turn part of the ammonium in the water into nitrite. Then anammox bacteria combine the remaining ammonium with that nitrite to make nitrogen gas. The microbes in this process are "autotrophic": they build their bodies from carbon dioxide instead of feeding on organic matter.

Engineers have built PN/A in different ways, depending on whether both steps share one tank (single-stage) or each gets its own tank (two-stage). In a two-stage system, each step can be fine-tuned in its own tank. This helps the different microbes grow where they are needed (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, two-stage PN/A usually removes nitrogen faster than single-stage PN/A (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusion

In this study, we set up an anammox treatment for the main flow of city wastewater in a sequencing batch reactor. This is a tank that repeatedly fills, treats, settles and empties in cycles.

When we ran the reactor without any easy-to-digest organic matter, a lot of nitrate built up in the water leaving the tank. This happened because unwanted nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) were active, and it made nitrogen removal less efficient.

Adding a small amount of easy-to-digest organic matter changed this. It rescued the reactor from the nitrate build-up and gave highly efficient nitrogen removal. Anammox remained the main way nitrogen was removed. Alongside it, partial denitrification working with anammox cleaned up the nitrate made by the anammox reaction itself.

The NOB were also held back effectively, because the tank contained even less oxygen than before. In addition, the sludge formed more granules, which helped the slow-growing anammox bacteria build up in the tank.

Overall, adding small amounts of easy-to-digest organic matter is a practical way to make nitrogen removal reliable and efficient in anammox reactors that treat the main flow of city wastewater.
parts.introduction_rest:
Even so, running PN/A at full scale on the main flow of city wastewater is still hard. One of the biggest worries is that too much nitrate stays in the water leaving the plant. That extra nitrate pushes total nitrogen above the legal limit for water released into the environment (Zhuang et al., 2022).

In a two-stage PN/A system, nitrate can form in both tanks. In the first tank, where partial nitritation happens, the unwanted nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) can turn nitrite into nitrate. In the second tank, nitrate comes from two sources. The anammox reaction itself gives off a little nitrate as a by-product, and NOB may also be active there.

Recent research shows that nitrate made in the first tank can be kept very low. Researchers have developed several ways to hold back NOB there (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021). One is to switch the air supply on and off rather than running it all the time. Another is to keep the sludge in the tank for only a very short time, so that slow-growing NOB are washed out. Engineers call this an ultra-low sludge retention time (SRT). A third is to take some sludge out to a side tank and treat it with substances that stop NOB from working.

That leaves the second tank, the anammox reactor, as the main source of nitrate. Several studies have reported too much nitrate from NOB activity in anammox reactors of different designs (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). These designs include sequencing batch reactors, fully mixed tanks, and tanks where the water flows upward through a bed of sludge grains (expanded granular sludge blanket reactors). Unfortunately, most of the tricks that hold back NOB in the first tank cannot be used in the anammox tank, because they may harm the anammox bacteria too. So we need to find new ways to stop nitrate from building up in anammox reactors.

Early studies saw easy-to-digest organic matter as a problem for anammox treatment of the main wastewater flow. They argued it should be removed beforehand. Otherwise, bacteria that feed on organic matter, called heterotrophs, might grow too fast and crowd out the anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies tell a different story. When anammox reactors were given the right amount of easy-to-digest organic matter, at carbon-to-nitrogen ratios of 0.5–1.5, the anammox bacteria kept working. In fact, the reactors removed more than 90% of the nitrogen (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

However, most of these studies treated wastewater with high nitrogen levels, of 100–300 mg of nitrogen per liter. At such high levels, forms of ammonia and nitrite known as free ammonia and free nitrous acid can hold back the growth of NOB (Ge et al., 2015). Because of this, too much nitrate was not a real problem in those studies. It is still unknown whether adding easy-to-digest organic matter can fix the nitrate build-up caused by NOB in anammox reactors that treat the weaker main flow of city wastewater.

Partial denitrification working with anammox (PD/A) could also help inside anammox reactors. In this process, other bacteria turn nitrate back into nitrite, and the anammox bacteria then use that nitrite. PD/A needs less organic matter to remove nitrogen, and it lessens the harm organic matter can do to anammox bacteria (Du et al., 2019). But in most PD/A studies, the incoming water mainly contained ammonium and nitrate (Du et al., 2019). The situation is different in anammox reactors treating the main wastewater flow. There, most of the oxidized nitrogen (nitrite and nitrate) arriving in the water is nitrite, and nitrate only appears gradually as the anammox reaction makes it. Very few studies have looked at how PD/A behaves in such reactors when easy-to-digest organic matter is present, so this needs more research (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up and ran an anammox reactor treating the main flow of city wastewater in two phases, one without and one with easy-to-digest organic matter. We compared the two phases in several ways: how well the reactor removed nitrogen, how steady the treatment was, which microbes lived in the tank, and what the sludge looked like. Using these data, we judged how low levels of easy-to-digest organic matter affect anammox treatment of the main wastewater flow. We also assessed how much such low levels could improve nitrogen removal.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and methods

2.1. How we set up the experiment

We treated the main flow of city wastewater with anammox bacteria in a 10-liter sequencing batch reactor (Figure 1). This is a tank that repeatedly fills, treats, settles and empties in cycles. To get it started, we seeded it with sludge from another small lab tank of anammox bacteria that had been treating wastewater rich in nitrogen. Right after seeding, the tank held 4.9 grams of microbes per liter of water.

The tank ran three cycles a day, and each cycle had five steps (Figure 1B). First, we fed in new wastewater for 10 minutes, swapping out half the water in the tank. Next came 360 minutes of stirring without any air. The sludge then settled for 30 minutes, treated water was drained off for 10 minutes, and the tank sat idle for 70 minutes before the next cycle. The tank stayed at room temperature, 24–26°C.

We never deliberately removed sludge from the tank. The only sludge that left was what washed out with the treated water and what we took as samples. Because of this, the microbes stayed in the tank for a long time. Engineers call this the sludge retention time, meaning the average time the microbes spend in the tank, and we estimate it was longer than 30 days.

Figure 1. (A) A diagram of the anammox reactor treating the main flow of city wastewater. (B) The steps in each cycle.

We ran the reactor in two phases, which differed in what we fed it (Figure 1A and Table 1).

In phase I (days 1–75), each cycle we fed the tank 5 liters of water coming out of a partial nitritation reactor. That earlier tank treated synthetic city wastewater, a man-made mixture that imitates real city wastewater, and turned part of its ammonium into nitrite. We describe it in the Supplementary material. The water we fed to the anammox tank held little organic matter. We measured organic matter as chemical oxygen demand, or COD, which tells us how much oxygen would be needed to break that matter down. The feed had 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L of COD. (The number after "±" shows how much the values usually varied around the average.) Since this water had already been treated by bacteria, most of what was left was probably organic matter that is hard to break down.

In phase II (days 76–135), we took 0.5 liters of the raw synthetic city wastewater and let it skip the partial nitritation reactor. We mixed it with 4.5 liters of water from the partial nitritation reactor in a middle tank, and then fed this mixture to the anammox tank. In this way, easy-to-digest organic matter entered the system as acetate, at 24.2 mg of COD per liter. Apart from this change in the organic matter in the feed, we ran the reactor in exactly the same way and under the same conditions in both phases.

Table 1. The main contents of the water fed to the anammox reactor. The columns show ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, total nitrogen and organic matter (COD), all in mg/L.

| | NH4+-N (mg/L) | NO2−-N (mg/L) | NO3−-N (mg/L) | TN (mg/L) | COD (mg/L) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8 |
| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2 |

2.2. Flask tests to see whether partial denitrification working with anammox could happen in the reactor

We ran two separate tests in flasks, outside the reactor, to find out whether partial denitrification working with anammox could happen with the microbes in our tank. We took sludge from the reactor and rinsed it three times with very pure water. Then we divided it among four separate 0.5-liter cone-shaped flasks. After adding organic matter and nitrogen compounds, we kept the flasks at 25°C in machines that shake them (200 turns per minute). Throughout the tests, we bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks to keep oxygen out.

In Batch Test I, we asked whether nitrite could build up while other bacteria were turning nitrate back toward nitrogen gas, a process called denitrification. So we added only nitrate (as sodium nitrate, NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. Every flask started with the same amount of nitrate, 15 mg/L, but we gave each one a different amount of acetate. The ratio of organic matter (COD) to nitrate nitrogen at the start was 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 in the four flasks.

In Batch Test II, we asked whether denitrification could work together with anammox. This time the flasks also got ammonium (as ammonium chloride, NH4Cl), in addition to nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate. Each flask started with 10 mg/L of ammonium and 15 mg/L of nitrate. Again, the four flasks got different amounts of acetate, so that their ratios of organic matter to nitrate nitrogen were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0.

2.3. How we measured things

We followed standard, widely used lab methods (APHA, 2005) to measure organic matter (COD), ammonium, nitrite, nitrate and total nitrogen. With these methods we also measured three properties of the sludge. The first was the amount of solid material in the tank water (mixed liquor suspended solids). The second was the part of those solids that burns away when heated, which is mostly living microbes (mixed liquor volatile suspended solids). The third was how well the sludge settles, given by the sludge volume index.

A WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany) kept continuous track of the temperature, the acidity (pH) and the dissolved oxygen in the reactor. To find the sizes of the sludge particles, we used a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4. How we worked out which routes the nitrogen took during typical cycles

Nitrogen can be changed from one form to another by several groups of microbes. To estimate how much each route contributed, we tracked how the amounts of the nitrogen compounds changed from the start to the end of typical cycles. We included only the main routes. Because the two phases were run differently, we used a different calculation for each.

In phase I, almost no easy-to-digest organic matter entered the reactor, so we left out denitrification. We worked out the nitrogen changed by three groups of microbes: anammox bacteria; ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which use oxygen to turn ammonium into nitrite; and NOB. For this we used Equations 1–3. In these equations, the numbers 2.04 and 0.26 come from the known recipe of the anammox reaction, which links how much ammonium it uses to how much nitrogen it removes and how much nitrate it makes.

(1) TN_anammox = ΔN = (NH4+-N_initial + NO2−-N_initial + NO3−-N_initial) − (NH4+-N_final + NO2−-N_final + NO3−-N_final)

(2) NH4+-N_AOB = NH4+-N_initial − NH4+-N_final − TN_anammox / 2.04

(3) NO3−-N_NOB = NO3−-N_final − NO3−-N_initial − TN_anammox × 0.26 / 2.04

What the symbols mean (all in mg of nitrogen per liter): TN_anammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria. NH4+-N_AOB is the ammonium used up by AOB. NO3−-N_NOB is the nitrate made by NOB. ΔN is how much the total dissolved inorganic nitrogen in the tank water dropped between the start and the end of the cycle. NH4+-N_initial, NO2−-N_initial and NO3−-N_initial are the ammonium, nitrite and nitrate in the tank water at the start of the cycle. NH4+-N_final, NO2−-N_final and NO3−-N_final are the same three at the end of the cycle.

In phase II, the tank held even less oxygen than in phase I, and overall the reactor removed nitrate (Section 3.2). So this time we left out nitrification, the oxygen-using route that turns ammonium into nitrite and nitrate. Instead, we worked out the nitrogen changed by three routes. The first was anammox. The second was denitratation, where bacteria turn nitrate into nitrite (NO3− → NO2−). The third was denitritation, where bacteria turn nitrite into nitrogen gas (NO2− → N2). For these we used Equations 4–6.

(4) TN_anammox = NH4+-N_initial − NH4+-N_final × 2.04

(5) NO3−-N_denitratation = NO3−-N_initial + TN_anammox × 0.26 / 2.04 − NO3−-N_final

(6) TN_denitritation = ΔN − TN_anammox

What the symbols mean (all in mg of nitrogen per liter): TN_anammox is the total nitrogen removed through the anammox route. NO3−-N_denitratation is the nitrate turned into nitrite by denitratation. TN_denitritation is the total nitrogen removed through denitritation.

2.5. Large-scale genetic sequencing

To find out which microbes lived in the tank, we took sludge samples on day 1, day 75 and day 134. We freeze-dried them (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States) and stored them at −20°C. We pulled the DNA out of the samples with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the maker's instructions. To make sure the DNA extract was pure, we measured its concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands).

Next we focused on one gene that all bacteria carry, the 16S rRNA gene. Some parts of this gene differ from one type of bacteria to another, so they work a bit like a name tag. We made many copies of one such part, the V3–V4 region, using a copying method called PCR. Short matching pieces of DNA, called primers, mark where the copying starts and ends. We used the bacterial primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′).

The copied DNA was then read on an Illumina MiSeq machine (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). From these readings, we worked out which microbes were present, and in what shares, in the same way as in our earlier report (Yang et al., 2017). We have placed the raw DNA readings in a public database, the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA), under Accession Number PRJNA942604.
parts.results:
## 3. Results

### 3.1. How well nitrogen was removed without and with easy-to-digest organic matter

In phase I, almost no easy-to-digest organic matter entered the reactor. We could see this because the tank removed hardly any organic matter at all. Engineers measure organic matter as chemical oxygen demand, or COD, which is how much oxygen it would take to break it down. The reactor removed only 3.8 mg/L of COD on average, give or take 2.1 mg/L from day to day (Figure 2A).

Nitrogen removal in phase I was unsteady (Figures 2B and 2C). It went well at first, during days 1–40. But from day 41 to day 75, nitrate in the water leaving the tank rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L. By the end of phase I, ammonium and nitrite were building up too. This showed that the anammox bacteria had become less active. As a result, the share of incoming nitrogen that the reactor removed fell from 83% to 30%.

**Figure 2.** How much organic matter, measured as COD (A), and total nitrogen (B) the anammox reactor removed, and the amounts of each nitrogen compound in the water entering and leaving the tank (C).

In phase II, we added acetate to the incoming water at 24.2 mg COD/L. This raised the ratio of easy-to-digest organic matter to total nitrogen to 0.9. On average, the reactor now removed 27.7 mg/L of COD, which means the bacteria used up all of the easy-to-digest food we supplied (Figure 2A).

The change was fast. Within 2 days, nitrate in the treated water dropped from 8.7 mg/L to 2.1 mg/L. It then stayed low for the rest of the run, at 1.1 mg/L on average, give or take 0.9 mg/L (Figure 2C). In other words, the reactor was now removing nitrate. This suggested that denitrification was happening in the tank. Denitrification is a process in which bacteria eat organic food and, in doing so, turn nitrate back into nitrite and then into nitrogen gas.

At the same time, ammonium and nitrite in the treated water also fell, which showed that the anammox bacteria had become active again. Over phase II, the reactor removed nitrogen very thoroughly. The treated water held only 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen on average, and the reactor removed 87.2% of the incoming nitrogen on average (Figure 2B).

### 3.2. How the nitrogen's route through the tank changed after adding easy-to-digest organic matter

To see which routes the nitrogen took, we followed the nitrogen compounds through single treatment cycles, from start to finish. In a typical cycle in phase I, before we added any easy-to-digest food, ammonium and nitrite slowly disappeared while a lot of nitrate built up (Figure 3A).

We compared how much nitrate appeared with how much ammonium was removed. For every unit of ammonium removed, 0.92 units of nitrate appeared. If the anammox reaction were working alone, only 0.26 units of nitrate would appear (Strous et al., 1998). So some other process had to be making the extra nitrate.

That process was nitrification. In nitrification, bacteria use oxygen to turn ammonium into nitrite, and then nitrite into nitrate. By tracking where the nitrogen went, we found that nitrification in the anammox reactor turned some ammonium into nitrite and some of that nitrite into nitrate (Figure 3B). Nitrification made 79% of all the nitrate produced, and this is why the reactor did not remove enough nitrogen.

**Figure 3.** Changes in the amounts of each nitrogen compound (A: phase I, C: phase II) and the routes the nitrogen took (B: phase I, D: phase II) during typical treatment cycles of the anammox reactor.

After we added easy-to-digest food in phase II, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell together during a typical cycle (Figure 3C). This shows that denitrification was removing two kinds of nitrate at once: the nitrate that came in with the wastewater and the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself makes.

Tracking the nitrogen also revealed partial denitrification. This is denitrification that stops halfway, turning nitrate into nitrite but not into nitrogen gas. It gave the anammox bacteria extra nitrite to use (Figure 3D), which boosted their activity inside the tank. Anammox still did most of the work: it accounted for 93% of the nitrogen removed (Figure 3D). Denitrification then raised the removal even further, leaving little total nitrogen in the treated water.

### 3.3. Small flask tests show that partial denitrification can work with anammox in the reactor

To look more closely at whether partial denitrification could work with anammox, we took sludge out of the reactor and ran short experiments with it in separate containers, called batch tests. In Batch Test I, we fed the sludge only nitrate and acetate, so we could study denitrification on its own. We tried four different ratios of organic food to nitrate.

At every ratio, nitrite built up (Figures 4A–D). The best result came when the food-to-nitrate ratio (COD to nitrate-nitrogen) was 2.0. At that ratio, 50.0% of the nitrate was turned into nitrite, the highest share we saw. These results suggest that denitrification in the anammox reactor could supply extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria.

**Figure 4.** Changes in the amounts of each nitrogen compound in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we added ammonium as well as nitrate and acetate. In the first hour, a lot of nitrate was removed while nitrite built up, again at every food-to-nitrate ratio. This showed that partial denitrification was taking place (Figures 4E–H).

After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell together. The batch tests were kept strictly free of oxygen, so the ammonium could only have been removed by anammox. The nitrite that the anammox bacteria used came from partial denitrification. This proves that partial denitrification working with anammox can happen in the reactor treating the main flow of city wastewater.

### 3.4. How the microbes in the reactor changed

We used large-scale genetic sequencing to see how small amounts of easy-to-digest organic matter affected the microbes in the reactor (Figure 5). All the percentages below are shares of the whole microbial community.

In phase I, with no easy-to-digest food, anammox bacteria (mostly a type called *Candidatus* Kuenenia) fell from 2.08% to 1.73%. Meanwhile, two groups of nitrifying bacteria rose markedly. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB, here *Nitrosomonas*), which turn ammonium into nitrite, rose from 0.29% to 0.40%. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB, here *Nitrospira*) rose from 0.14% to 0.56%. These trends match what we saw in the water: nitrate built up and nitrogen removal got worse as the reactor ran.

After we added easy-to-digest food in phase II, anammox bacteria recovered to 2.48%. At the same time, AOB fell to 0.05% and NOB fell to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding easy-to-digest organic matter in the right way helps anammox bacteria thrive and holds back the nitrifying bacteria.

The mix of denitrifying bacteria also changed after we added the food. In phase I, the main denitrifier was *Denitratisoma*, which can carry out complete denitrification, turning nitrate all the way into nitrogen gas. Its share fell from 3.91% to 2.00% in phase II. In contrast, *Thauera* and *Candidatus* Competibacter grew much more common in phase II. Earlier studies have identified both as bacteria that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020). *Thauera* rose from 0.18% to 2.15%, and *Candidatus* Competibacter from 0.15% to 1.35%. These results gave further evidence that partial denitrification was working with anammox in the reactor.

**Figure 5.** Changes in which microbes made up the community in the anammox reactor.

### 3.5. How the sludge formed granules in the reactor

The sludge we used to start the reactor already contained some granules. We counted a clump as a granule if it was more than 200 μm across (a micrometre, μm, is a thousandth of a millimetre). Granules made up 17.4% of this starting sludge, and the sludge clumps were 130.8 μm across on average (Figure 6).

The size of the sludge stayed steady in phase I. In phase II, it grew clearly, reaching an average of 195.6 μm. In the end, granules made up 52.5% of all the microbial mass in the reactor. This shows that adding easy-to-digest organic matter in phase II encouraged the sludge to form granules. Granules can help anammox bacteria build up in the tank, because these bacteria tend to grow better in large clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

**Figure 6.** Changes in the size of the sludge clumps in the anammox reactor.
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion

### 4.1. Why nitrogen removal improved after we added easy-to-digest organic matter

In this study, adding easy-to-digest organic matter quickly rescued the anammox reactor treating the main flow of city wastewater from a heavy build-up of nitrate (Figure 2). With only low amounts of this food present, the reactor removed nitrogen very thoroughly. Several mechanisms may lie behind this improvement.

First, nitrification was held back more strongly, so less nitrate was made inside the tank. Nitrification is the oxygen-using process in which microbes turn ammonium into nitrite and then into nitrate. In phase I, we ran the reactor without any easy-to-digest organic matter. Nitrification was fairly active, so more nitrate was made and nitrogen removal got worse (Figures 2, 3). Other studies have shown the same thing (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020).

The oxygen dissolved in the water, at 0.06–0.08 mg/L, is what allowed nitrification to happen. It came in with the incoming wastewater and from the air at the top of the reactor while the tank was being stirred by machine (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying microbes are very good at grabbing oxygen even when there is little of it (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). These include complete ammonia oxidizers, or comammox, which can turn ammonium all the way into nitrate by themselves, and NOB belonging to the group (genus) Nitrospira. These microbes may have added to nitrification in our reactor, because the amount of Nitrospira increased significantly (Figure 5).

In phase II, after we added easy-to-digest organic matter, the dissolved oxygen fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L. This was possibly because aerobic heterotrophic bacteria, which use oxygen and feed on organic matter, used it up (Figure 3C). So the tank held even less oxygen in phase II than in phase I, and this held back nitrification. As a result, during phase II there were fewer ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which turn ammonium into nitrite, and fewer NOB (Figure 5).

Second, partial denitrification working with anammox took place in the reactor. At the same time, it removed the nitrate that arrived with the incoming wastewater and the nitrate made by the anammox reaction itself. Batch tests, which are short, separate experiments in small containers, proved that nitrite can build up while nitrate is being denitrified (Figures 4A–D). Our analysis of what happened during one reactor cycle (Figure 3D), along with further batch tests (Figures 4E–H), showed that anammox bacteria can then use up and remove this nitrite. They do so with ammonium as the electron donor, meaning the compound that supplies the electrons for their reaction. In this way, the nitrate in the reactor was cleaned up while using only a little organic matter, and this raised the reactor's nitrogen removal efficiency to a high level.

There is more to this second mechanism. The easy-to-digest organic matter came in with the wastewater at the start of each cycle. Even so, nitrate was made (by anammox) and removed (by denitrification) nonstop during the whole cycle (Figure 3). We therefore expected endogenous denitrification to occur. This is denitrification powered by food that bacteria have stored inside their cells. In this study, the bacteria Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter did the work of partial denitrification during phase II (Figure 5). Both can store easy-to-digest organic matter inside their cells as reserves, such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates, a kind of natural plastic (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). So the organic matter in the incoming water may have been turned into stored reserves at the start of each cycle, and those reserves may then have fed partial denitrification for the whole cycle.

Third, the anammox bacteria became more active and grew more, which makes the process work better and more steadily. In this study, the acetate we added may have had only a limited direct effect on anammox activity. Low amounts of acetate do not slow anammox bacteria down (Huang et al., 2014). Some kinds of anammox bacteria, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can get energy from short-chain fatty acids, a family of simple organic compounds that includes acetate (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this route may not have mattered much here, because anammox bacteria of the genus Candidatus Kuenenia made up most of the anammox population in the reactor throughout the experiment.

The easy-to-digest organic matter therefore mainly helped anammox bacteria in indirect ways. For example, when other bacteria broke it down using oxygen, they used up dissolved oxygen in the water, and this weakened oxygen's harmful effect on anammox activity (Strous et al., 1999). In addition, when bacteria used the organic matter without oxygen for partial denitrification of nitrate, they supplied extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria, which boosted anammox activity (Figure 3). Furthermore, the organic matter made the microbes release more extracellular polymers, a sticky material they give off around themselves, and made the sludge form more granules (Figure 6). Other studies have shown this too (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). Granules helped keep the slow-growing anammox bacteria in the tank and let them build up (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b).

As a result, after we added low amounts of easy-to-digest organic matter, anammox bacteria rose from 1.73% to 2.48% of the microbial community (Figure 5). Meanwhile, the anammox route stayed the main way nitrogen was removed (Figure 3).

### 4.2. Putting this approach to use, and what to study next

In this study, we used an effective, practical strategy to solve the nitrate build-up caused by unwanted NOB activity in anammox reactors treating the main flow of city wastewater. Other ways to cut the amount of nitrate made have been reported (Díaz et al., 2020). They include pushing the oxygen out of the incoming wastewater with nitrogen gas, building the reactor tall and narrow so that less of its surface touches the air, and putting protective covers on the anammox reactor. However, these measures may not be affordable or workable in some cases. This is especially true when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because they require major rebuilding of the reactor.

That is why we tested adding low amounts of easy-to-digest organic matter instead. This can reduce nitrate build-up with only a small change: sending part of the untreated city wastewater to the anammox reactor, or adding a small amount of organic carbon from outside (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). The organic matter can also come from the liquid produced when sludge ferments, if a treatment plant has it available (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). Finally, our proposed way of running an anammox process on the main flow of city wastewater also works for continuous flow reactors, where water flows in and out all the time instead of in cycles. However, such reactors may need extra measures to keep the anammox bacteria inside. Examples are filling the tank with suitable carriers, which are small objects that bacteria can grow on, and using a cyclone, a swirling device that separates out granular sludge so it can be kept (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).

Even when NOB are not making too much nitrate, it helps to run the anammox reactor with a low amount of easy-to-digest organic matter, because this could remove all of the nitrogen (Zhuang et al., 2022). As other studies have reported, partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) and partial denitrification working with anammox both played a part in removing nitrogen (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen without needing organic food, while partial denitrification with anammox removed the nitrate made by the anammox reaction.

In Table 2, we give a theoretical equation for this combined process, called Case III. We compare it with two other anammox-based processes that also aim to remove all the nitrogen, called Cases I and II. We measure oxygen needs in milligrams of oxygen for each milligram of nitrogen removed. We measure organic matter as chemical oxygen demand (COD), a standard way of counting organic matter, again per milligram of nitrogen removed.

In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without organic food, but 11% of the ammonium ends up as nitrate. Cleaning up that nitrate through denitrification still uses organic carbon. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 mg of organic matter (as COD) for each mg of nitrogen. In Case II, the nitrite that anammox needs comes from first turning all the ammonium into nitrate (complete nitrification) and then turning that nitrate back into nitrite by partial denitrification. This route needs more oxygen and more organic carbon than making nitrite by partial nitritation. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg of oxygen and 0.73 mg of organic matter (as COD) for each mg of nitrogen.

In theory, Case III has advantages over both. First, most of its nitrite comes from partial nitritation, so we expect it to save oxygen and organic carbon compared with Case II. Second, it cleans up nitrate through partial denitrification with anammox, which uses less organic carbon than Case I. In addition, this partial denitrification with anammox can remove some ammonium without using any oxygen, so Case III also needs less oxygen than Case I. Overall, Case III can remove 100% of the nitrogen while needing the least oxygen (1.76 mg of oxygen per mg of nitrogen) and the least organic matter (0.14 mg COD per mg of nitrogen) of the three cases.

Table 2

Theoretical oxygen and organic matter needed by three anammox-based processes to remove all the nitrogen. Reactions are written as chemical equations; the numbered steps (i), (ii) and (iii) are combined as shown to give the total reaction.

| Case | Reactions | Oxygen needed (mg O2 per mg N) | Organic matter needed (mg COD per mg N) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Case I: PN/A + denitrification | Partial nitrification: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i); Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii); Denitrification: NO3− + 0.625CH3COO− + 0.625H+ → 0.5 N2 + HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.75H2O (iii); Total reaction by (i × 1.32 + ii)/2.32 + iii × 0.11: NH3 + 0.85O2 + 0.07CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.11HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.51H2O + 0.07H+ | 1.94 | 0.32 |
| Case II: Complete nitrification + partial denitrification with anammox | Complete nitrification: NH3 + 2O2 → NO3− + H2O + H+ (i); Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (ii); Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (iii); Total reaction by ((ii × 1.32 + iii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 1.03O2 + 0.16CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.16HCO3− + 0.16CO2 + 1.65H2O + 0.03H+ | 2.35 | 0.73 |
| Case III: PN/A + partial denitrification with anammox | Partial nitrification: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i); Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii); Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (iii); Total reaction by ((iii × 0.26 + ii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 0.77O2 + 0.03CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.03HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.52H2O + 0.03H+ | 1.76 | 0.14 |

Despite these advantages in theory and in practice, several questions need answers before our nitrate control strategy can be put to use. First, how the nitrogen is removed should be studied further. When we worked out how nitrogen changed from one form to another in the reactor, we left out some minor nitrogen pathways, and this might affect how accurate our calculations are. Future studies should untangle the complex networks through which microbes pass nitrogen around. Advanced tools can help: isotope labeling, which tags atoms so they can be followed, and metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, which read all the genes in a microbial community and which of those genes are switched on (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020).

Second, it should be checked further whether the strategy works with real city wastewater. Other studies have already reported partial denitrification, and partial denitrification with anammox, running on the mixed organic matter found in real city wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to see the long-term effects of adding organic matter, especially as temperatures change with the seasons. Third, future studies should find the best range for the amount of easy-to-digest organic matter, and for its ratio to total nitrogen, so that as little organic matter as possible is used in real treatment plants.

parts.title: Keeping nitrogen removal steady and highly effective in a city-wastewater anammox reactor by adding small amounts of easily digested organic matter
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We ran an anammox reactor to treat wastewater with low levels of nitrogen, like the water in ordinary city sewage. Anammox bacteria are tiny organisms that turn ammonium and nitrite into harmless nitrogen gas. The water we fed the reactor held 25–35 mg/L of ammonium plus nitrite. We ran the reactor in two phases. In phase I, the water had no readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), which is organic matter that bacteria can digest easily. In phase II, it did.

In phase I, the reactor removed nitrogen efficiently at first. After long-term operation (75 days), however, nitrate built up in the treated water leaving the reactor (the effluent), and the nitrogen removal efficiency fell to 30%. Analysis of the microbes showed that anammox bacteria dropped from 2.15 to 1.78% of the community. Over the same time, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, rose from 0.14 to 0.56%.

In phase II, we added rbCOD in the form of acetate, with a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 0.9. Within 2 days, the nitrate concentration in the effluent went down. The reactor then achieved advanced nitrogen removal, with an average effluent total nitrogen of 3.4 mg/L. Even with the added organic matter, the anammox pathway still did most of the nitrogen removal. High-throughput sequencing, a method that reads the DNA of the microbes in a sample, showed a high anammox abundance of 2.48%, which further supports anammox as the main nitrogen remover.

We attribute the improvement to three things. First, the activity of NOB was suppressed more strongly. Second, the leftover nitrate was cleaned up by partial denitrification working together with anammox. Third, the sludge formed more granules, which are small round clumps of microbes. Overall, adding low concentrations of rbCOD is a feasible strategy for achieving robust and efficient nitrogen removal in anammox reactors treating city wastewater.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, mainstream, nitrogen removal, readily biodegradable organics
parts.introduction_first: Cleaning nitrogen out of city wastewater without using much energy or added carbon has drawn a lot of attention over the past decade. One way to do it is called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A). In this process, bacteria first turn some of the ammonium in the water into nitrite (partial nitritation), and then anammox bacteria convert ammonium and nitrite into nitrogen gas. This approach can make a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) energy-neutral (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017). Engineers have built PN/A systems in different forms, depending on the number of stages, meaning that the process is run in either one tank or two. In a two-stage system, partial nitritation and anammox take place in two separate reactors, so each step can be tuned for the different microorganisms that carry it out (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). For this reason, a two-stage PN/A process typically removes nitrogen at a higher rate than a single-stage one (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We set up an anammox treatment for ordinary city wastewater in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a tank that treats water in repeated fill-and-empty cycles. When we ran it with no rbCOD, unwanted NOB activity let high levels of nitrate build up in the effluent, and the nitrogen removal efficiency dropped. When we ran it with a low concentration of rbCOD, the reactor recovered from the nitrate buildup and removed nitrogen very efficiently.

With a low concentration of rbCOD, anammox stayed the main way nitrogen was removed. Partial denitrification combined with anammox (PD/A) removed the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself produced. The NOB were also effectively suppressed, because the conditions in the reactor were stricter anoxic, meaning even less oxygen was present. In addition, the sludge formed more granules, which helped build up the slow-growing anammox bacteria.

Overall, adding low concentrations of rbCOD is a feasible strategy for achieving robust and efficient nitrogen removal in anammox reactors treating city wastewater.
parts.introduction_rest:
Even so, using the popular PN/A systems at full scale is still hard. One of the biggest worries is the high concentration of nitrate in the treated water leaving the reactor. Nitrate is a form of nitrogen, and it can push the total nitrogen (TN) in the effluent above the legal discharge limit (Zhuang et al., 2022).

In a two-stage PN/A process, nitrate can form in both reactors. In the first reactor, where partial nitritation happens, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) turn nitrite into nitrate. In the second reactor, the anammox reactor, nitrate comes from the anammox reaction itself and also from unwanted NOB activity. Recent work shows that nitrate in the first reactor can be kept very low, because engineers have developed several ways to hold NOB back. These include switching the air on and off at intervals (intermittent aeration), keeping the sludge in the reactor for only a very short time (an ultra-low sludge retention time, or SRT), and treating a side stream of sludge with chemicals that inhibit NOB (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021).

The second reactor has therefore become the main source of nitrate. Too much nitrate caused by unwanted NOB activity has been reported in anammox reactors of many designs, including sequencing batch reactors (SBR), completely stirred tank reactors, and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most of the ways of holding back NOB that work in the first reactor cannot be used in the second one, because they could also harm the anammox bacteria. So we need to look for other ways to reduce nitrate buildup in anammox reactors.

Early studies treated readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), the easily digested organic matter, as a problem for anammox treatment of city wastewater. Its presence lets ordinary bacteria called heterotrophs overgrow and outcompete the anammox bacteria, so researchers thought it should be removed beforehand (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies, however, report that anammox bacteria can stay active. When anammox reactors received a suitable amount of rbCOD, with a carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio of 0.5–1.5, nitrogen removal efficiency even rose above 90% (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

But most of those studies treated wastewater with a lot of nitrogen, 100–300 mg N/L. At such levels, free ammonia or free nitrous acid (two forms of nitrogen that are toxic to many bacteria) can stop NOB from growing (Ge et al., 2015). Because of this, extra nitrate was hardly a problem in those studies. So we still do not know whether adding rbCOD can solve the nitrate problem caused by NOB in anammox reactors treating city wastewater, where nitrogen levels are low.

There is a second idea. In partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A), bacteria use organic matter to turn nitrate into nitrite, and anammox bacteria then use that nitrite. This can lower the amount of organic matter needed for nitrogen removal and reduce the harm that organic matter does to anammox bacteria (Du et al., 2019). Yet in most PD/A studies, the water entering the reactor has ammonium and nitrate as its main nitrogen compounds (Du et al., 2019). City-wastewater anammox reactors are different. There the main oxidized nitrogen going in is nitrite, and nitrate builds up slowly as the anammox reaction makes it. How PD/A behaves in this kind of reactor when rbCOD is present has rarely been reported, and it needs more study (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we built and ran an anammox reactor for city wastewater in two phases, one without rbCOD and one with it. We compared the two phases in four ways: how well the reactor removed nitrogen, how stable the process was, which microbes lived in it, and what the sludge looked like. With these data, we assessed how low concentrations of rbCOD affect anammox treatment of city wastewater, and whether they could improve nitrogen removal.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we set up the reactor

We treated the wastewater in a 10 L sequencing batch reactor (Figure 1). We seeded it with sludge, the mix of microbes and water that does the cleaning, taken from a small laboratory anammox reactor that treated wastewater very rich in nitrogen. Right after we added this sludge, the reactor held 4.9 g of biomass per liter. The reactor ran three cycles a day. Each cycle had five steps: 10 min of feeding, during which half of the water in the tank was replaced (a volume exchange ratio of 50%), then 360 min of gentle mixing without oxygen (anoxic mixing), 30 min of settling, 10 min of discharging the treated water, and 70 min of idling (Figure 1B). The reactor sat at room temperature, 24–26°C.

We did not remove any sludge on purpose during the run. The only sludge that left was what washed out with the effluent and what we took out for samples. We estimated that the sludge retention time (SRT), meaning how long the sludge stays in the reactor, was longer than 30 days.

Figure 1

The layout (A) and the cycle steps (B) of our anammox reactor for ordinary city wastewater.

We ran the reactor in two phases, which differed in what we fed it (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the reactor with 5 L of effluent from a partial nitritation (PN) reactor. That reactor treated synthetic city wastewater, and we describe it in the Supplementary material. This feed held little chemical oxygen demand (COD), which is a measure of the organic matter in water. It averaged 25.1 mg/L, with a typical spread of 8.8 mg/L around that average. Because the water had already been treated once, we expect most of this organic matter to be the kind that bacteria can hardly digest.

In phase II (days 76–135), we sent a small part of the raw synthetic city wastewater (0.5 L) around the PN reactor. We mixed it with 4.5 L of PN effluent in a middle tank and fed this mix to the anammox reactor. In this way, easily digested organic matter (rbCOD) entered the system as acetate, at 24.2 mg COD/L. Apart from this difference in the organic matter we fed, the way we ran the reactor and its conditions were the same in both phases.

Table 1

Main features of the water fed to the anammox reactor (averages, with the typical spread after the ± sign). All nitrogen values are in mg/L; TN is total nitrogen.

| | Ammonium (NH4+-N) | Nitrite (NO2−-N) | Nitrate (NO3−-N) | TN | COD |
| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8 |
| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2 |

2.2.

Batch tests of partial denitrification working with anammox in the reactor

We ran two batch tests outside the reactor (ex situ) to see whether partial denitrification working together with anammox (PD/A) could happen in the reactor sludge. We took sludge from the reactor and washed it three times with deionized water. Then we divided it among four separate 0.5-L conical flasks. After adding food for the microbes (organic matter and nitrogen compounds), we kept the flasks in shaking incubators at 200 rpm and 25°C. Throughout the tests we bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks, which kept oxygen out.

Batch Test I asked whether nitrite can pile up when bacteria carry out denitrification, the process that turns nitrate into nitrogen gas. For this test, we added only nitrate (as NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. Every flask started with 15 mg/L of nitrate, and each got a different amount of acetate. The starting ratios of COD to nitrate nitrogen in the four flasks were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.

Batch Test II asked whether denitrification could work together with the anammox process. Besides nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate, the feed also held ammonium (as NH4Cl). We started with 10 mg/L of ammonium and 15 mg/L of nitrate. Again we gave the four flasks different amounts of acetate, so the COD to nitrate nitrogen ratios were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.

2.3.

How we measured things

We measured COD, ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, and total nitrogen with standard methods (APHA, 2005). We used the same standard methods for three sludge measurements: mixed liquor suspended solids (how much sludge is floating in the water), mixed liquor volatile suspended solids (how much of that is organic, living-type material), and the sludge volume index (how well the sludge settles). Inside the reactor, we tracked temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen (DO) continuously with a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the sizes of the sludge particles with a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4.

Calculating where the nitrogen went in typical cycles

We worked out which pathways moved nitrogen in the reactor by looking at how the nitrogen compounds changed in typical cycles. We counted only the major pathways. We used different calculations in the two phases.

In phase I, almost no easily digested organic matter came in, so we left denitrification out of the calculation. We calculated the nitrogen changes caused by anammox bacteria, by ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB, which turn ammonium into nitrite), and by NOB with Equations 1–3.

(1)TNanammox=ΔN=(NH4+−Ninitial+NO2−−Ninitial+NO3−−Ninitial)−(NH4+−Nfinal+NO2−−Nfinal+NO3−−Nfinal)

(2)NH4+−NAOB=NH4+−Ninitial−NH4+−Nfinal−TNanammox/2.04

(3)NO3−−NNOB=NO3−−Nfinal−NO3−−Ninitial−TNanammox×0.26/2.04

In these equations, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in mg N/L. NH4+−NAOB is the ammonium used by AOB, and NO3−−NNOB is the nitrate made by NOB, both in mg N/L. ΔN is the difference between the total inorganic nitrogen in the water at the start of the cycle and at its end, in mg N/L. NH4+−Ninitial, NO2−−Ninitial, and NO3−−Ninitial are the ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate concentrations in the water at the start of the cycle, in mg N/L. NH4+−Nfinal, NO2−−Nfinal, and NO3−−Nfinal are the same three concentrations at the end of the cycle, in mg N/L.

In phase II, the reactor ran under stricter anoxic conditions than in phase I, meaning even less oxygen was present, and nitrate was removed overall (Section 3.2). So this time we left the nitrification pathways out of the calculation. We calculated nitrogen changes through three routes with Equations 4–6: anammox, denitratation (nitrate turned into nitrite, NO3− → NO2−), and denitritation (nitrite turned into nitrogen gas, NO2− → N2).

(4)TNanammox=NH4+−Ninitial−NH4+−Nfinal×2.04

(5)NO3−−Ndenitratation=NO3−−Ninitial+TNanammox×0.26/2.04−NO3−−Nfinal

(6)TNdenitritation=ΔN−TNanammox

Here TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed through the anammox pathway, in mg N/L. NO3−−Ndenitratation is the nitrate reduced by denitratation, and TNdenitritation is the total nitrogen removed by denitritation, both in mg N/L.

2.5.

Reading the microbes' DNA (high-throughput sequencing)

We took sludge samples from the reactor on day 1, day 75, and day 134. We freeze-dried them (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States) and stored them at −20°C. We pulled the DNA out of the samples with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the maker's instructions. To make sure the extract was pure, we measured its DNA concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands).

Next we copied the V3–V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene, a stretch of DNA that differs from one kind of bacterium to another, so it works a little like a name tag. For this we used the bacterial primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). Primers are short pieces of DNA that mark the start and end of the stretch to copy. We read the copied DNA (PCR products) on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). From these data, we worked out which microbes were present and how common each was, as described in our previous report (Yang et al., 2017). We have deposited the raw reads in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database (Accession Number: PRJNA942604).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

How well the reactor removed nitrogen without and with easily digested organic matter

In phase I, we fed the reactor almost no easily digested organic matter (rbCOD). The reactor removed very little chemical oxygen demand (COD, a measure of how much organic matter is in the water): only 3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L (Figure 2A). Nitrogen removal was not steady (Figures 2B,C). It was good at the start, during days 1–40. But on days 41–75, the nitrate in the treated water leaving the reactor (the effluent) rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L. By the end of phase I, ammonium and nitrite were piling up as well, which tells us that the anammox bacteria were becoming less active. As a result, the nitrogen removal efficiency fell from 83% to 30%.

Figure 2

How well the reactor removed COD (A) and total nitrogen, TN (B), and the amounts of each nitrogen compound in the water going in and out (C).

In phase II, we added acetate, which supplied 24.2 mg/L of COD. This raised the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen (TN) to 0.9. The reactor removed 27.7 mg/L of COD on average, so it used up all of the easily digested organic matter we fed it (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, the effluent nitrate dropped from 8.7 mg/L to 2.1 mg/L, and it then stayed low at 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L for the rest of the run (Figure 2C). In other words, nitrate was being removed. This suggested that denitrification, in which bacteria use organic matter to turn nitrate into nitrogen compounds with less oxygen, was happening in the reactor.

Effluent ammonium and nitrite also fell at the same time, which shows that the anammox bacteria had recovered their activity. In phase II, the reactor reached advanced nitrogen removal: the effluent held an average of 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen, and the average nitrogen removal efficiency was 87.2% (Figure 2B).

3.2.

How the path of nitrogen changed after we added easily digested organic matter

To see how nitrogen moved through the reactor, we followed the water through single treatment cycles. In a typical phase I cycle, before we added rbCOD, ammonium and nitrite were slowly used up, while nitrate built up a great deal (Figure 3A). For every unit of ammonium nitrogen removed, 0.92 units of nitrate nitrogen were produced (ΔNO3−-N/ΔNH4+-N = 0.92). That is much higher than the value of 0.26 expected from the anammox reaction alone (Strous et al., 1998), so something else must have been making nitrate.

Our nitrogen mass flow, a tally of where the nitrogen went, showed that nitrification was at work inside the anammox reactor. Some ammonium was oxidized to nitrite, and part of that nitrite was oxidized further to nitrate (Figure 3B). Nitrification produced 79% of the nitrate. This is why the reactor could not remove enough nitrogen in phase I.

Figure 3

Changes in the amounts of each nitrogen compound (A: phase I, C: phase II) and the paths nitrogen took (B: phase I, D: phase II) in typical cycles of the reactor.

After we added rbCOD in phase II, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all dropped together during a typical cycle (Figure 3C). So denitrification removed both the nitrate that came in with the water and the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself made.

The nitrogen mass flow also showed partial denitrification (PD), in which nitrate is turned into nitrite (NO3− → NO2−). This gave the anammox bacteria extra nitrite to work with (Figure 3D), so anammox activity inside the reactor went up. Even so, anammox stayed the main way nitrogen was removed, accounting for 93% of the nitrogen removal (Figure 3D). Denitrification then pushed the removal a little higher, leaving a low effluent TN concentration.

3.3.

Batch tests show that partial denitrification and anammox can work together in the reactor

We tested this idea further with batch tests, which we ran outside the reactor using sludge taken from it. In Batch Test I, we fed the sludge only nitrate and acetate, so that we could study denitrification alone. At every ratio of COD to nitrate nitrogen (COD/NO3−-N) we tried, nitrite built up (Figures 4A–D). The most nitrate was turned into nitrite, 50.0%, when the COD/NO3−-N ratio was 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the reactor can supply extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria.

Figure 4

Changes in the amounts of each nitrogen compound in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we added ammonium to the nitrate and acetate. During the first hour, a lot of nitrate was removed and nitrite built up at every COD/NO3−-N ratio, which means partial denitrification was happening (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all went down together.

The conditions in the test were strictly anoxic, with no oxygen, so the ammonium could only have been removed by the anammox pathway. The nitrite that anammox needed came from partial denitrification. This proves that partial denitrification working together with anammox (PD/A) can happen in the reactor.

3.4.

How the microbes in the reactor changed

To see how low levels of rbCOD affected the microbes, we read their DNA with high-throughput sequencing (Figure 5). In phase I, without rbCOD, anammox bacteria, mainly Candidatus Kuenenia, fell from 2.08% to 1.73% of the community. Meanwhile, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB, called Nitrosomonas here) rose significantly, from 0.29% to 0.40%, and NOB (Nitrospira) rose significantly from 0.14% to 0.56%. Here "significantly" means that a rise this big would rarely show up by chance alone if nothing had really changed. These trends match the nitrate buildup and the weaker nitrogen removal we saw as the reactor ran.

After we added rbCOD in phase II, anammox bacteria recovered to 2.48%. AOB dropped to 0.05% and NOB dropped to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding the right amount of rbCOD helps anammox bacteria build up and holds back the bacteria that cause nitrification.

The group of denitrifying bacteria changed too. In phase I, the main denitrifier was Denitratisoma, which can denitrify all the way to nitrogen gas (NO3− → N2). Its share fell from 3.91% to 2.00% in phase II. Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter, on the other hand, have been identified as the working microbes of partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020). They grew a lot in phase II: Thauera rose from 0.18% to 2.15%, and Candidatus Competibacter rose from 0.15% to 1.35%. This gives us more evidence that PD/A took place in the reactor.

Figure 5

Changes in the mix of microbes in the reactor.

3.5.

How granules formed in the reactor

The sludge we started with already held some granules, which we counted as clumps wider than 200 μm; they made up 17.4% of the sludge. The average clump size was 130.8 μm (Figure 6). The size stayed steady in phase I, then rose significantly to 195.6 μm in phase II. By the end, granules made up 52.5% of all the biomass in the reactor. This shows that adding rbCOD in phase II helped granules form.

Granules help build up anammox bacteria, because these bacteria tend to grow best in large clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

4.1.

How adding easily digested organic matter improved nitrogen removal

In our experiment, adding easily digested organic matter (rbCOD) quickly brought the anammox reactor for ordinary city wastewater back from a state of heavy nitrate buildup (Figure 2). With only low concentrations of rbCOD, the reactor reached advanced nitrogen removal. We think several things worked together to make this happen.

First, nitrification was held back more strongly, so less nitrate was made inside the reactor. Nitrification is the process in which bacteria use oxygen to turn ammonium into nitrite and then into nitrate. In phase I, we added no rbCOD. Nitrification was fairly active, so nitrate production rose and nitrogen removal got worse (Figures 2, 3). Other researchers have seen the same thing (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020).

The oxygen that fed nitrification was dissolved oxygen (DO) at 0.06–0.08 mg/L. It came in with the incoming water and from the air at the top of the reactor during mechanical mixing (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying bacteria hold on to oxygen very well even when there is very little of it. These include complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox), which do the whole job from ammonium to nitrate on their own, and NOB from the genus Nitrospira (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have helped drive nitrification in our reactor, because the amount of Nitrospira rose significantly (Figure 5). ("Significantly" here means a statistical test showed that a rise this large would rarely happen by chance alone.)

In phase II, after we added rbCOD, the dissolved oxygen fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L. This was possibly because aerobic heterotrophic bacteria, which use oxygen to digest organic matter, were using it up (Figure 3C). So the conditions in phase II were stricter anoxic than in phase I, meaning even less oxygen was around, and that held nitrification back. As a result, both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and NOB became less abundant during phase II (Figure 5).

Second, partial denitrification working together with anammox (PD/A) took place in the reactor. It removed the nitrate that came in with the wastewater and also the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself produces. Our batch tests, which are small separate experiments, showed that nitrite can pile up when bacteria denitrify nitrate (Figures 4A–D). They also showed that anammox bacteria can then use this nitrite, with ammonium as their electron donor (Figures 4E–H). The analysis of one full reactor cycle agreed (Figure 3D). In this way the nitrate in the reactor was cleaned up using only a small amount of organic matter, and that lifted the nitrogen removal efficiency to a high level.

There is more. We added rbCOD with the incoming water at the start of each cycle. Even so, nitrate was made (by anammox) and used up (by denitrification) all the way through the cycle (Figure 3). So we expected endogenous denitrification, which means bacteria using carbon they have stored inside their own cells. In phase II, the bacteria doing partial denitrification were Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter (Figure 5). Both can store rbCOD as internal carbon reserves such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). So the rbCOD in the incoming water may have been turned into these reserves at the start of the cycle, and the reserves may then have fed partial denitrification for the rest of the cycle.

Third, anammox bacteria became more active and grew better, which makes the process work better and stay steadier. In our reactor, the direct effect of rbCOD (acetate) on anammox activity may have been small. Low concentrations of acetate do not inhibit anammox bacteria (Huang et al., 2014). A few anammox species, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can even use short-chain fatty acids like acetate as an energy source (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). But this route is probably not important here, because the anammox bacteria in our reactor were mostly from the genus Candidatus Kuenenia throughout the experiment.

So rbCOD mostly helped anammox bacteria in indirect ways. First, when bacteria use oxygen to digest rbCOD, they use up dissolved oxygen in the water, and oxygen is known to slow anammox bacteria down (Strous et al., 1999). Second, when bacteria use rbCOD without oxygen to turn nitrate into nitrite, they give the anammox bacteria extra nitrite to work with, which raised anammox activity (Figure 3). Third, rbCOD encouraged the microbes to make more extracellular polymers, the sticky material that holds cells together, and to form granules in the reactor (Figure 6). Other studies have found this too (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). Granules help the reactor keep and build up the slow-growing anammox bacteria (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). As a result, anammox bacteria rose from 1.73 to 2.48% of the microbes after we added low concentrations of rbCOD (Figure 5). At the same time, anammox stayed the main way nitrogen was removed (Figure 3).

4.2.

Using this approach and what we still need to study

We used an effective and practical strategy to fix the nitrate buildup that unwanted NOB activity causes in anammox reactors for ordinary city wastewater. Other ways to cut nitrate production have been reported. One is to flush the oxygen out of the incoming water with nitrogen gas. Another is to build a tall, narrow reactor so less of its surface touches the air. A third is to put protective covers on the reactor (Díaz et al., 2020). But these measures may not be affordable or workable in some cases, especially when upgrading an existing wastewater treatment plant, because they mean major changes to the reactor's design.

The strategy we tested needs only a small change. A plant can send part of its raw city wastewater to the anammox reactor, or add a small amount of organic carbon from outside (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). If the plant has sludge fermentation liquid, that can supply the rbCOD (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). We also note that our operating strategy can be used in continuous flow reactors, where water moves through without stopping. Those reactors may need extra steps to keep the anammox bacteria inside, such as filling the reactor with suitable carriers for the microbes to grow on, or using a cyclone to hold back the granular sludge selectively (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).

Even when NOB are not making too much nitrate, running an anammox reactor with a low concentration of rbCOD is useful, because it could lead to complete nitrogen removal (Zhuang et al., 2022). Both partial nitritation followed by anammox (PN/A) and PD/A have been reported to contribute to nitrogen removal (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our reactor, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen without needing organic matter, and PD/A removed the nitrate that the anammox reaction produced.

Table 2 gives a theoretical equation for this process as Case III. We compare it with two other anammox-based processes aimed at complete nitrogen removal (Cases I and II). In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without organic matter, but in the end 11% of the ammonium turns into nitrate. Cleaning up that nitrate by denitrification still uses organic carbon. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 mg COD/mg N. In Case II, the nitrite that anammox bacteria need is made by complete nitrification of ammonium followed by partial denitrification of the nitrate. This takes more oxygen and more organic carbon than making nitrite by partial nitritation. In total, Case II uses 2.35 mg O2/mg N and 0.73 mg COD/mg N.

In theory, Case III has advantages over both. First, nitrite is made mainly by partial nitritation, so we expect it to save oxygen and organic carbon compared with Case II. Second, nitrate is cleaned up by PD/A, which uses less organic carbon than Case I. PD/A in Case III can also remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it needs less oxygen than Case I too. Overall, Case III can remove 100% of the nitrogen with the least oxygen (1.76 mg O2/mg N) and the least organic matter (0.14 mg COD/mg N) of the three cases.
