Despite these advantages in theory and in practice, several questions need answers before our nitrate control strategy can be put to use.

First, we need to study how the nitrogen is removed in more depth. When we worked out how nitrogen changed form in the reactor, we left out some minor nitrogen pathways, and that might have affected how accurate our calculation is. Future studies should untangle the complex web in which microbes pass nitrogen around. They can use advanced tools such as isotope labeling (tracking nitrogen atoms with a special tag), metagenomics (reading the DNA of all the microbes in a sample) and metatranscriptomics (reading which genes are switched on) (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020).

Second, we need to check the strategy with real city wastewater. Partial denitrification, and PD/A, using the mixed organic carbon found in real city wastewater have already been reported (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). We also need longer experiments to learn the long-term effects of adding organic matter, especially as temperatures change with the seasons.

Third, future studies should find the best range of rbCOD concentration and the best ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen (rbCOD/TN), so that real plants can use as little organic matter as possible.

parts.title: Adding small amounts of easy-to-break-down organic matter makes anammox nitrogen removal reliable and highly efficient in the main wastewater flow
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We tested a wastewater treatment tank that uses anammox: a process in which bacteria turn ammonium and nitrite, two forms of nitrogen in water, into nitrogen gas. The wastewater had a low combined concentration of ammonium and nitrite (NH4+ + NO2−, 25–35 mg/L). In phase I, we ran the tank without organic matter that bacteria can easily break down. In phase II, we supplied this material, measured as readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD). This measure describes how much oxygen would be needed to break the material down.

In phase I, nitrogen removal worked well at first. But after long-term operation (75 days), nitrate, another form of nitrogen, built up in the treated water. As a result, nitrogen removal efficiency fell to 30%. Our analysis of the microbes showed that the share of anammox bacteria fell from 2.15 to 1.78%, while the share of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB)—bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate—increased from 0.14 to 0.56%.

In phase II, we added easy-to-break-down organic matter in the form of acetate, with a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 0.9. The nitrate concentration in the treated water dropped within 2 days. During the operation that followed, we achieved very thorough nitrogen removal: the treated water contained an average total nitrogen concentration of 3.4 mg/L. Even with the added organic matter, anammox still accounted for most of the nitrogen removed. DNA sequencing, which we used to identify the bacteria present, showed a high share of anammox bacteria (2.48%), further supporting their leading role.

We linked the improvement to three changes. The activity of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate was held back more strongly. Remaining nitrate was removed through partial denitrification, which turns nitrate into nitrite, followed by anammox. The sludge—the mixture of microbes and other solids in the tank—also formed more granules, or compact clusters. Overall, adding low concentrations of easy-to-break-down organic matter is a workable way to achieve reliable, efficient nitrogen removal in anammox tanks treating the main wastewater flow.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, main wastewater flow, nitrogen removal, easy-to-break-down organic matter
parts.introduction_first: Over the past decade, researchers have paid considerable attention to a way of removing nitrogen from municipal wastewater—the wastewater collected from homes and other buildings—that could help treatment plants produce as much energy as they use (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017). This approach combines partial nitritation, in which bacteria turn some ammonium into nitrite, with anammox, in which other bacteria use ammonium and nitrite to make nitrogen gas. Together, these processes are called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A). They remove nitrogen without relying on organic matter as their energy source. Treatment plants can carry out PN/A in either one stage or two. In a two-stage system, partial nitritation and anammox take place in separate treatment tanks. This lets operators adjust conditions for each process and help the different microbes build up in the tank where they work best (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, two-stage PN/A typically removes nitrogen at a higher rate than the single-stage process (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We set up anammox treatment for the main wastewater flow in a sequencing batch reactor: a tank that treats wastewater in repeated cycles of filling, mixing, settling and draining. When we ran it without easy-to-break-down organic matter, unwanted activity by bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate caused high levels of nitrate to build up in the treated water. This reduced nitrogen removal efficiency. Adding a low concentration of easy-to-break-down organic matter reversed the nitrate buildup and restored highly efficient nitrogen removal.

With this small addition, anammox remained the main process removing nitrogen. Meanwhile, partial denitrification followed by anammox removed the nitrate produced by the anammox reaction itself. The tank also had even less dissolved oxygen, which effectively held back the bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate. In addition, the organic matter helped the sludge form compact clusters, allowing slow-growing anammox bacteria to build up. Overall, adding low concentrations of easy-to-break-down organic matter is a workable way to achieve reliable, efficient nitrogen removal in anammox tanks treating the main wastewater flow.
parts.introduction_rest:
Using partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) to treat the main wastewater flow at full scale remains difficult. One major concern is that too much nitrate remains in the treated water, pushing total nitrogen—the amount of all forms of nitrogen combined—above the discharge limit (Zhuang et al., 2022). In a two-stage system, bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate can produce nitrate in the first tank, where partial nitritation takes place. In the second tank, nitrate comes from both the anammox reaction itself and unwanted activity by these same nitrate-producing bacteria. Recent research shows that several methods can keep nitrate production very low in the first tank. These include switching the air supply on and off, keeping sludge in the tank for a very short time, and treating sludge in a separate flow with substances that hold back the unwanted bacteria (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021).

The second-stage anammox tank has therefore become a major source of nitrate. Researchers have reported too much nitrate production from unwanted activity by bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate in several tank designs. These include sequencing batch reactors, which treat wastewater in repeated cycles; completely stirred tanks, where the contents are mixed throughout; and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors, where water flows upward through a bed of sludge granules, or compact clusters (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most methods developed to hold back these bacteria in the first tank cannot be used in the second because they may also slow anammox activity. We therefore need to investigate ways to reduce nitrate buildup in anammox tanks.

Early studies treated easy-to-break-down organic matter, measured as readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), as a problem for anammox treatment of the main wastewater flow. The view was that pretreatment should remove this material because it can allow bacteria that feed on organic matter to grow too much and outcompete anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies, however, have found that anammox bacteria can remain active with a suitable amount of this organic matter. In particular, tanks operated at carbon/nitrogen ratios of 0.5–1.5 achieved nitrogen removal efficiencies above 90% (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023). Most of these studies, though, treated wastewater with high nitrogen concentrations of 100–300 mg N/L. At these concentrations, free ammonia or free nitrous acid—particular chemical forms of ammonia and nitrite—can hold back the growth of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate (Ge et al., 2015). As a result, these bacteria produce almost no excess nitrate. It is still unknown whether adding easy-to-break-down organic matter can solve the problem of excess nitrate production by these bacteria in anammox tanks treating the main wastewater flow.

Another approach combines partial denitrification, which turns nitrate into nitrite, with anammox. This combination, called partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A), can reduce the organic matter needed to remove nitrogen and minimize its harmful effects on anammox activity (Du et al., 2019). In most studies of this approach, however, ammonium and nitrate are the main nitrogen compounds in the incoming water (Du et al., 2019). The situation is different in anammox tanks treating the main wastewater flow. There, nitrite is the main form of incoming NOx−, a term that groups nitrite and nitrate together, and the anammox reaction gradually produces nitrate. Few studies have reported on the role of partial denitrification/anammox in these tanks when easy-to-break-down organic matter is present, so this needs further investigation (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up an anammox tank to treat the main wastewater flow and ran it in two phases, with and without easy-to-break-down organic matter. We compared how well it removed nitrogen, how steadily the process worked, which microbes were present, and the shape and structure of the sludge in the two phases. Using these comparisons, we assessed how low concentrations of easy-to-break-down organic matter affected anammox treatment of the main wastewater flow and evaluated their potential to improve nitrogen removal.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

Experimental setup

We carried out anammox treatment for the main wastewater flow in a 10 L sequencing batch reactor (SBR): a tank that treats wastewater in repeated cycles (Figure 1). We started it with sludge—the mixture of microbes and other solids—from a laboratory anammox tank treating wastewater with high nitrogen levels. After we added this sludge, the tank contained 4.9 g/L of biomass, or microbial material. We ran three cycles each day. Each cycle began with 10 min of filling, replacing 50% of the water. We then mixed the contents for 360 min under anoxic conditions, meaning without dissolved oxygen, and allowed the sludge to settle for 30 min. Finally, we drained treated water for 10 min and left the tank idle for 70 min (Figure 1B). The tank ran at room temperature, 24–26°C. We did not deliberately remove sludge during operation, apart from sampling; some biomass also escaped with the treated water. We estimated that the solids retention time (SRT)—the average time solids stayed in the tank—was longer than 30 days.

Figure 1

Layout (A) and operating cycle (B) of the anammox treatment tank for the main wastewater flow.

We divided operation into two phases based on the incoming water (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the anammox tank with 5 L of treated water from a partial nitritation (PN) tank. In that tank, bacteria turned some ammonium into nitrite while treating synthetic municipal wastewater: a prepared mixture representing wastewater from homes and other buildings. The Supplementary material describes the PN tank. The water entering the anammox tank had a low chemical oxygen demand (COD), 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. COD measures the amount of oxygen needed to chemically break down material in water. Most of this remaining organic matter was likely hard to break down because the water had already undergone biological treatment.

In phase II (days 76–135), we sent 0.5 L of the untreated synthetic municipal wastewater around the PN tank and mixed it with 4.5 L of PN-treated water in the middle tank. We then fed this mixture into the anammox tank. This introduced easy-to-break-down organic matter, measured as readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), in the form of acetate at 24.2 mg COD/L. Apart from the differences in the organic matter entering the tank, the operating cycles and conditions were identical in phases I and II.

Table 1

| | NH4+-N (mg/L) | NO2−-N (mg/L) | NO3−-N (mg/L) | TN (mg/L) | COD (mg/L) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8 |
| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2 |

2.2.

Batch tests of the tank's potential for partial denitrification/anammox

We carried out two batch tests outside the tank to explore whether partial denitrification could work together with anammox (PD/A). Partial denitrification turns nitrate into nitrite, which anammox bacteria can then use. We washed sludge collected from the tank three times with deionized water, which has dissolved ions removed, and transferred it to four separate 0.5-L conical flasks. After adding organic matter and nitrogen compounds for the bacteria to use, we placed the flasks in shaking incubators at 25°C and 200 revolutions per minute (rpm). Throughout the tests, we continuously passed nitrogen gas through the flasks to remove oxygen and keep the conditions anoxic.

Batch Test I checked whether nitrite could build up during denitrification, the process that reduces nitrate through nitrite toward nitrogen gas. We therefore added only nitrate, as sodium nitrate (NaNO3), and acetate to the flasks. Each flask started with a nitrate concentration of 15 mg/L, but received a different amount of acetate. The starting ratios of COD to nitrate nitrogen (COD/NO3−-N) in the four flasks were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0, respectively.

Batch Test II checked whether denitrification could work together with anammox. Along with nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate, the feed contained ammonium as ammonium chloride (NH4Cl). The starting ammonium concentration was 10 mg/L, and the starting nitrate concentration was 15 mg/L. We added different amounts of acetate to the four flasks, giving COD/NO3−-N ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0, respectively.

2.3.

Measurement methods

We used standard methods (APHA, 2005) to measure COD, nitrogen present as ammonium (NH4+-N), nitrite (NO2−-N) and nitrate (NO3−-N), and total nitrogen (TN). We also measured mixed liquor suspended solids, the solids suspended in the tank's water; mixed liquor volatile suspended solids, the portion lost when heated under the test conditions; and sludge volume index, a measure of how much space settled sludge takes up for a given mass. We monitored temperature, pH—a measure of acidity—and dissolved oxygen (DO) directly in the tank using a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the range of sludge particle sizes with a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4.

Calculating how nitrogen changed during typical cycles

We calculated how nitrogen moved through different reaction pathways from changes in nitrogen compound concentrations during typical cycles. These calculations included only the main pathways. We used different calculation methods for the two operating phases. In phase I, the tank received a negligible amount of easy-to-break-down organic matter, so we left denitrification pathways out of the calculations. We calculated nitrogen changes caused by anammox bacteria, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB)—bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite—and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, using Equations 1–3.

(1) TNanammox = ΔN = (NH4+−Ninitial + NO2−−Ninitial + NO3−−Ninitial) − (NH4+−Nfinal + NO2−−Nfinal + NO3−−Nfinal)

(2) NH4+−NAOB = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal − TNanammox/2.04

(3) NO3−−NNOB = NO3−−Nfinal − NO3−−Ninitial − TNanammox × 0.26/2.04

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria; NH4+−NAOB is the ammonium used by AOB; and NO3−−NNOB is the nitrate produced by NOB. All are measured in mg N/L, meaning milligrams of nitrogen per liter. ΔN is the difference between the total inorganic nitrogen concentrations in the tank water at the start and end of a cycle. Inorganic nitrogen here is the combined nitrogen in ammonium, nitrite and nitrate. NH4+−Ninitial, NO2−−Ninitial and NO3−−Ninitial are the concentrations of these three forms in the tank water at the start of the cycle. NH4+−Nfinal, NO2−−Nfinal and NO3−−Nfinal are their concentrations at the end. These concentrations and ΔN are also in mg N/L.

In phase II, the tank had even less dissolved oxygen than in phase I, and nitrate decreased overall (Section 3.2). We therefore left nitrification—the oxygen-using conversion of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate—out of the calculations. We calculated nitrogen changes through anammox, denitratation, which turns nitrate into nitrite (NO3− → NO2−), and denitritation, which turns nitrite into nitrogen gas (NO2− → N2), using Equations 4–6.

(4) TNanammox = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal × 2.04

(5) NO3−−Ndenitratation = NO3−−Ninitial + TNanammox × 0.26/2.04 − NO3−−Nfinal

(6) TNdenitritation = ΔN − TNanammox

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed through anammox; NO3−−Ndenitratation is the nitrate reduced through denitratation; and TNdenitritation is the total nitrogen removed through denitritation. All three are in mg N/L.

2.5.

DNA sequencing analysis

We collected sludge samples from the tank on days 1, 75 and 134, freeze-dried them with a BT2KXL instrument (Virtis, United States), and stored them at −20°C. We extracted genomic DNA—the microbes' genetic material—with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the manufacturer's instructions. We measured DNA concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands) to ensure the extract was pure.

We copied the V3–V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene, a section of bacterial DNA used to identify bacteria. For this step, we used bacterial primers—short DNA pieces that mark the region to copy—338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). We sequenced the resulting PCR products, the DNA copies made by the polymerase chain reaction, on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). We used these data to analyze which microbes were present, following the method in our earlier report (Yang et al., 2017). The raw DNA sequence reads are available in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database under Accession Number PRJNA942604.
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

Nitrogen removal without and with easy-to-break-down organic matter

In phase I, we ran the anammox treatment tank for the main wastewater flow with almost no easy-to-break-down organic matter, measured as readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD). Chemical oxygen demand (COD) measures the oxygen needed to break down organic material. The small, insignificant amount of COD removed—3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L—showed how little of this material entered the tank (Figure 2A). Nitrogen removal was unstable (Figures 2B,C). It worked well at first, on days 1–40, but the nitrate concentration in the treated water rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L over days 41–75. Ammonium and nitrite also built up at the end of phase I, indicating that anammox activity in the tank had declined. As a result, the percentage of incoming nitrogen removed fell from 83 to 30%.

Figure 2

Removal of COD (A) and total nitrogen (TN) (B), and concentrations of different nitrogen compounds in the incoming and treated water (C), in the anammox tank treating the main wastewater flow.

In phase II, we added acetate, an easy-to-break-down organic material, at 24.2 mg COD/L. This raised the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen to 0.9. The tank removed an average of 27.7 mg/L of COD, indicating that all the rbCOD in the incoming water was used (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, the nitrate concentration in the treated water fell from 8.7 to 2.1 mg/L. It then stayed low, at 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L, during the operation that followed (Figure 2C). Overall, the tank removed nitrate. This suggested that denitrification—a bacterial process that converts nitrate toward nitrogen gas—was taking place. Ammonium and nitrite concentrations in the treated water also fell at the same time, indicating that anammox activity had recovered. In phase II, we achieved very thorough nitrogen removal: the treated water contained an average total nitrogen concentration of 3.4 mg/L, and the tank removed an average of 87.2% of incoming nitrogen (Figure 2B).

3.2.

Changes in how nitrogen was transformed after adding easy-to-break-down organic matter

By following nitrogen through individual treatment cycles, we found changes in how the tank transformed it. In a typical phase I cycle, before we added easy-to-break-down organic matter, ammonium and nitrite were gradually removed, but nitrate built up considerably (Figure 3A). We compared the amount of nitrogen appearing as nitrate with the amount removed as ammonium. This ratio, written as ΔNO3−-N/ΔNH4+-N, was 0.92—much higher than the theoretical ratio of 0.26 for anammox alone (Strous et al., 1998). This indicated that another process was also making nitrate. Our accounting of nitrogen moving between its different forms suggested that nitrification was taking place: bacteria were using oxygen to turn some ammonium into nitrite and some nitrite into nitrate (Figure 3B). Nitrification accounted for 79% of the nitrate produced, leaving the tank unable to remove enough nitrogen.

Figure 3

Changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations during typical treatment cycles (A: phase I; C: phase II), and the processes that transformed nitrogen during those cycles (B: phase I; D: phase II).

After we added easy-to-break-down organic matter in phase II, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate concentrations all fell together during a typical reaction cycle (Figure 3C). This indicates that denitrification removed both the nitrate entering with the incoming water and the nitrate made by anammox. Tracking nitrogen between its different forms also revealed that partial denitrification (PD), which turns nitrate into nitrite (NO3− → NO2−), supplied extra nitrite for anammox (Figure 3D). This increased anammox activity inside the tank. Anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal process, accounting for 93% of the nitrogen removed (Figure 3D). Denitrification improved removal further, leaving a low total nitrogen concentration in the treated water.

3.3.

Separate batch tests reveal the potential for partial denitrification followed by anammox

We further demonstrated the potential for partial denitrification followed by anammox (PD/A) using separate batch tests outside the main treatment tank. In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the feed to investigate denitrification. Nitrite built up at every tested ratio of COD to nitrate nitrogen, written as COD/NO3−-N (Figures 4A–D). The highest percentage of nitrate converted to nitrite was 50.0%, reached at a COD/NO3−-N ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the tank could supply extra nitrite for anammox.

Figure 4

Changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we added ammonium to the feed alongside nitrate and acetate. During the first hour, nitrate was removed significantly, while nitrite built up at every tested COD/NO3−-N ratio. This indicated that partial denitrification was taking place (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate concentrations all fell together. Under the strictly oxygen-free conditions of the batch test, anammox removed the ammonium. Partial denitrification supplied the nitrite needed for that reaction. These results therefore prove the potential for partial denitrification followed by anammox in the tank treating the main wastewater flow.

3.4.

Changes in the microbes in the anammox treatment tank

We used DNA sequencing to identify microbes and investigate how a low concentration of easy-to-break-down organic matter affected their community in the tank (Figure 5). In phase I, without this addition, the share of anammox bacteria fell from 2.08 to 1.73% of the microbial community. Most of these anammox bacteria belonged to the group Candidatus Kuenenia. Meanwhile, the shares of two groups of nitrifying bacteria increased significantly. Ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which turn ammonium into nitrite and were represented by Nitrosomonas, rose from 0.29 to 0.40% of the community. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate and were represented by Nitrospira, rose from 0.14 to 0.56%. These trends matched the nitrate buildup and worsening nitrogen removal during tank operation.

After we added easy-to-break-down organic matter in phase II, the share of anammox bacteria recovered to 2.48% of the microbial community. The shares of AOB and NOB fell to 0.05 and 0.23%, respectively. These results suggest that adding a suitable amount of easy-to-break-down organic matter helps anammox bacteria build up and holds back nitrifying bacteria.

The denitrifying bacteria also changed after the addition. Denitratisoma, which can carry out complete denitrification from nitrate to nitrogen gas (NO3− → N2), was the leading group of denitrifying bacteria in phase I. Its share of the microbial community fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II. In contrast, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter became much more common in phase II. These groups have been identified as microbes that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020). Thauera rose from 0.18 to 2.15% of the community, while Candidatus Competibacter rose from 0.15 to 1.35%. These results provided further evidence of partial denitrification followed by anammox in the tank.

Figure 5

Changes in the microbial community in the anammox tank treating the main wastewater flow.

3.5.

Sludge forming compact clusters in the anammox treatment tank

The sludge used to start the tank contained some granules—compact clusters of microbes and other solids. Granules with a diameter greater than 200 μm (D > 200 μm) made up 17.4% of this starting sludge, and the average sludge particle diameter was 130.8 μm (Figure 6). A micrometre (μm) is one-thousandth of a millimetre. Sludge particle size stayed stable in phase I, then increased significantly to an average diameter of 195.6 μm in phase II. Granules eventually made up 52.5% of the total biomass—the living material—in the tank. This indicates that adding easy-to-break-down organic matter in phase II helped the sludge form granules. Forming these clusters can help anammox bacteria build up in the tank because they are more likely to grow in large clusters (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

parts.discussion:
4. Discussion 4.1. How adding easy-to-break-down organic matter improved nitrogen removal Adding easy-to-break-down organic matter, measured as readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), quickly restored our anammox treatment tank after nitrate had built up to high levels (Figure 2). With low concentrations of this material, the tank achieved very thorough nitrogen removal from the main wastewater flow. Several mechanisms may explain this improvement. First, the addition more strongly held back nitrification—the oxygen-using process that turns ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate. This reduced nitrate production inside the tank. In phase I, we supplied no easy-to-break-down organic matter. Relatively high nitrification activity increased nitrate production and reduced nitrogen removal performance (Figures 2, 3), as other studies have also shown (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Oxygen entered with the incoming water and from the air above the tank during mechanical mixing. This supplied enough dissolved oxygen (DO), at 0.06–0.08 mg/L, to support nitrification (Figure 3A). Some bacteria that carry out nitrification can use oxygen even when very little is available. These include complete ammonia oxidizers, called comammox, which carry out both steps from ammonium to nitrate, and bacteria in the genus Nitrospira that turn nitrite into nitrate (NOB) (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have contributed to nitrification in our tank: the share of Nitrospira increased significantly (Figure 5). In phase II, after we added easy-to-break-down organic matter, dissolved oxygen fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L. This may have happened because bacteria used oxygen while breaking down the added material (Figure 3C). The tank therefore had even less dissolved oxygen than in phase I, which held back nitrification. As a result, the shares of both ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which turn ammonium into nitrite, and NOB decreased during phase II (Figure 5). Second, the tank achieved partial denitrification followed by anammox, or PD/A. Partial denitrification turns nitrate into nitrite, which anammox bacteria can then use. Together, these processes removed both nitrate entering with the incoming water and nitrate produced by anammox. Tests on separate batches showed that nitrite could build up as nitrate was broken down through denitrification (Figures 4A–D). Measurements during a treatment cycle (Figure 3D) and further batch tests (Figures 4E–H) also showed that anammox bacteria could use and remove this nitrite. They did so with ammonium as the electron donor—the substance that supplies electrons for the reaction. In this way, the tank removed the remaining nitrate while using little organic matter, bringing nitrogen removal efficiency to a high level. Although we supplied the easy-to-break-down organic matter with the incoming water at the start, anammox kept producing nitrate and denitrification kept reducing it throughout the treatment cycle (Figure 3). We therefore expected denitrification to use carbon stored inside the bacteria. In phase II, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter were the bacteria responsible for partial denitrification (Figure 5). Both can store easy-to-break-down organic matter as internal carbon supplies, such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). The bacteria may therefore have stored the incoming organic matter at the start and used it to support partial denitrification throughout the cycle. Third, the addition promoted anammox activity and growth, improving treatment performance and stability. The direct effects of the added organic matter—acetate—on anammox activity may have been limited. Low concentrations of acetate do not inhibit anammox activity (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox species, including Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can gain energy from short-chain fatty acids, a group of small organic molecules (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this route may have played only a small role here because Candidatus Kuenenia was the main genus of anammox bacteria throughout our experiment. The added organic matter therefore mainly promoted anammox indirectly. For example, bacteria breaking it down with oxygen can use up dissolved oxygen in the tank water. This reduces oxygen's inhibitory effect on anammox (Strous et al., 1999). Also, when bacteria used the organic matter for partial denitrification under conditions with little oxygen, they supplied extra nitrite for anammox and promoted its activity (Figure 3). The organic matter also encouraged microbes to release polymers—large molecules—outside their cells, and helped the sludge form compact clusters (Figure 6). Other studies have shown these effects too (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). These changes helped keep slow-growing anammox bacteria in the tank and allowed them to build up (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). As a result, their share of the bacterial community rose from 1.73 to 2.48% after we introduced low concentrations of easy-to-break-down organic matter (Figure 5). Anammox also remained the main process removing nitrogen (Figure 3). 4.2. Practical use and further study We used an effective, workable strategy to address nitrate buildup caused by unwanted activity of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate in anammox tanks treating the main wastewater flow. Other reported ways to reduce nitrate production include using nitrogen gas to remove oxygen from incoming water, making tanks tall and narrow to reduce the water surface exposed to air, and adding protective covers (Díaz et al., 2020). However, these measures may be too costly or unsuitable in some cases, especially when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because they require major changes to the tank's design. Our strategy instead adds a low concentration of easy-to-break-down organic matter. It can reduce nitrate buildup with only a small modification: operators can redirect some untreated municipal wastewater to the anammox tank or add a small amount of organic carbon from an outside source (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). Liquid from sludge fermentation, a process that breaks down sludge, can also supply this material if it is available at the plant (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). Our operating strategy also applies to tanks with continuous water flow. However, these tanks may need extra measures to keep anammox bacteria inside. Options include adding suitable carriers—surfaces for the bacteria to grow on—and using a cyclone separator to selectively retain sludge that has formed compact clusters (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017). Even without excessive nitrate production by NOB, running an anammox tank with a low concentration of easy-to-break-down organic matter is beneficial because it offers the potential for complete nitrogen removal (Zhuang et al., 2022). Both partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) and partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) contributed to nitrogen removal, as reported in other studies (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen without relying on organic matter for energy. PD/A removed the nitrate produced by the anammox reaction. Table 2 presents a theoretical equation for this combined process as Case III and compares it with two other anammox-based approaches aimed at complete nitrogen removal, Cases I and II. In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without using organic matter for energy, but 11% of the ammonium ends up as nitrate. Removing this remaining nitrate through denitrification still uses organic carbon. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 mg COD/mg N: the organic matter required, measured as chemical oxygen demand (COD), for each milligram of nitrogen. In Case II, complete nitrification first turns ammonium into nitrate. Partial denitrification then turns that nitrate into the nitrite needed by anammox. This route needs more oxygen and organic carbon than making nitrite through partial nitritation (PN). Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg O2/mg N and 0.73 mg COD/mg N. Case III has theoretical advantages over both alternatives. Most nitrite comes from partial nitritation, so we expect it to save oxygen and organic carbon compared with Case II. It also removes the remaining nitrate through PD/A, which uses less organic carbon than the nitrate-removal step in Case I. In addition, PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, saving oxygen compared with Case I. Overall, Case III can achieve 100% nitrogen removal with the lowest requirements of the three cases: 1.76 mg O2/mg N for oxygen and 0.14 mg COD/mg N for organic matter. First, we need to investigate the nitrogen-removal mechanisms further. When calculating how nitrogen changed form in our tank, we left out some secondary routes by which microbes process nitrogen. This might affect the accuracy of our calculations. Future studies should untangle these complex networks of microbial nitrogen recycling using advanced tools. These include isotope labeling, which tracks specially marked atoms; metagenomics, which examines the genes in a microbial community; and metatranscriptomics, which examines which genes the microbes are using (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Second, we need to further check whether the strategy works with real municipal wastewater. Other studies have already reported partial denitrification and PD/A using the complex organic carbon sources found in that wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to investigate the long-term effects of adding organic matter, particularly as temperatures change with the seasons. Third, future studies should identify the best ranges for both the concentration of easy-to-break-down organic matter and its ratio to total nitrogen, called the rbCOD/TN ratio. This will help minimize organic matter use in practical applications.

parts.title: Removing nitrogen reliably and efficiently from municipal wastewater by adding a small amount of easily broken-down organic matter
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We ran an anammox reactor—a tank where bacteria remove nitrogen—to treat wastewater containing 25–35 mg/L of ammonium and nitrite combined. For the first 75 days, we added no easily broken-down organic matter. Nitrogen removal worked well at first, but nitrate built up in the treated water, and removal efficiency fell to 30%. The share of anammox bacteria fell from 2.15% to 1.78%, while the share of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate rose from 0.14% to 0.56%.

In the second phase, we added acetate, an easily broken-down organic substance, at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 0.9. Nitrate in the treated water fell within 2 days. During the following operation, the treated water contained an average of 3.4 mg/L total nitrogen. Anammox remained the main route by which nitrogen was removed, and DNA sequencing found that anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the community, further supporting their leading role. We attribute the improvement to stronger suppression of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate, removal of remaining nitrate through partial denitrification working alongside anammox, and the growth of sludge into larger clumps. Adding a small amount of easily broken-down organic matter is a workable way to make nitrogen removal in municipal-wastewater anammox reactors reliable and efficient.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, municipal wastewater, nitrogen removal, easily broken-down organic matter
parts.introduction_first: Removing nitrogen from municipal wastewater through partial nitritation and anammox has attracted much attention over the past decade because it could help wastewater treatment plants operate without a net energy demand (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017). In partial nitritation, bacteria turn some ammonium into nitrite; anammox bacteria then use ammonium and nitrite to remove nitrogen. Treatment plants can carry out these steps in one reactor or two. Using separate reactors lets each step run under suitable conditions and helps the different bacteria grow (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, the two-reactor process typically removes nitrogen faster than the one-reactor process (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We set up an anammox reactor for municipal-strength wastewater in a tank that runs in repeated batches. Without easily broken-down organic matter, unwanted bacteria turned nitrite into nitrate. Nitrate built up in the treated water, and nitrogen removal became less efficient. Adding a small amount of easily broken-down organic matter reversed the nitrate buildup and restored highly efficient nitrogen removal. Anammox remained the main way nitrogen was removed, while partial denitrification working alongside anammox removed the nitrate made by the anammox reaction. The added organic matter also helped keep oxygen levels lower, suppressing the unwanted bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate. It promoted the formation of larger sludge clumps, which helped the slow-growing anammox bacteria build up. Overall, adding a small amount of easily broken-down organic matter is a workable way to make nitrogen removal in municipal-wastewater anammox reactors reliable and efficient.
parts.introduction_rest:
Using partial nitritation and anammox to treat municipal wastewater at full scale remains difficult. One major concern is nitrate in the treated water: when too much builds up, total nitrogen can exceed the discharge limit (Zhuang et al., 2022). In a two-reactor system, bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate can produce nitrate in the first reactor, where partial nitritation takes place. In the second reactor, both the anammox reaction and unwanted activity by those bacteria can produce nitrate. Recent studies show that several methods can limit nitrate production in the first reactor: switching the air supply on and off, removing sludge after a very short time, or treating sludge separately with substances that inhibit the unwanted bacteria (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021).

The second, anammox reactor has therefore become a major source of nitrate. Excess nitrate caused by bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate has been reported in reactors that run in repeated batches, reactors that keep their contents mixed, and reactors that treat wastewater as it flows upward through clumps of sludge (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most methods used to suppress these bacteria in the first reactor cannot be used in the anammox reactor because they may also inhibit anammox bacteria. We therefore need ways to reduce nitrate buildup in anammox reactors.

Early studies saw easily broken-down organic matter as a problem for anammox treatment of municipal wastewater. They recommended removing it before treatment because other bacteria could grow too much and outcompete anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies found that anammox bacteria could remain active when reactors received an appropriate amount of this organic matter. With carbon-to-nitrogen ratios of 0.5–1.5, more than 90% of the nitrogen could be removed (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

Most of those studies, however, treated wastewater with high nitrogen concentrations of 100–300 mg N/L. At those concentrations, free ammonia or free nitrous acid can inhibit the growth of bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate, so excessive nitrate production is negligible (Ge et al., 2015). We still do not know whether adding easily broken-down organic matter can address the excess nitrate that these bacteria produce in anammox reactors treating municipal wastewater.

Partial denitrification working alongside anammox could also reduce the amount of organic matter needed for nitrogen removal and limit its unfavorable effects on anammox activity (Du et al., 2019). But in most studies of this approach, ammonium and nitrate are the main forms of nitrogen entering the reactor (Du et al., 2019). In anammox reactors treating municipal wastewater, nitrite is the main form of incoming oxidized nitrogen, while the anammox reaction gradually produces nitrate. Few studies have examined how partial denitrification works alongside anammox under these conditions when easily broken-down organic matter is present (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up and ran an anammox reactor for municipal wastewater in two phases: one without easily broken-down organic matter and one with it. We compared how well the phases removed nitrogen, how stable the process was, which microorganisms were present, and the form of the sludge. We used these results to assess how a low concentration of easily broken-down organic matter affected the process and whether it could improve nitrogen removal.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we ran the reactor

We treated municipal-strength wastewater in a 10 L anammox reactor: a tank that runs in repeated batches (Figure 1). To start it, we added sludge from a laboratory anammox reactor that treated wastewater high in nitrogen. The starting concentration of living material in the reactor was 4.9 g/L. We ran three cycles each day. In each cycle, we fed the tank for 10 minutes, replacing 50% of its volume; mixed it without added oxygen for 360 minutes; let the sludge settle for 30 minutes; released treated water for 10 minutes; and left the tank idle for 70 minutes (Figure 1B). Room temperature was 24–26°C. We did not remove sludge except when it left with the treated water or when we took samples. We estimated that sludge stayed in the reactor for longer than 30 days on average.

Figure 1

The municipal-strength wastewater anammox reactor (A) and its operating cycle (B).

We ran the reactor in two phases, changing what we fed it (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), each feed was 5 L of treated water from a partial nitritation reactor, which treated synthetic municipal wastewater. We describe that reactor in the Supplementary material. The feed to the anammox reactor had little organic matter, measured as chemical oxygen demand (COD): 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. Because the wastewater had already been biologically treated, most of this organic matter would likely have been difficult for microorganisms to break down. In phase II (days 76–135), we diverted 0.5 L of raw synthetic municipal wastewater around the partial nitritation reactor and mixed it with 4.5 L of that reactor’s treated water in a middle tank. We then fed the mixture to the anammox reactor. This added easily broken-down organic matter as acetate, equivalent to 24.2 mg COD/L. Apart from the organic matter in the feed, we kept the operating cycle and conditions the same in both phases.

2.2.

Separate tests of partial denitrification working alongside anammox

We ran two batch tests outside the reactor to examine whether partial denitrification could work alongside anammox. We collected sludge from the reactor, washed it three times with deionized water, and placed it in four separate 0.5 L cone-shaped flasks. After adding organic matter and nitrogen compounds, we kept the flasks in shaking incubators at 200 revolutions per minute and 25°C. Throughout the tests, we passed nitrogen gas through the flasks to keep oxygen out.

In Batch Test I, we asked whether nitrite would build up as bacteria reduced nitrate. We added only nitrate, as sodium nitrate (NaNO₃), and acetate. Every flask started with 15 mg/L nitrate. We varied the acetate dose so that the starting ratios of COD to nitrate nitrogen in the four flasks were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.

In Batch Test II, we asked whether nitrate reduction could work alongside anammox. We added ammonium, as ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl), as well as nitrate (NaNO₃) and acetate. Every flask started with 10 mg/L ammonium and 15 mg/L nitrate. We again varied the acetate dose to give starting COD-to-nitrate-nitrogen ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 across the four flasks.

2.3.

What we measured

Using standard methods (APHA, 2005), we measured COD; nitrogen in ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate; total nitrogen (TN); the amount of suspended sludge and its organic portion; and the sludge volume index, which describes how the sludge settles. We monitored temperature, acidity (pH), and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the reactor continuously with a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the range of sludge particle sizes with a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4.

How we calculated nitrogen changes during typical cycles

We used the changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations during typical reactor cycles to calculate the main ways nitrogen was transformed. We did not include minor pathways. We used different calculations for the two phases. In phase I, almost no easily broken-down organic matter entered the reactor, so we left nitrate- and nitrite-reducing pathways out of the calculation. We calculated the contributions of anammox bacteria, bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite (AOB), and bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate (NOB) using Equations 1–3.

(1) TN_anammox = ΔN = (NH₄⁺-N_initial + NO₂⁻-N_initial + NO₃⁻-N_initial) − (NH₄⁺-N_final + NO₂⁻-N_final + NO₃⁻-N_final)

(2) NH₄⁺-N_AOB = NH₄⁺-N_initial − NH₄⁺-N_final − TN_anammox/2.04

(3) NO₃⁻-N_NOB = NO₃⁻-N_final − NO₃⁻-N_initial − TN_anammox × 0.26/2.04

Here, TN_anammox is total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria; NH₄⁺-N_AOB is ammonium nitrogen used by AOB; and NO₃⁻-N_NOB is nitrate nitrogen produced by NOB. ΔN is the difference between the total dissolved inorganic nitrogen at the start and end of a cycle. The terms ending in “initial” are the ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate nitrogen concentrations at the start of the cycle; those ending in “final” are their concentrations at the end. All these quantities are in mg N/L.

In phase II, conditions in the reactor had less oxygen than in phase I, and nitrate decreased overall (Section 3.2). We therefore left nitrification—the conversion of ammonium or nitrite to more oxidized nitrogen compounds—out of this calculation. Using Equations 4–6, we calculated nitrogen changes through anammox, the conversion of nitrate to nitrite (denitratation, NO₃⁻ → NO₂⁻), and the conversion of nitrite to nitrogen gas (denitritation, NO₂⁻ → N₂).

(4) TN_anammox = NH₄⁺-N_initial − NH₄⁺-N_final × 2.04

(5) NO₃⁻-N_denitratation = NO₃⁻-N_initial + TN_anammox × 0.26/2.04 − NO₃⁻-N_final

(6) TN_denitritation = ΔN − TN_anammox

Here, TN_anammox is total nitrogen removed through anammox; NO₃⁻-N_denitratation is nitrate nitrogen reduced to nitrite; and TN_denitritation is total nitrogen removed by converting nitrite to nitrogen gas. Each is in mg N/L.

2.5.

DNA sequencing of the sludge community

We collected sludge samples on days 1, 75, and 134, freeze-dried them (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States), and stored them at −20°C. We extracted DNA with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the manufacturer’s instructions. We measured DNA concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands) to check the purity of the extract. To identify bacteria, we copied the V3–V4 region of their 16S rRNA gene using the 338F primer (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and the 806R primer (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). We sequenced the resulting DNA pieces on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). We then analyzed which microorganisms were present as described in our previous report (Yang et al., 2017). The raw sequencing reads are available in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA), accession number PRJNA942604.

3.

Results

3.1.

Nitrogen removal without and with easily broken-down organic matter

In phase I, we added almost no easily broken-down organic matter to the municipal-wastewater anammox reactor. The small amount of chemical oxygen demand (COD) removed—3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L—showed that there was little of this material to use (Figure 2A). Nitrogen removal was unstable (Figures 2B,C). It worked well at first, during days 1–40, but nitrate in the treated water rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L during days 41–75. Ammonium and nitrite also built up near the end of phase I, indicating that anammox activity had declined. The share of nitrogen removed fell from 83% to 30%.

Figure 2

Removal of chemical oxygen demand (A) and total nitrogen (B), and nitrogen-compound concentrations in water entering and leaving the municipal-wastewater anammox reactor (C).

In phase II, we added acetate equal to 24.2 mg COD/L, bringing the ratio of easily broken-down organic matter to total nitrogen to 0.9. The reactor removed an average of 27.7 mg COD/L, indicating that it used all the easily broken-down organic matter in the feed (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, nitrate in the treated water fell from 8.7 to 2.1 mg/L. It stayed low during the following operation, averaging 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L (Figure 2C). The reactor was now removing nitrate, which suggested that bacteria were converting nitrate through denitrification. Ammonium and nitrite in the treated water fell at the same time, indicating that anammox activity had recovered. In phase II, the treated water contained an average of 3.4 mg/L total nitrogen, and the reactor removed an average of 87.2% of the incoming nitrogen (Figure 2B).

3.2.

How nitrogen changed form after we added easily broken-down organic matter

Measurements during a reactor cycle showed that the routes by which nitrogen changed form had shifted. In a typical phase I cycle, before we added easily broken-down organic matter, ammonium and nitrite gradually fell while nitrate built up substantially (Figure 3A). For each amount of ammonium removed, the amount of nitrate produced gave a ratio of 0.92. Anammox alone would give a ratio of 0.26 (Strous et al., 1998), so another route was producing nitrate. Tracking where the nitrogen went suggested that bacteria converted some ammonium to nitrite and some nitrite to nitrate inside the reactor (Figure 3B). This process, called nitrification, accounted for 79% of the nitrate produced and left the reactor removing too little nitrogen.

Figure 3

Nitrogen-compound concentrations during typical reactor cycles (A: phase I; C: phase II) and the routes by which nitrogen changed form (B: phase I; D: phase II).

In a typical phase II cycle, after we added easily broken-down organic matter, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell together (Figure 3C). This showed that denitrification removed both nitrate entering the reactor and nitrate made by the anammox reaction. Tracking the nitrogen also showed that partial denitrification changed nitrate into nitrite, providing more nitrite for anammox (Figure 3D). As a result, anammox activity in the reactor increased. Anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal route: it accounted for 93% of the nitrogen removed (Figure 3D). Denitrification improved removal further, leaving little total nitrogen in the treated water.

3.3.

Batch tests of partial denitrification working alongside anammox

We used separate batch tests to examine whether partial denitrification could work alongside anammox in this reactor. In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the feed so we could examine denitrification. Nitrite built up at every ratio of acetate, measured as COD, to nitrate nitrogen (Figures 4A–D). The largest share of nitrate converted to nitrite was 50.0%, at a COD-to-nitrate-nitrogen ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the reactor could supply extra nitrite for anammox.

Figure 4

Nitrogen-compound concentrations in Batch Tests I (A–D) and II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we added ammonium as well as nitrate and acetate. During the first hour, nitrate fell substantially while nitrite built up at every COD-to-nitrate-nitrogen ratio, showing that partial denitrification was occurring (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell together. The batch test had strictly oxygen-free conditions, so anammox removed the ammonium. Partial denitrification supplied the nitrite that anammox needed. These results prove that partial denitrification can work alongside anammox in the municipal-wastewater reactor.

3.4.

How the bacteria in the reactor changed

We used high-throughput DNA sequencing to examine how a small amount of easily broken-down organic matter affected the reactor’s mix of microorganisms (Figure 5). In phase I, without this added material, the share of anammox bacteria—mostly *Candidatus Kuenenia*—fell from 2.08% to 1.73% of the community. Meanwhile, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (*Nitrosomonas*) rose from 0.29% to 0.40%, and bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate (*Nitrospira*) rose from 0.14% to 0.56%. These changes matched the nitrate buildup and worsening nitrogen removal. After we added easily broken-down organic matter in phase II, the anammox bacteria’s share recovered to 2.48%, while the shares of *Nitrosomonas* and *Nitrospira* fell to 0.05% and 0.23%, respectively. These results suggest that adding an appropriate amount of this material helps anammox bacteria grow while suppressing bacteria that produce nitrate.

The types of denitrifying bacteria changed too. *Denitratisoma*, which can carry denitrification all the way from nitrate to nitrogen gas, was the most common denitrifying bacterium in phase I. Its share fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II. By contrast, *Thauera* and *Candidatus Competibacter*, which have been identified as bacteria that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020), increased from 0.18% to 2.15% and from 0.15% to 1.35%, respectively. These changes provided further evidence that partial denitrification was working alongside anammox in the reactor.

Figure 5

Changes in the mix of microorganisms in the municipal-wastewater anammox reactor.

3.5.

Growth of sludge into larger clumps

The sludge used to start the reactor already contained some large clumps: 17.4% had diameters greater than 200 μm. Its average clump diameter was 130.8 μm (Figure 6). Clump size stayed stable in phase I, then increased substantially in phase II, reaching an average diameter of 195.6 μm. By the end, large clumps made up 52.5% of all the sludge in the reactor. This indicated that adding easily broken-down organic matter in phase II promoted the growth of sludge into larger clumps. Larger clumps can help anammox bacteria build up because these bacteria are more likely to grow in large groups (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

Figure 6

Changes in the size distribution of sludge clumps in the municipal-wastewater anammox reactor.
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion 4.1. How easily broken-down organic matter improved nitrogen removal In our reactor treating municipal-strength wastewater, adding easily broken-down organic matter (rbCOD) quickly reversed the buildup of nitrate (Figure 2). Even at low concentrations, it helped the reactor remove nitrogen efficiently. Several processes may explain the improvement. First, the added organic matter strengthened the suppression of nitrification—the conversion of ammonium and nitrite into nitrate—so the reactor made less nitrate. During phase I, when we added no rbCOD, relatively high nitrification activity increased nitrate production and worsened nitrogen removal (Figures 2, 3), as other studies have also shown (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). The reactor contained 0.06–0.08 mg/L dissolved oxygen (DO), which supported nitrification. This oxygen came in with the wastewater and from air at the top of the reactor during mechanical mixing (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying bacteria can grow at very low oxygen levels, including complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox) and bacteria in the genus Nitrospira that turn nitrite into nitrate (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have contributed to nitrification in our reactor: Nitrospira became much more abundant (Figure 5). In phase II, after we added rbCOD, dissolved oxygen fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L, possibly because oxygen-using bacteria consumed the organic matter (Figure 3C). The reactor thus had less oxygen than in phase I, suppressing nitrification. The shares of both bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite and bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate fell during phase II (Figure 5). Second, partial denitrification working alongside anammox removed nitrate both from the incoming wastewater and from the anammox reaction. In partial denitrification, bacteria change nitrate into nitrite. Our batch tests showed that nitrite could build up during this change (Figures 4A–D). Anammox bacteria could then use that nitrite with ammonium and remove both, as our analysis of a treatment cycle and further batch tests showed (Figures 3D, 4E–H). This combination removed the remaining nitrate while using little organic matter, raising the reactor’s nitrogen removal efficiency. Although we supplied rbCOD only with the wastewater at the start of each cycle, the anammox reaction produced nitrate and denitrification reduced it throughout the cycle (Figure 3). We therefore expected bacteria to use carbon they had stored inside their cells for denitrification later in the cycle. During phase II, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter were the bacteria responsible for partial denitrification (Figure 5). Both can store rbCOD as internal carbon sources, including glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). The rbCOD supplied at the start may therefore have supported partial denitrification throughout the cycle. Third, anammox bacteria became more active and grew, improving performance and stability. The acetate we supplied as rbCOD probably had little direct effect on anammox activity: low acetate concentrations do not inhibit it (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox species, including Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can use short-chain fatty acids to obtain energy (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). That route was probably minor here, because Candidatus Kuenenia dominated the reactor’s anammox bacteria throughout the experiment. Instead, rbCOD mainly helped anammox indirectly. Bacteria using oxygen to break down rbCOD can lower dissolved oxygen in the water and reduce its inhibitory effect on anammox (Strous et al., 1999). Partial denitrification can also use rbCOD without oxygen to make more nitrite for anammox bacteria (Figure 3). In addition, rbCOD promoted the release of substances outside microbial cells that help sludge grow into larger clumps (Figure 6), as other studies have shown (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). These clumps help keep slow-growing anammox bacteria in the reactor so they can build up (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). After we added low concentrations of rbCOD, the anammox share of the microbial community rose from 1.73% to 2.48% (Figure 5). Anammox remained the main route for nitrogen removal (Figure 3). 4.2. Putting the approach to use and what we need to study next We used a practical strategy to address nitrate buildup caused by unwanted bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate in anammox reactors treating municipal wastewater. Other proposed ways to reduce nitrate production include using nitrogen gas to remove oxygen from incoming wastewater, making the reactor tall and narrow to reduce its contact with air, and covering it (Díaz et al., 2020). These measures may be costly or impractical, especially when upgrading an existing wastewater treatment plant, because they can require major changes to the reactor. Adding a low concentration of rbCOD needs only a small change: a plant could send part of its raw municipal wastewater to the anammox reactor or add a small amount of an outside organic carbon source (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). Liquid produced by fermenting sludge could also supply rbCOD if the plant has it available (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). This operating approach also applies to reactors where wastewater flows through continuously. Such reactors may need extra ways to retain anammox bacteria, however, such as suitable surfaces for them to grow on or a cyclone device that selectively keeps larger sludge clumps (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017). A low concentration of rbCOD could also help a municipal-wastewater anammox reactor remove all its nitrogen even when bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate are not making excess nitrate (Zhuang et al., 2022). Other studies have reported that partial nitritation and anammox, together with partial denitrification working alongside anammox, both contribute to nitrogen removal (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our reactor, partial nitritation and anammox removed most nitrogen without organic carbon, while partial denitrification working alongside anammox removed nitrate made by the anammox reaction. Table 2 compares the theoretical reactions and oxygen and organic-matter needs of three anammox-based ways to remove all nitrogen. Case III represents the combined approach in our reactor. In Case I, partial nitritation and anammox remove nitrogen without organic carbon, but 11% of the ammonium ends up as nitrate. Removing that remaining nitrate by denitrification still takes organic carbon: the overall requirement is 0.32 mg of chemical oxygen demand (COD), a measure of organic matter, per mg of nitrogen. In Case II, complete nitrification turns ammonium into nitrate; partial denitrification then makes nitrite for anammox. Compared with making nitrite through partial nitritation, this route takes more oxygen and organic carbon. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg O₂ and 0.73 mg COD per mg of nitrogen. Case III has theoretical advantages over both. It makes most nitrite through partial nitritation, so it is expected to save oxygen and organic carbon compared with Case II. It removes remaining nitrate through partial denitrification working alongside anammox, using less organic carbon than Case I. That combined route also removes some ammonium without oxygen, further lowering oxygen demand compared with Case I. Of the three, Case III can theoretically remove 100% of the nitrogen with the lowest requirements: 1.76 mg O₂ and 0.14 mg COD per mg of nitrogen. First, we need to investigate nitrogen removal in more detail. We left out some less prominent ways bacteria process nitrogen when calculating how nitrogen changed in the reactor; this might affect the calculation’s accuracy. Future studies should examine these connected microbial processes using methods such as isotope labeling, which traces nitrogen atoms, and metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, which examine microbial genes and their activity (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Second, we need to check the strategy using real municipal wastewater. Other studies have reported partial denitrification and partial denitrification working alongside anammox using the varied organic matter in real municipal wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to examine the long-term effects of adding organic matter, especially as temperatures change with the seasons. Third, future studies should find the best ranges for rbCOD concentration and the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen, so real plants use as little added organic matter as possible.

parts.title: Reliable, highly efficient nitrogen removal in a mainstream anammox reactor by adding small amounts of easy-to-use organic matter
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We ran an anammox reactor to treat low-strength wastewater containing ammonium and nitrite (NH4+ + NO2−, 25–35 mg/L). In phase I, we added no readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), meaning organic matter that microbes can break down easily. In phase II, we added rbCOD. At first in phase I, nitrogen removal was efficient. However, after 75 days, nitrate built up in the treated water, and nitrogen removal efficiency fell to 30%. Microbial analysis showed that anammox bacteria decreased from 2.15 to 1.78%, while nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) increased from 0.14 to 0.56%.

In phase II, we added rbCOD as acetate at a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 0.9. Nitrate in the treated water fell within 2 days. Nitrogen removal then became highly effective, with average total nitrogen in the treated water of 3.4 mg/L. Even after rbCOD was added, the anammox pathway remained the main route by which nitrogen was removed. High-throughput sequencing showed that anammox bacteria were abundant (2.48%), further supporting their leading role. Nitrogen removal improved because NOB activity was more strongly suppressed, partial denitrification and anammox removed nitrate together, and the sludge formed more granules. Overall, adding low concentrations of rbCOD is a practical way to achieve reliable and efficient nitrogen removal in mainstream anammox reactors.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, mainstream, nitrogen removal, readily biodegradable organics
parts.introduction_first:
Removing nitrogen from municipal wastewater without adding organic carbon, using partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A), has received much attention over the past decade because it can help a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) operate without needing net energy input (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017). In PN/A, partial nitritation changes some ammonium into nitrite, and anammox bacteria then use ammonium and nitrite to remove nitrogen.

Researchers have developed single-stage and two-stage PN/A systems for wastewater treatment plants. In a two-stage system, partial nitritation (PN) and anammox happen in separate reactors. This lets each reactor favor the microbes needed for its own job (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). Therefore, two-stage PN/A usually removes nitrogen faster than single-stage PN/A (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

In this study, we established mainstream anammox treatment in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a reactor that treats water in repeated batches. When we operated the reactor without rbCOD, nitrate built up to high levels in the treated water because of unwanted NOB activity. This reduced nitrogen removal efficiency.

In contrast, adding a low concentration of rbCOD restored the anammox reactor after nitrate accumulation and achieved highly efficient nitrogen removal. At this low rbCOD concentration, anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal pathway, while partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) removed nitrate made by the anammox reaction. NOB were also effectively suppressed because conditions were more strictly anoxic, meaning they had even less oxygen. In addition, sludge granulation increased, which helped enrich slow-growing anammox bacteria. Overall, adding low concentrations of rbCOD is a practical strategy for reliable and efficient nitrogen removal in mainstream anammox reactors.
parts.introduction_rest:
A major challenge still limits full-scale use of mainstream PN/A: high nitrate concentrations in the treated water can cause total nitrogen (TN) to exceed discharge limits (Zhuang et al., 2022). In a two-stage PN/A system, nitrate can form in both reactors. In the first-stage PN reactor, bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate can produce it. In the second-stage anammox reactor, nitrate can come from the anammox reaction itself and from unwanted NOB activity.

Recent research shows that nitrate production in the first-stage PN reactor can be kept low. Useful ways to suppress NOB include turning aeration on and off, keeping sludge in the reactor for an extremely short time, and treating some sludge separately with substances that inhibit NOB (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021). The second-stage anammox reactor has therefore become a major source of nitrate. Excess nitrate caused by unwanted NOB has been reported in several reactor types, including sequencing batch reactors, completely mixed reactors, and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most methods used to suppress NOB in first-stage PN reactors cannot be used in second-stage anammox reactors because they may also inhibit anammox activity. We therefore need strategies that reduce nitrate buildup in anammox reactors.

Early studies viewed rbCOD, or organic matter that microbes can break down easily, as a problem for mainstream anammox. They suggested removing it before treatment because it can encourage too many heterotrophs—microbes that use organic matter for food—to grow and compete with anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies, however, have shown that anammox bacteria can remain active when an appropriate amount of rbCOD is present. In particular, nitrogen removal can exceed 90% when anammox reactors receive rbCOD at carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratios of 0.5–1.5 (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

However, most of these studies treated wastewater with high nitrogen concentrations, 100–300 mg N/L. At these concentrations, free ammonia or free nitrous acid can inhibit NOB growth (Ge et al., 2015), so excess nitrate production is usually minor. It is still unclear whether adding rbCOD can solve the excess nitrate production caused by NOB in mainstream anammox reactors. In addition, partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) can lower the amount of organic matter needed for nitrogen removal and reduce the harmful effects that organics can have on anammox activity (Du et al., 2019). Yet, in most PD/A studies, ammonium and nitrate were the main nitrogen compounds entering the reactor (Du et al., 2019). In mainstream anammox reactors, nitrite is the main incoming form of oxidized nitrogen (NOx−), while nitrate is gradually produced by the anammox reaction. PD/A in mainstream anammox reactors with rbCOD has rarely been reported and needs further investigation (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we established a mainstream anammox reactor and operated it in two phases: first without rbCOD and then with rbCOD. We compared nitrogen-removal performance, process stability, the microbial community, and sludge shape in the two phases. Using these results, we assessed how low rbCOD concentrations affect mainstream anammox and evaluated whether small amounts of rbCOD can improve nitrogen removal.

## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1. Experimental setup

We treated typical municipal wastewater with anammox in a 10 L sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a reactor that treats water in repeated batches (Figure 1). We seeded the reactor with sludge from a lab-scale anammox reactor treating wastewater with high nitrogen concentrations. After seeding, the reactor contained 4.9 g/L of biomass.

We operated the SBR for three cycles each day. Each cycle included 10 min of feeding, with 50% of the reactor volume replaced; 360 min of mixing under anoxic conditions, meaning with very little or no oxygen; 30 min of settling; 10 min of discharging; and 70 min of idling (Figure 1B). We kept the reactor at room temperature, 24–26°C. We did not remove sludge during operation, except when biomass left with the treated water or when we collected sludge samples. We estimated that the sludge retention time (SRT), the average time sludge stayed in the reactor, was longer than 30 days.

**Figure 1**

Diagram (A) and operating cycle (B) of the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox.

Based on the incoming wastewater, we divided reactor operation into two phases (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the reactor 5 L of treated water from a partial nitritation (PN) reactor that treated synthetic municipal wastewater. Details of the PN reactor are available in the Supplementary material. This incoming water had a low chemical oxygen demand (COD), 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. Because the wastewater had already been biologically treated, most of this organic matter was likely difficult for microbes to break down.

In phase II (days 76–135), we bypassed 0.5 L of raw synthetic municipal wastewater and mixed it with 4.5 L of treated water from the PN reactor in a middle tank. We then fed this mixed water into the anammox reactor. This added readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), meaning organic matter that microbes can break down easily, as acetate at 24.2 mg COD/L. Other than the different organic matter in the incoming water, the operating cycle and conditions were the same in phases I and II.
