### 2.2. Batch tests of the potential for partial denitrification/anammox in the reactor

We carried out two batch tests outside the reactor to examine the potential for partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A), in which nitrate is partly reduced to nitrite and anammox bacteria use that nitrite with ammonium to remove nitrogen. We washed sludge collected from the reactor three times with deionized water, then divided it among four separate 0.5-L conical flasks. After adding organic and nitrogen sources, we incubated the flasks at 25°C in shaking incubators at 200 rpm. Throughout the tests, we continuously bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks to maintain anoxic conditions.

In Batch Test I, we examined whether nitrite could build up during denitrification, the microbial reduction of nitrate or nitrite. We added only nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. The starting nitrate concentration was 15 mg/L in every flask, while the acetate dose differed among flasks. The starting COD/NO3−-N ratios were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 in the four flasks, respectively.

In Batch Test II, we examined whether denitrification could work together with anammox. Along with nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate, we added ammonium (NH4Cl). The starting ammonium and nitrate concentrations were 10 mg/L and 15 mg/L, respectively. We added different acetate doses to the four flasks, giving starting COD/NO3−-N ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0, respectively.

### 2.3. Analytical methods

We measured COD; ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate nitrogen; total nitrogen (TN); mixed liquor suspended solids; mixed liquor volatile suspended solids; and sludge volume index using standard methods (APHA, 2005). We monitored temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the reactor online using a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured sludge particle-size distribution with a laser particle-size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

### 2.4. Calculating nitrogen transformation pathways during typical cycles

We calculated nitrogen transformation pathways in the reactor from changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations during typical operating cycles. These calculations included only the main nitrogen pathways. Because the reactor operated differently in the two phases, we used different calculation methods for each phase.

In phase I, the reactor received negligible rbCOD. We therefore did not include denitrification pathways in the calculation. We calculated nitrogen conversions by anammox bacteria, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), and NOB using Eqs. 1–3.

(1) TNanammox=ΔN=(NH4+−Ninitial+NO2−−Ninitial+NO3−−Ninitial)−(NH4+−Nfinal+NO2−−Nfinal+NO3−−Nfinal)

(2) NH4+−NAOB=NH4+−Ninitial−NH4+−Nfinal−TNanammox/2.04

(3) NO3−−NNOB=NO3−−Nfinal−NO3−−Ninitial−TNanammox×0.26/2.04

Here, TNanammox is total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in mg N/L. NH4+−NAOB is ammonium consumed by AOB, in mg N/L. NO3−−NNOB is nitrate produced by NOB, in mg N/L. ΔN is the difference in total inorganic nitrogen concentration in the bulk liquid between the start and end of a cycle, in mg N/L. NH4+−Ninitial, NO2−−Ninitial, and NO3−−Ninitial are the bulk-liquid ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate concentrations at the start of a cycle, respectively, in mg N/L. NH4+−Nfinal, NO2−−Nfinal, and NO3−−Nfinal are the corresponding concentrations at the end of a cycle, in mg N/L.

In phase II, we operated the reactor under more strictly anoxic conditions than in phase I. Overall nitrate removal occurred (Section 3.2). We therefore did not include nitrification, the oxygen-using conversion of ammonium or nitrite, in the calculation. We calculated nitrogen conversions through anammox, denitratation (NO3− → NO2−), and denitritation (NO2− → N2) using Eqs. 4–6.

(4) TNanammox=NH4+−Ninitial−NH4+−Nfinal×2.04

(5) NO3−−Ndenitratation=NO3−−Ninitial+TNanammox×0.26/2.04−NO3−−Nfinal

(6) TNdenitritation=ΔN−TNanammox

Here, TNanammox is total nitrogen removed through the anammox pathway, in mg N/L. NO3−−Ndenitratation is nitrate reduced through denitratation, in mg N/L. TNdenitritation is total nitrogen removed through denitritation, in mg N/L.

### 2.5. High-throughput sequencing analysis

We collected sludge samples from the reactor on days 1, 75, and 134. We freeze-dried the samples with a BT2KXL freeze dryer (Virtis, United States) and stored them at −20°C. We extracted genomic DNA using the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the manufacturer’s instructions. We measured DNA concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands) to check the purity of the extracted DNA.

We copied the V3–V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene using bacterial primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). We sequenced the PCR products on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). We analyzed microbial composition from these data as described in our previous report (Yang et al., 2017). We deposited the raw sequencing reads in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database under accession number PRJNA942604.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Nitrogen removal without and with easily used organic matter

In phase I, we ran the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox with almost no readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), or organic matter that microbes can break down easily. Very little chemical oxygen demand (COD) was removed: 3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L (Figure 2A). Nitrogen removal was unstable (Figures 2B,C). Although removal was good at the start, from days 1–40, nitrate in the treated water rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L between days 41 and 75. Near the end of phase I, ammonium and nitrite also built up. This showed that anammox activity in the reactor was declining. As a result, nitrogen removal efficiency fell from 83% to 30%.

**Figure 2.** COD removal (A), total nitrogen (TN) removal (B), and nitrogen-compound concentrations in the incoming and treated water (C) of the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox.

In phase II, we added acetate at 24.2 mg COD/L to the reactor. This raised the rbCOD/TN ratio to 0.9. The reactor removed an average of 27.7 mg COD/L, showing that it used all of the easily used organic matter in the feed (Figure 2A). Nitrate in the treated water dropped from 8.7 mg/L to 2.1 mg/L within 2 days. It then stayed low, at 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L, during the following operation (Figure 2C). Overall, nitrate was removed. This suggested that denitrification, in which microbes reduce nitrate, was occurring in the reactor.

At the same time, treated-water ammonium and nitrite concentrations fell, showing that anammox activity had recovered. In phase II, we achieved advanced nitrogen removal: the average treated-water TN concentration was 3.4 mg/L, and the average nitrogen removal efficiency was 87.2% (Figure 2B).

### 3.2. How nitrogen conversion changed after adding easily used organic matter

Our analysis of individual treatment cycles showed that the reactor’s nitrogen-conversion pathway changed. In a typical phase I cycle, before rbCOD was added, ammonium and nitrite gradually decreased, but nitrate built up strongly (Figure 3A). The amount of nitrate nitrogen produced per amount of ammonium nitrogen removed, ΔNO3−-N/ΔNH4+-N, was 0.92. This was much higher than the theoretical anammox value of 0.26 (Strous et al., 1998), showing that nitrate was also being produced by another pathway.

The nitrogen mass flow indicated that nitrification changed some ammonium into nitrite and then changed part of that nitrite into nitrate in the anammox reactor (Figure 3B). Nitrification produced 79% of the nitrate. This caused the reactor to remove nitrogen insufficiently.

**Figure 3.** Changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations during typical reactor cycles (A: phase I; C: phase II) and nitrogen-conversion pathways (B: phase I; D: phase II).

After we added rbCOD in phase II, ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate all decreased at the same time during a typical reaction cycle (Figure 3C). This showed that denitrification removed both the nitrate entering with the feed and the nitrate made by the anammox reaction.

The nitrogen mass flow also showed that partial denitrification (PD), which changes nitrate into nitrite (NO3− → NO2−), supplied extra nitrite for anammox (Figure 3D). As a result, anammox activity within the reactor was promoted. Figure 3D shows that anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal pathway, accounting for 93% of nitrogen removal. Denitrification further improved nitrogen removal efficiency, producing a low TN concentration in the treated water.

### 3.3. Batch tests show the potential for partial denitrification linked with anammox

We used batch tests outside the reactor to further show the potential for partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A), in which nitrate is partly changed into nitrite and anammox then uses that nitrite with ammonium.

In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the feed to examine denitrification. Nitrite built up at every COD/NO3−-N ratio tested (Figures 4A–D). The highest nitrate-to-nitrite conversion ratio was 50.0%, at a COD/NO3−-N ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox could supply extra nitrite for anammox.

**Figure 4.** Changes in nitrogen-compound concentrations in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we also added ammonium, along with nitrate and acetate. During the first hour, nitrate was removed strongly and nitrite built up at every COD/NO3−-N ratio. This showed that partial denitrification occurred (Figures 4E–H). Afterward, ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate concentrations all fell together.

Because the batch test was under strictly anoxic conditions, with very little or no oxygen, ammonium was removed through the anammox pathway. Partial denitrification generated the nitrite needed for the anammox reaction. Therefore, these tests prove the potential for PD/A in the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox.

### 3.4. Changes in the reactor’s microbial community

We used high-throughput sequencing, a method that identifies many microbes at once, to examine how low-concentration rbCOD affected the microbial community in the reactor (Figure 5). In phase I, without rbCOD, the share of anammox bacteria, mainly *Candidatus Kuenenia*, fell from 2.08% to 1.73%. Meanwhile, the shares of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), *Nitrosomonas*, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), *Nitrospira*, increased from 0.29% to 0.40% and from 0.14% to 0.56%, respectively. These changes match the nitrate buildup and worsening nitrogen removal during reactor operation.

After we added rbCOD in phase II, the share of anammox bacteria recovered to 2.48%. The shares of AOB and NOB fell to 0.05% and 0.23%, respectively. These results suggest that adding an appropriate amount of rbCOD helps enrich anammox bacteria and suppress nitrifying bacteria.

We also saw a change in the denitrifying-bacteria population after rbCOD was added. *Denitratisoma*, which can carry out complete denitrification from nitrate to nitrogen gas (NO3− → N2), was the main denitrifying bacterium in phase I. Its abundance fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II. In contrast, *Thauera* and *Candidatus Competibacter*—microorganisms identified as important for partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020)—were strongly enriched in phase II. Their abundances rose from 0.18% to 2.15% and from 0.15% to 1.35%, respectively. These results provide further evidence of PD/A in the reactor.

**Figure 5.** Changes in microbial composition in the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox.

### 3.5. Sludge forming larger clumps in the reactor

The starting sludge in the reactor already contained some granular sludge: particles larger than 200 μm made up 17.4% of the sludge. Its average particle diameter was 130.8 μm (Figure 6). Sludge size stayed stable in phase I, then increased strongly to 195.6 μm in phase II. By the end, granular sludge made up 52.5% of all biomass in the reactor. This showed that adding rbCOD in phase II promoted sludge granulation, or sludge forming larger clumps.

Granulation can help enrich anammox bacteria because these bacteria are more likely to grow in large clusters (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

**Figure 6.** Changes in sludge particle-size distribution in the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox.
parts.discussion:
## 4. Discussion ### 4.1. How adding rbCOD improved nitrogen removal In our study, adding rbCOD, or organic matter that microbes can break down easily, quickly restored the reactor treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox after nitrate had built up to high levels (Figure 2). Efficient nitrogen removal was achieved even with low rbCOD concentrations. Several processes may have helped improve nitrogen removal after rbCOD was added. First, nitrification was more strongly suppressed, reducing nitrate made inside the reactor. In phase I, we operated the reactor without rbCOD. Nitrification activity was relatively high, which increased nitrate production and worsened nitrogen removal (Figures 2 and 3), as other studies have also shown (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Dissolved oxygen (DO), at 0.06–0.08 mg/L, entered with the influent and from air at the top of the reactor during mechanical mixing (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying microbes, including complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox) and Nitrospira NOB, can use oxygen very efficiently even when oxygen is scarce (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have contributed to nitrification because Nitrospira became much more abundant (Figure 5). After we added rbCOD in phase II, DO in the reactor fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L, possibly because aerobic heterotrophic bacteria used it while breaking down the organic matter (Figure 3C). Phase II therefore had more strictly anoxic conditions than phase I, which suppressed nitrification. As a result, the abundance of both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which change ammonium into nitrite, and NOB decreased during phase II (Figure 5). Second, partial nitrate reduction linked with anammox (PD/A) occurred in the reactor. This process removed nitrate entering with the influent as well as nitrate made by the anammox reaction. Our batch tests showed that nitrate reduction can build up nitrite (Figures 4A–D). Cycle analysis (Figure 3D) and batch tests (Figures 4E–H) further showed that anammox bacteria can use this nitrite, together with ammonium as the electron donor, and remove it. In this way, nitrate was polished from the reactor with only a small use of organic matter, helping nitrogen removal efficiency reach a high level. Although rbCOD entered with the influent at the start of each cycle, nitrate was continuously made by anammox and reduced by denitrification throughout the cycle (Figure 3). We therefore expected endogenous denitrification, meaning nitrate reduction supported by carbon stored inside microbial cells. In phase II, Thauera and *Candidatus Competibacter* were the bacteria responsible for partial denitrification (Figure 5). Both can store rbCOD as internal carbon sources, such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). Thus, rbCOD in the influent may have been stored at the beginning of the cycle and then supported partial denitrification throughout the cycle. Third, rbCOD promoted anammox activity and growth, improving process performance and stability. Acetate, the rbCOD used here, may have had limited direct effects on anammox activity. Low acetate concentrations do not inhibit anammox activity (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox species, including *Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus* and *Candidatus Brocadia fulgida*, can use short-chain fatty acids to generate energy (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this route may have been unimportant here because *Candidatus Kuenenia* dominated the anammox population throughout the experiment. Instead, rbCOD mainly promoted anammox indirectly. For example, aerobic breakdown of rbCOD can use DO in the bulk liquid and reduce its harmful effect on anammox activity (Strous et al., 1999). Also, when partial denitrification used rbCOD under anoxic conditions, it supplied additional nitrite for anammox bacteria and promoted anammox activity (Figure 3). In addition, rbCOD promoted secretion of extracellular polymers and sludge forming larger clumps in the reactor (Figure 6), as reported previously (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). These changes helped retain and enrich slow-growing anammox bacteria (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). Consequently, anammox bacteria increased from 1.73% to 2.48% after we added low rbCOD concentrations (Figure 5). At the same time, anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal pathway (Figure 3). ### 4.2. Practical use and future research We used an effective and practical strategy to address nitrate buildup caused by unwanted NOB activity in reactors treating typical municipal wastewater with anammox. Other reported ways to lower nitrate production include removing oxygen from the influent with nitrogen gas, reducing the reactor surface exposed to air by using a high height-to-diameter ratio, and placing protective covers on the reactor (Díaz et al., 2020). However, these approaches may not be economical or practical in some situations, especially when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because they require major changes to reactor design. In contrast, adding a low concentration of rbCOD can reduce nitrate buildup with only minor changes. For example, a treatment plant could redirect some raw municipal wastewater to the anammox reactor or add a small amount of external organic carbon (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). If available at the wastewater treatment plant, liquid from sludge fermentation can also provide rbCOD (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). This operating strategy can also be used in continuous-flow reactors. However, extra measures may be needed to keep anammox bacteria in the system, such as adding suitable carriers or using a cyclone to selectively retain granular sludge (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017). Even when NOB do not make too much nitrate, operating a mainstream anammox reactor with a low rbCOD concentration can still be useful because it may achieve complete nitrogen removal (Zhuang et al., 2022). As reported previously, both partial ammonium-to-nitrite conversion followed by anammox (PN/A) and PD/A can contribute to nitrogen removal (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most nitrogen without using organic matter, while PD/A removed nitrate made during the anammox reaction. Table 2 gives the theoretical reaction for this process in Case III and compares it with two other anammox-based approaches for complete nitrogen removal, Cases I and II. In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without organic matter, but 11% of ammonium is ultimately changed into nitrate. Denitrification is still needed to polish this nitrate, and it uses organic matter. Overall, Case I requires 0.32 mg COD per mg N. In Case II, ammonium is fully nitrified to nitrate, and partial denitrification then makes the nitrite that anammox needs. Compared with making nitrite through PN, this approach needs additional oxygen and organic matter. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg O2/mg N and 0.73 mg COD/mg N. Case III has theoretical advantages over Cases I and II. First, PN produces most nitrite, so it should save oxygen and organic matter compared with Case II. Second, PD/A polishes nitrate while using less organic matter than Case I. In addition, PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it can also reduce oxygen demand compared with Case I. Overall, among the three cases, Case III can theoretically achieve 100% nitrogen removal with the lowest oxygen demand, 1.76 mg O2/mg N, and the lowest organic-matter demand, 0.14 mg COD/mg N. First, the nitrogen-removal mechanisms need further investigation. When we calculated nitrogen changes in the reactor, we did not include some smaller nitrogen-conversion pathways. This may have affected the accuracy of the calculations. Future studies should clarify the complex networks through which microbes recycle nitrogen by using advanced methods such as isotope labeling, metagenomics, and metatranscriptomics (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Second, the nitrate-control strategy should be tested further with real municipal wastewater. Partial denitrification and PD/A using the complex organic matter in real municipal wastewater have been reported previously (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to examine the long-term effects of adding organic matter, especially as temperatures change with the seasons. Third, future studies should identify the best rbCOD concentration range and rbCOD-to-total-nitrogen ratio, so that real applications use as little organic matter as possible.

parts.title: Improving nitrogen removal in a mainstream anammox reactor with small amounts of easy-to-use organic matter
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We used an anammox reactor to treat wastewater with low nitrogen levels (ammonium + nitrite, 25–35 mg/L). We first ran it without readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), a measure of organic matter that microbes can quickly use (phase I), and then added it (phase II). In phase I, nitrogen removal was efficient at first, but after 75 days nitrate built up in the treated water and nitrogen removal efficiency fell to 30%. The share of anammox bacteria in the microbial community fell from 2.15 to 1.78%, while the share of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, rose from 0.14 to 0.56%. In phase II, we added acetate as rbCOD at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 0.9. Effluent nitrate fell within 2 days. During the following operation, nitrogen removal was strong, and average total nitrogen in the treated water was 3.4 mg/L. Even with rbCOD added, anammox remained the main pathway removing nitrogen. DNA sequencing showed that anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the community, further supporting their leading role. Better nitrogen removal was linked to stronger suppression of NOB activity, nitrate removal by partial denitrification and anammox, and the formation of larger sludge clumps. Overall, adding a small amount of rbCOD is a practical way to achieve steady, efficient nitrogen removal in mainstream anammox reactors.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, mainstream, nitrogen removal, readily biodegradable organic matter
parts.introduction_first: Autotrophic nitrogen removal from municipal wastewater uses microbes that remove nitrogen without needing organic matter as their food. One such process, partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A), has received much attention over the past decade because it could help wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) use no more energy than they produce (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017). PN/A systems can use one reactor or two. In a two-reactor system, partial nitritation (PN)—the first step that changes some ammonium into nitrite—and anammox, which uses ammonium and nitrite to remove nitrogen, happen in separate reactors. This can help each process's microbes grow well (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, two-reactor PN/A systems usually remove nitrogen faster than one-reactor systems (Liu et al., 2018).

Conclusion

We set up a mainstream anammox process in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR), which treats wastewater in repeated batches. Without rbCOD, unwanted activity by nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) led to nitrate building up in the treated water and reduced nitrogen removal efficiency. When we added a small amount of rbCOD, the reactor recovered from nitrate buildup and removed nitrogen very effectively.

With this small addition of rbCOD, anammox remained the main pathway for removing nitrogen, while partial denitrification and anammox (PD/A) removed nitrate produced by the anammox reaction. The more oxygen-poor conditions also suppressed NOB effectively. The addition of rbCOD encouraged sludge granules to form, helping slow-growing anammox bacteria become more abundant. Overall, adding a small amount of rbCOD is a practical way to achieve steady, efficient nitrogen removal in mainstream anammox reactors.
parts.introduction_rest:
To date, using mainstream partial nitritation and anammox (PN/A) at full scale remains challenging. One major concern is that treated water can contain too much nitrate, causing total nitrogen (TN) levels to exceed discharge limits (Zhuang et al., 2022). In a two-reactor PN/A system, nitrate can form in both reactors: in the first, when nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria (NOB) are active, and in the second, through anammox and unwanted NOB activity.

Recent studies show that nitrate production in the first reactor can be reduced using strategies that suppress NOB. These include switching aeration on and off, using an extremely short sludge retention time (SRT)—the time sludge stays in the reactor—or treating sludge from a side stream with inhibitors (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021). The second, anammox reactor has therefore become a major source of nitrate. High nitrate production linked to unwanted NOB activity has been reported in several reactor types, including sequencing batch reactors (SBRs), completely stirred tank reactors, and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most methods used to suppress NOB in the first reactor cannot be used in the anammox reactor because they may also inhibit anammox bacteria. We therefore need strategies to reduce nitrate buildup in anammox reactors.

Early studies treated readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), or easy-to-use organic matter, as a problem for mainstream anammox. They proposed removing it before treatment because it could cause other microbes, called heterotrophs, to grow too much and outcompete anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). More recent studies, however, found that anammox bacteria can remain active when a suitable amount of rbCOD is present. In particular, nitrogen removal efficiency exceeded 90% when reactors were run at carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratios of 0.5–1.5 (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

Most of these studies treated wastewater with high nitrogen concentrations, 100–300 mg N/L. Such concentrations can limit NOB growth because of free ammonia or free nitrous acid (Ge et al., 2015), so excessive nitrate production was negligible. It is still unknown whether adding rbCOD can reduce the excessive nitrate production caused by NOB in mainstream anammox reactors.

Partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) can also reduce the amount of organic matter needed for nitrogen removal and limit the harmful effects of organic matter on anammox activity (Du et al., 2019). However, in most PD/A studies, ammonium and nitrate were the main nitrogen compounds entering the reactor (Du et al., 2019). In mainstream anammox reactors, nitrite is the main form of incoming nitrogen oxides (NOx−), while the anammox reaction gradually produces nitrate. PD/A in mainstream anammox reactors with rbCOD has rarely been reported and needs further study (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up a mainstream anammox reactor and ran it in two phases, with and without rbCOD. We compared nitrogen removal, process stability, the microbial community, and sludge shape between the phases. Using these data, we assessed how low amounts of rbCOD affect the mainstream anammox process and evaluated whether they can improve nitrogen removal.

## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1. Experimental setup

We ran the mainstream anammox process in a 10 L sequencing batch reactor (SBR; Figure 1). We seeded it with sludge from a laboratory-scale anammox reactor that treated wastewater with a high nitrogen level. After adding the sludge, the reactor contained 4.9 g of biomass per liter.

We ran three treatment cycles per day. Each cycle included 10 minutes of feeding, during which half the reactor volume was replaced; 360 minutes of anoxic mixing, with oxygen kept out; 30 minutes for the sludge to settle; 10 minutes to discharge treated water; and 70 minutes with no operation (Figure 1B). The reactor was kept at room temperature, 24–26°C. We did not remove sludge during operation, except when some left with the treated water or was taken for sampling. We estimated that the sludge age, called the solids retention time (SRT), was longer than 30 days.

**Figure 1.** Diagram of the mainstream anammox reactor (A) and its operating cycle (B).

We operated the reactor in two phases, based on what was in its incoming wastewater (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed it 5 L of treated water from a partial nitritation (PN) reactor that had processed synthetic municipal wastewater. Details of the PN reactor are provided in the Supplementary material. The incoming water had a low chemical oxygen demand (COD), 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. Because the wastewater had already been treated by microbes, most of this organic matter was likely difficult for microbes to break down.

In phase II (days 76–135), we sent 0.5 L of raw synthetic municipal wastewater around the PN reactor and mixed it with 4.5 L of PN-treated water in an intermediate tank. We then fed this mixture to the anammox reactor. This introduced readily biodegradable chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD)—easy-to-use organic matter—in the form of acetate, at 24.2 mg COD/L. The reactor's operating schedule and conditions were otherwise the same in both phases.

**Table 1.** Main characteristics of the water fed to the mainstream anammox reactor.

| Phase | Ammonium as nitrogen (mg/L) | Nitrite as nitrogen (mg/L) | Nitrate as nitrogen (mg/L) | Total nitrogen (mg/L) | Chemical oxygen demand (mg/L) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8 |
| II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2 |

### 2.2. Batch tests of the reactor's potential for partial nitrate conversion and anammox

We ran two separate batch tests outside the reactor to examine whether partial denitrification and anammox (PD/A) could occur in its sludge. We washed sludge collected from the reactor three times with deionized water, then divided it among four 0.5 L conical flasks. After adding organic and nitrogen compounds for the microbes to use, we placed the flasks in shaking incubators at 25°C and 200 rpm. We continuously bubbled nitrogen gas through them to keep oxygen out.

In Batch Test I, we tested whether nitrite could build up while nitrate was being reduced. We added nitrate, as sodium nitrate (NaNO₃), and acetate to the flasks. Each flask started with 15 mg/L nitrate, while the acetate amounts differed. The starting ratios of COD to nitrate-as-nitrogen in the four flasks were 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.

In Batch Test II, we tested whether nitrate reduction could occur alongside anammox. We added ammonium, as ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl), as well as nitrate and acetate. The starting concentrations were 10 mg/L ammonium and 15 mg/L nitrate. The four flasks received different amounts of acetate, giving starting COD-to-nitrate-as-nitrogen ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0.

### 2.3. How we measured the water and sludge

We measured chemical oxygen demand (COD), ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, total nitrogen (TN), suspended solids in the mixed water, volatile suspended solids in the mixed water, and the sludge volume index using standard methods (APHA, 2005). The sludge volume index describes how well sludge settles. We monitored temperature, pH (a measure of acidity), and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the reactor online with a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the distribution of sludge-particle sizes using a laser particle-size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

### 2.4. Calculating nitrogen pathways during typical cycles

We calculated the nitrogen pathways in the reactor from how the concentrations of nitrogen compounds changed over typical treatment cycles. We included only the main pathways. Because the reactor ran differently in the two phases, we used different calculations for each.

In phase I, little rbCOD entered the reactor, so we left denitrification out of the calculations. We calculated nitrogen changes due to anammox bacteria, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) using Equations 1–3:

(1) TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ = ΔN = (NH₄⁺–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ + NO₂⁻–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ + NO₃⁻–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ) − (NH₄⁺–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ + NO₂⁻–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ + NO₃⁻–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ)

(2) NH₄⁺–Nₐₒᵦ = NH₄⁺–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ − NH₄⁺–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ − TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ/2.04

(3) NO₃⁻–Nₙₒᵦ = NO₃⁻–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ − NO₃⁻–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ − TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ × 0.26/2.04

Here, TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ is the amount of total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in mg N/L; NH₄⁺–Nₐₒᵦ is ammonium used by AOB, in mg N/L; and NO₃⁻–Nₙₒᵦ is nitrate produced by NOB, in mg N/L. ΔN is the change in the total amount of inorganic nitrogen in the water between the start and end of a cycle, in mg N/L. The terms with “initial” and “final” indicate the ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate concentrations at the start and end of the cycle, respectively, in mg N/L.

In phase II, the reactor was kept under more strictly oxygen-free conditions than in phase I. Overall nitrate removal occurred (Section 3.2), so we left nitrification out of the calculations. We calculated nitrogen changes due to anammox, denitratation (nitrate changing into nitrite), and denitritation (nitrite changing into nitrogen gas) using Equations 4–6:

(4) TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ = (NH₄⁺–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ − NH₄⁺–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ) × 2.04

(5) NO₃⁻–N𝒹ₑₙᵢₜᵣₐₜₐₜᵢₒₙ = NO₃⁻–Nᵢₙᵢₜᵢₐₗ + TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ × 0.26/2.04 − NO₃⁻–N𝒻ᵢₙₐₗ

(6) TN𝒹ₑₙᵢₜᵣᵢₜₐₜᵢₒₙ = ΔN − TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ

Here, TNₐₙₐₘₘₒₓ is total nitrogen removed through anammox, NO₃⁻–N𝒹ₑₙᵢₜᵣₐₜₐₜᵢₒₙ is nitrate reduced through denitratation, and TN𝒹ₑₙᵢₜᵣᵢₜₐₜᵢₒₙ is total nitrogen removed through denitritation; all are in mg N/L.

### 2.5. DNA sequencing to identify microbes

We collected sludge from the reactor on days 1, 75, and 134. We freeze-dried the samples (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States) and stored them at −20°C. We extracted DNA with the Fast DNA Kit (MP Biomedicals, CA, United States), following the manufacturer's instructions. We measured DNA concentration with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands) to check the purity of the extract.

We copied the V3–V4 region of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene using the primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). We sequenced the resulting PCR products using an Illumina MiSeq platform (MajorBio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). We analyzed the microbial community composition from these data as described in our previous report (Yang et al., 2017). We deposited the raw sequencing reads in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under accession number PRJNA942604.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Nitrogen removal with and without easy-to-use organic matter

In phase I, the mainstream anammox reactor received almost no easy-to-use organic matter (rbCOD). The reactor removed very little chemical oxygen demand (COD): 3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L (Figure 2A). Nitrogen removal was unstable (Figures 2B and 2C). At first, during days 1–40, the reactor removed nitrogen well. But from day 41 to day 75, nitrate in the treated water rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L. By the end of phase I, ammonium and nitrite had also built up, showing that anammox activity in the reactor had declined. As a result, nitrogen removal efficiency fell from 83% to 30%.

**Figure 2**

COD removal (A), total nitrogen (TN) removal (B), and nitrogen-compound levels in the incoming and treated water (C) in the mainstream anammox reactor.

In phase II, we added acetate, an easy-to-use organic matter, at 24.2 mg COD/L. This raised the rbCOD-to-TN ratio to 0.9. The reactor removed an average of 27.7 mg/L COD, showing that it used all the rbCOD supplied in the feed (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, nitrate in the treated water fell from 8.7 to 2.1 mg/L. It remained low during the rest of the operation, averaging 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L (Figure 2C). This shows that nitrate was removed, suggesting that denitrification took place in the reactor. Ammonium and nitrite in the treated water also fell, showing that anammox activity recovered. Overall, nitrogen removal was strong in phase II: average TN in the treated water was 3.4 mg/L, and average nitrogen removal efficiency was 87.2% (Figure 2B).

### 3.2. How nitrogen pathways changed after adding easy-to-use organic matter

Cycle tests showed that the way nitrogen changed in the mainstream anammox reactor shifted after we added rbCOD. In a typical phase I cycle, before rbCOD was added, ammonium and nitrite gradually fell while nitrate built up considerably (Figure 3A). For each unit of ammonium removed, the reactor produced 0.92 units of nitrate (ΔNO₃⁻-N/ΔNH₄⁺-N = 0.92). This was much higher than the theoretical anammox value of 0.26 (Strous et al., 1998), showing that another pathway was also producing nitrate. The nitrogen balance showed that nitrification changed some ammonium into nitrite and some of that nitrite into nitrate in the reactor (Figure 3B). Nitrification accounted for 79% of nitrate production, leaving the mainstream anammox reactor unable to remove enough nitrogen.

**Figure 3**

Changes in nitrogen-compound levels during typical reactor cycles (A: phase I; C: phase II) and the nitrogen pathways in those cycles (B: phase I; D: phase II).

After we added rbCOD in phase II, ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate all fell at the same time during a typical cycle (Figure 3C). This shows that denitrification removed both nitrate that entered with the feed and nitrate produced by anammox. The nitrogen balance also showed that partial denitrification—changing nitrate into nitrite—provided extra nitrite for anammox (Figure 3D). This promoted anammox activity inside the reactor. Anammox remained the main nitrogen-removal pathway in phase II, accounting for 93% of nitrogen removal (Figure 3D). Denitrification further improved nitrogen removal, resulting in low TN in the treated water.

### 3.3. Batch tests show the reactor could use partial nitrate conversion and anammox

We used batch tests outside the reactor to further show the potential for partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) in the mainstream anammox reactor. In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the feed to examine denitrification. Nitrite built up at every tested COD-to-nitrate-nitrogen ratio (Figures 4A–D). The largest share of nitrate changed into nitrite was 50.0%, at a COD/NO₃⁻-N ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the mainstream anammox reactor could provide extra nitrite for anammox.

**Figure 4**

Changes in nitrogen-compound levels in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we added ammonium as well as nitrate and acetate to the feed. During the first hour, nitrate fell sharply while nitrite built up at every COD/NO₃⁻-N ratio, showing that partial denitrification (PD) occurred (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite, and nitrate all fell together. The batch test was kept strictly oxygen-free, so ammonium was removed through the anammox pathway. PD supplied the nitrite needed for anammox. These results therefore show the potential for PD/A in the mainstream anammox reactor.

### 3.4. Microbial changes in the mainstream anammox reactor

We used high-throughput DNA sequencing to examine how low levels of rbCOD affected the microbial community in the mainstream anammox reactor (Figure 5). During phase I, when no rbCOD was added, anammox bacteria—mainly *Candidatus Kuenenia*—made up 2.08% of the community at first and 1.73% later. Over the same phase, ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), mainly *Nitrosomonas*, rose from 0.29% to 0.40%, while nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria (NOB), mainly *Nitrospira*, rose from 0.14% to 0.56%. These changes match the nitrate buildup and the decline in nitrogen removal during reactor operation.

After rbCOD was added in phase II, anammox bacteria increased to 2.48% of the community. AOB decreased to 0.05% and NOB to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding the right amount of rbCOD benefits the growth of anammox bacteria and suppresses nitrifying bacteria.

The denitrifying bacteria also changed after rbCOD was added. In phase I, *Denitratisoma*, which can complete denitrification by changing nitrate into nitrogen gas (NO₃⁻ → N₂), was the main denitrifying bacterium. Its share of the community fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II. In contrast, *Thauera* and *Candidatus Competibacter*, which have been identified as microbes that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020), increased from 0.18% to 2.15% and from 0.15% to 1.35%, respectively, between the phases. These results provide further evidence for partial denitrification and anammox in the reactor.

**Figure 5**

Changes in the microbial community in the mainstream anammox reactor.

### 3.5. Sludge clumps grew in the mainstream anammox reactor

The seed sludge in the mainstream anammox reactor already contained some granules larger than 200 μm in diameter: they made up 17.4% of the sludge. The average sludge diameter was 130.8 μm (Figure 6). Sludge size stayed stable in phase I, then increased significantly to an average of 195.6 μm in phase II. By the end, granules made up 52.5% of all biomass in the reactor, showing that granule formation was promoted after rbCOD was added in phase II. Granules may help anammox bacteria become more abundant because these bacteria tend to grow in larger clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

**Figure 6**

Changes in sludge size distribution in the mainstream anammox reactor.
