## 4. Discussion ### 4.1. How adding easy-to-use organic matter improved nitrogen removal In our study, adding easy-to-use organic matter (rbCOD) quickly helped the mainstream anammox reactor recover from nitrate buildup (Figure 2). The reactor removed nitrogen very well even when rbCOD levels were low. Several processes may explain this improvement. First, adding rbCOD strengthened the conditions that suppress nitrification, so less nitrate was made inside the reactor. During phase I, when we did not add rbCOD, nitrification was relatively active. This increased nitrate production and worsened nitrogen removal (Figures 2 and 3), as other studies have also shown (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Oxygen entered with the wastewater and from the air at the top of the reactor while it was mechanically mixed. The oxygen level was 0.06–0.08 mg/L (Figure 3A). Some bacteria that make nitrate, including complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox) and Nitrospira nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria, can use oxygen even when very little is available (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have helped nitrification continue, because the amount of Nitrospira rose significantly (Figure 5). After we added rbCOD in phase II, the oxygen level fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L, possibly because oxygen-using bacteria consumed it (Figure 3C). Conditions were therefore more oxygen-poor than in phase I, which suppressed nitrification. As a result, the amounts of both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria fell during phase II (Figure 5). Second, partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) took place in the reactor. Together, these processes removed nitrate that came in with the wastewater and nitrate produced by anammox. Batch tests showed that nitrate could first be partly changed into nitrite during denitrification (Figures 4A–D). Cycle analysis and batch tests also showed that anammox bacteria could use this nitrite, with ammonium as their partner, and remove it (Figures 3D and 4E–H). In this way, the reactor removed nitrate using only a small amount of organic matter, raising its nitrogen removal efficiency to a high level. Although rbCOD entered with the wastewater at the start of a treatment cycle, anammox kept producing nitrate and denitrification kept reducing it throughout the cycle (Figure 3). This means that denitrification using stored, internally produced carbon was expected to occur. During phase II, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter were the bacteria responsible for partial denitrification (Figure 5). Both can store rbCOD as internal carbon sources, including glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). The rbCOD entering with the wastewater may therefore have been stored at the beginning of the cycle and supported partial denitrification throughout it. Third, anammox activity and growth increased, improving how well the process worked and how steadily it performed. The direct effect of rbCOD (acetate) on anammox activity may have been limited. Low acetate levels do not inhibit anammox activity (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox species, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can use short-chain fatty acids to obtain energy (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). But this route may have been minor in our study because the reactor's anammox population was dominated throughout the experiment by Candidatus Kuenenia. Instead, rbCOD mainly helped anammox indirectly. For example, aerobic bacteria can use rbCOD and consume oxygen in the water, reducing oxygen's inhibitory effect on anammox bacteria (Strous et al., 1999). Also, partial denitrification of nitrate using rbCOD supplied extra nitrite for anammox and helped increase its activity (Figure 3). The rbCOD also encouraged bacteria to release sticky materials around their cells, helping sludge form granules (Figure 6), as earlier studies have shown (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). These granules helped retain and build up slow-growing anammox bacteria (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). After we added low levels of rbCOD, anammox bacteria increased from 1.73% to 2.48% of the microbial community (Figure 5). Anammox nevertheless remained the main route for removing nitrogen (Figure 3). ### 4.2. Uses and questions for future research In this study, we used a practical strategy to address nitrate buildup caused by unwanted activity of nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria in mainstream anammox reactors. Other strategies to reduce nitrate production have been reported: removing oxygen from incoming wastewater with nitrogen gas, reducing the reactor's surface area exposed to air by making it taller relative to its width, and covering the reactor (Díaz et al., 2020). These approaches may not be affordable or practical in some situations, especially when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), because they require major changes to the reactor. By contrast, our strategy adds a low level of rbCOD and needs only a small modification: redirecting some untreated municipal wastewater to the anammox reactor or adding a small amount of outside organic carbon (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). If available at the WWTP, sludge fermentation liquid can also supply rbCOD (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). This operating strategy can also be used in continuous-flow reactors. However, extra steps may be needed to keep anammox bacteria in the reactor, such as adding suitable carriers or using a cyclone to retain granular sludge selectively (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017). Running a mainstream anammox reactor with a low level of rbCOD may be useful even when nitrite-to-nitrate bacteria do not produce too much nitrate, because it could allow complete nitrogen removal (Zhuang et al., 2022). Earlier studies have reported that both partial nitritation and anammox (PN/A) and partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) can contribute to nitrogen removal (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen without using organic matter, while PD/A removed nitrate produced by the anammox reaction. Table 2 gives the theoretical reaction and compares the oxygen and organic matter needed for this process (Case III) with two other anammox-based approaches to complete nitrogen removal (Cases I and II). In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without organic matter, but 11% of the ammonium is eventually changed into nitrate. Removing this nitrate by denitrification still takes organic matter. In total, Case I needs 0.32 mg COD per mg of nitrogen. In Case II, nitrite for anammox is made by fully changing ammonium into nitrate and then partly changing the nitrate into nitrite through partial denitrification. This approach needs more oxygen and organic matter than making nitrite through partial nitritation. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg oxygen and 0.73 mg COD per mg of nitrogen. Case III has theoretical advantages over Cases I and II. It makes most of the nitrite through partial nitritation, which is expected to save oxygen and organic matter compared with Case II. It also removes nitrate through PD/A, which uses less organic matter than the denitrification in Case I. In addition, PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it can save oxygen compared with Case I. Overall, of the three cases, Case III can remove 100% of the nitrogen with the lowest requirements: 1.76 mg oxygen and 0.14 mg COD per mg of nitrogen. **Table 2. Theoretical oxygen and organic matter needed for different anammox-based approaches to complete nitrogen removal.** | | Reaction | Oxygen needed (mg O₂/mg N) | Organic matter needed (mg COD/mg N) | |---|---|---:|---:| | Case I: partial nitritation and anammox (PN/A) + denitrification | Partial nitritation: NH₃ + 1.5O₂ → NO₂⁻ + H₂O + H⁺ (i)
Anammox: NH₃ + 1.32NO₂⁻ + H⁺ → 1.02 N₂ + 0.26NO₃⁻ + 2H₂O (ii)
Denitrification: NO₃⁻ + 0.625CH₃COO⁻ + 0.625H⁺ → 0.5 N₂ + HCO₃⁻ + 0.25CO₂ + 0.75H₂O (iii)
Total reaction by (i × 1.32 + ii)/2.32 + iii × 0.11: NH₃ + 0.85O₂ + 0.07CH₃COO⁻ → 0.5 N₂ + 0.11HCO₃⁻ + 0.03CO₂ + 1.51H₂O + 0.07H⁺ | 1.94 | 0.32 | | Case II: complete nitrification + partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) | Complete nitrification: NH₃ + 2O₂ → NO₃⁻ + H₂O + H⁺ (i)
Partial denitrification: NO₃⁻ + 0.25CH₃COO⁻ → NO₂⁻ + 0.25HCO₃⁻ + 0.25CO₂ + 0.25H₂O (ii)
Anammox: NH₃ + 1.32NO₂⁻ + H⁺ → 1.02 N₂ + 0.26NO₃⁻ + 2H₂O (iii)
Total reaction by ((ii × 1.32 + iii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH₃ + 1.03O₂ + 0.16CH₃COO⁻ → 0.5 N₂ + 0.16HCO₃⁻ + 0.16CO₂ + 1.65H₂O + 0.03H⁺ | 2.35 | 0.73 | | Case III: partial nitritation and anammox (PN/A) + partial nitrate conversion and anammox (PD/A) | Partial nitritation: NH₃ + 1.5O₂ → NO₂⁻ + H₂O + H⁺ (i)
Anammox: NH₃ + 1.32NO₂⁻ + H⁺ → 1.02 N₂ + 0.26NO₃⁻ + 2H₂O (ii)
Partial denitrification: NO₃⁻ + 0.25CH₃COO⁻ → NO₂⁻ + 0.25HCO₃⁻ + 0.25CO₂ + 0.25H₂O (iii)
Total reaction by ((iii × 0.26 + ii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH₃ + 0.77O₂ + 0.03CH₃COO⁻ → 0.5 N₂ + 0.03HCO₃⁻ + 0.03CO₂ + 1.52H₂O + 0.03H⁺ | 1.76 | 0.14 | Although the strategy has theoretical and practical advantages, several questions need to be addressed before it is used to control nitrate. First, we need to investigate the nitrogen-removal pathways further. When calculating nitrogen changes in the reactor, we left out some secondary nitrogen processes, which may have affected the accuracy of the calculations. Future studies should use advanced methods, including isotope labeling, metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, to work out the complex networks through which microbes transform and recycle nitrogen (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Second, we need to test the strategy with real municipal wastewater. Earlier studies have reported partial denitrification and PD/A using the complex organic matter in real municipal wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to investigate the lasting effects of adding organic matter, especially across seasonal temperature changes. Third, future work should determine the best ranges for rbCOD concentration and the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen (TN), so that organic matter use can be kept as low as possible in real applications.

parts.title: Adding a little easy-to-eat food helps a main-treatment anammox tank remove nitrogen reliably and efficiently
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We ran an anammox tank to clean wastewater that was low in nitrogen. Anammox is a way of removing nitrogen in which special bacteria turn ammonium and nitrite into harmless nitrogen gas without using oxygen. The wastewater held 25–35 mg/L of ammonium plus nitrite. We ran the tank in two phases. In phase I we added no readily biodegradable organic matter, meaning food that bacteria can easily break down. In phase II we added a small amount of it. We measured this food as rbCOD, the part of the chemical oxygen demand (a measure of how much organic matter is in the water) that bacteria can easily use.

In phase I, the tank removed nitrogen well at first. But after long operation (75 days), nitrate built up in the water leaving the tank, and the share of nitrogen removed fell to 30%. When we looked at the microbes, anammox bacteria made up 2.15% of the community at the start and 1.78% at the end. Meanwhile, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, rose from 0.14% to 0.56%.

In phase II, we fed the tank acetate, a simple food, as rbCOD. We added 0.9 parts of carbon for every 1 part of nitrogen. Within 2 days, the nitrate in the outgoing water dropped. After that, the tank removed nitrogen much better, with an average of 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen left in the outgoing water. Even with the added food, most of the nitrogen was still removed by anammox.

We read the DNA of the microbes in the sludge (high-throughput sequencing). It showed that anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the community, which further supports their leading role. We put the better nitrogen removal down to three things. NOB were held back more strongly. Nitrate was cleaned up at the same time by partial denitrification (bacteria turning nitrate into nitrite) and by anammox. And the sludge formed more granules, which are small, dense clumps of bacteria. Overall, adding small amounts of rbCOD is a workable way to make main-treatment anammox tanks remove nitrogen reliably and efficiently.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, main-treatment (mainstream), nitrogen removal, readily biodegradable organic matter
parts.introduction_first:
Over the past ten years, many researchers have become interested in removing nitrogen from city wastewater with a method called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A). In this method, bacteria do the work without adding any carbon-based food. They first turn some of the ammonium into nitrite, and then anammox bacteria turn the nitrite and the rest of the ammonium into nitrogen gas. Because the process needs no extra food, it can make a wastewater treatment plant that uses no more energy than it produces (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017).

Plants can use PN/A in two ways, depending on how many stages they run. In a single-stage system, both steps happen in one tank. In a two-stage system, each step happens in its own tank. Keeping the two steps apart lets each kind of microbe grow in its own tank, which suits them better (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). For this reason, the two-stage system usually removes nitrogen faster than the single-stage system (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

In this study, we set up a main-treatment anammox system in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a tank that goes through a repeating cycle of filling, treating, settling and draining. When we ran the tank without rbCOD, a lot of nitrate built up in the outgoing water because unwanted NOB were active, and less nitrogen was removed. When we ran the tank with a small amount of rbCOD, the anammox tank recovered from the nitrate build-up and removed nitrogen very efficiently.

With this small amount of rbCOD, anammox was still the main way nitrogen was removed. Meanwhile, partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) removed the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself produced. NOB were also held back well, because the tank had less oxygen in it. In addition, the sludge formed more granules, which helped the slow-growing anammox bacteria thrive. Overall, adding small amounts of rbCOD is a workable way to make main-treatment anammox tanks remove nitrogen reliably and efficiently.
parts.introduction_rest:
Even so, using PN/A on a full scale to clean real city wastewater is still hard. One of the biggest worries is that the water leaving the system can still carry a lot of nitrate. That pushes the total nitrogen above the limits that the rules for releasing water into rivers and lakes allow (Zhuang et al., 2022). In a two-stage system, nitrate can come from both tanks. In the first tank, where ammonium is turned into nitrite, NOB can turn some of the nitrite into nitrate. In the second tank, the anammox tank, nitrate can come from anammox itself and from unwanted NOB.

Recent studies show that nitrate can be kept low in the first tank. Researchers have developed several ways to hold back NOB there. One is to give the tank air only at certain times instead of all the time. Another is to keep the sludge in the tank for a very short time, so that NOB have little chance to grow. A third is to take sludge out of the system, treat it separately with chemicals that block NOB, and then return it (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021). The second tank, the anammox tank, has become the main place where nitrate is made. Other researchers have reported too much nitrate in anammox tanks because unwanted NOB were active. This happened in several kinds of tanks: sequencing batch reactors (SBRs), completely stirred tank reactors, and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors, which are tanks filled with floating clumps of sludge (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most of the ways of holding back NOB that were developed for the first tank do not work in the second tank, because they may also block anammox. So we need to find ways to stop nitrate from building up in anammox tanks.

In early studies, rbCOD was seen as a problem for main-treatment anammox. The idea was that rbCOD should be removed before the water reached the tank. Otherwise, heterotrophs, which are bacteria that feed on organic matter, could grow too much and outcompete the anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). However, recent studies have reported that anammox bacteria can still stay active when the tank is run with a suitable amount of rbCOD. In particular, the share of nitrogen removed can rise above 90% when the tank is given 0.5 to 1.5 parts of carbon for every 1 part of nitrogen (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

However, most of these studies treated wastewater that was high in nitrogen, with 100 to 300 mg of nitrogen per litre. At such high levels, free ammonia or free nitrous acid (forms of ammonia and nitrite that are not bound to other substances) can hold back the growth of NOB (Ge et al., 2015). So in those studies, the extra nitrate made by NOB hardly mattered. We still do not know whether adding rbCOD can solve the problem of too much nitrate made by NOB in main-treatment anammox tanks.

There is another point to consider. In an anammox tank, partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) can mean that less organic matter is needed to remove nitrogen, and it can reduce the harm that organic matter does to anammox (Du et al., 2019). However, in most PD/A studies, the incoming water held mostly ammonium and nitrate (Du et al., 2019). In main-treatment anammox tanks, the incoming water holds mostly nitrite, and nitrate is made slowly by the anammox reaction itself. Very few studies have reported how PD/A works in main-treatment anammox tanks when rbCOD is present, and this needs more research (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up a main-treatment anammox tank and ran it in two phases, once with rbCOD and once without. We compared the two phases in four ways: how well they removed nitrogen, how steady they ran, which microbes lived in the sludge, and what the sludge looked like. From these results, we judged how small amounts of rbCOD affect main-treatment anammox, and we tested whether small amounts of rbCOD could help the tank remove more nitrogen.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we set up the experiment

We ran the main-treatment anammox tank in a 10 L sequencing batch reactor (SBR) (Figure 1). To start it, we added sludge from a small lab-scale anammox tank that was already treating nitrogen-rich wastewater. After this, the reactor held 4.9 g of sludge per litre.

The reactor ran three cycles a day. Each cycle had five steps (Figure 1B). First came 10 min of feeding, when we replaced half of the liquid in the tank (a volume exchange ratio of 50%). Next came 360 min of mixing without oxygen, then 30 min of settling, then 10 min of draining, and finally 70 min of standing still. The reactor ran at room temperature, 24–26°C. We never removed sludge from the reactor, apart from the sludge that washed out with the outgoing water and the sludge we took for samples. From this, we estimated that the sludge stayed in the reactor for more than 30 days on average. This average time is called the sludge retention time (SRT).

Figure 1

The main-treatment anammox tank: (A) a diagram of the setup and (B) the steps of each cycle.

The way we fed the tank changed with the wastewater, so we split its operation into two phases (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the tank with 5 L of outgoing water from a partial nitritation (PN) tank. This PN tank treated artificial city wastewater, a lab-made copy of real city wastewater. We describe the PN tank in the Supplementary material. The water fed to the anammox tank in phase I had little organic matter, a chemical oxygen demand (COD) of 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. Most of this was probably organic matter that bacteria find hard to break down, because the wastewater had already been treated by bacteria.

In phase II (days 76–135), we sent part of the raw artificial city wastewater (0.5 L) around the PN tank and mixed it with the PN tank's outgoing water (4.5 L) in a middle tank. This mixed water then went into the anammox tank. In this way, rbCOD, the food that bacteria can easily use, entered the system as acetate, at 24.2 mg COD/L. Apart from the different mix of organic matter in the incoming water, the tank was run in exactly the same way and under the same conditions in both phases.

Table 1

Main features of the water fed into the main-treatment anammox tank. The ± values show how much the measurements varied.

| | Ammonium nitrogen, NH4+-N (mg/L) | Nitrite nitrogen, NO2−-N (mg/L) | Nitrate nitrogen, NO3−-N (mg/L) | Total nitrogen, TN (mg/L) | COD (mg/L)

| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8

| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2

2.2.

Jar tests on how well partial denitrification/anammox could work in the tank

To find out how well partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) could work in the tank, we ran two batch tests. In a batch test, we take sludge out of the tank and grow the microbes in a closed container. We washed the sludge three times with deionized water (very pure water with the dissolved salts removed). We then split it among four separate cone-shaped flasks, each holding 0.5 L. After adding the food and nitrogen sources, we kept the flasks in shaking incubators at 25°C, shaking at 200 turns per minute. Throughout the tests, we bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks all the time to keep oxygen out.

Batch Test I asked whether nitrite could build up while denitrification was happening. So we added only nitrate (as sodium nitrate, NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. The starting nitrate was the same in every flask, 15 mg/L, but we added different amounts of acetate. This gave four flasks with starting ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 parts of carbon (COD) for every 1 part of nitrate nitrogen.

Batch Test II asked whether denitrification could be combined with the anammox process. Besides nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate, this test's feed also contained ammonium (as ammonium chloride, NH4Cl). The starting ammonium was 10 mg/L and the starting nitrate was 15 mg/L. Again, we added different amounts of acetate to four flasks, giving the same four ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 parts of carbon for every 1 part of nitrate.

2.3.

How we measured things

We measured chemical oxygen demand (COD), ammonium nitrogen, nitrite nitrogen, nitrate nitrogen, total nitrogen, and three measures of the sludge using standard methods (APHA, 2005). The three sludge measures were the mixed liquor suspended solids (the total amount of solid material floating in the tank), the mixed liquor volatile suspended solids (the part of those solids that burns away, which is mostly organic matter), and the sludge volume index (how much space the sludge takes up in water, which shows how well it settles). We tracked the temperature, pH (how acidic or alkaline the water is) and dissolved oxygen in the reactor continuously with a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the sizes of the sludge particles with a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4.

Working out how nitrogen changed during typical cycles

We worked out how nitrogen changed in the tank by looking at how the amounts of each nitrogen compound rose and fell over typical cycles. We only included the main routes by which nitrogen changes from one form to another. We used different calculations for the two phases of the tank.

In phase I, almost no rbCOD entered the tank. So we left out denitrification in our calculations. Instead, we calculated how much nitrogen was changed by anammox bacteria, by ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB, which turn ammonium into nitrite) and by NOB (which turn nitrite into nitrate) using Eqs. 1–3.

(1) TNanammox = ΔN = (NH4+-Ninitial + NO2−-Ninitial + NO3−-Ninitial) − (NH4+-Nfinal + NO2−-Nfinal + NO3−-Nfinal)

(2) NH4+-NAOB = NH4+-Ninitial − NH4+-Nfinal − TNanammox/2.04

(3) NO3−-NNOB = NO3−-Nfinal − NO3−-Ninitial − TNanammox × 0.26/2.04

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in mg N/L. NH4+-NAOB is the ammonium used up by AOB, in mg N/L. NO3−-NNOB is the nitrate made by NOB, in mg N/L. ΔN is the difference between the total inorganic nitrogen in the tank at the start and at the end of the cycle, in mg N/L. NH4+-Ninitial, NO2−-Ninitial and NO3−-Ninitial are the ammonium, nitrite and nitrate in the tank at the start of the cycle, in mg N/L. NH4+-Nfinal, NO2−-Nfinal and NO3−-Nfinal are the same three at the end of the cycle, in mg N/L.

In phase II, the tank had less oxygen than in phase I, and overall it removed nitrate (Section 3.2). So we left out nitrification, the step in which bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite, in our calculations. Instead, we calculated how much nitrogen was changed by anammox, by denitratation (turning nitrate into nitrite) and by denitritation (turning nitrite into nitrogen gas) using Eqs. 4–6.

(4) TNanammox = NH4+-Ninitial − NH4+-Nfinal × 2.04

(5) NO3−-Ndenitratation = NO3−-Ninitial + TNanammox × 0.26/2.04 − NO3−-Nfinal

(6) TNdenitritation = ΔN − TNanammox

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by the anammox route, in mg N/L. NO3−-Ndenitratation is the nitrate used up by denitratation, in mg N/L. TNdenitritation is the total nitrogen removed by denitritation, in mg N/L.

2.5.

Reading the microbes' DNA

We collected sludge from the reactor on day 1, day 75 and day 134. We freeze-dried it (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States) and stored it at −20°C. We pulled out the DNA using the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the maker's instructions. To check that the DNA was clean, we measured how much there was with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands).

Next, we copied one stretch of a gene called 16S rRNA, known as the V3–V4 region. This stretch differs between kinds of bacteria, so it works like a name tag. To copy it, we used PCR, a method that makes many copies of a chosen piece of DNA. Short starter pieces of DNA called primers mark where copying begins and ends. We used the bacterial primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). The copied DNA was then read on an Illumina MiSeq machine (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China).

From these data, we worked out which microbes were present, as described in our earlier report (Yang et al., 2017). The raw DNA readings are stored in the public NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database (Accession Number: PRJNA942604).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

How well the tank removed nitrogen with and without rbCOD

In phase I, we fed the main-treatment anammox tank almost no rbCOD. We could tell this because the tank hardly used any of it: the chemical oxygen demand (COD) in the tank fell by only 3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L (Figure 2A). The "±" shows how much the measurements varied. Nitrogen removal was also unsteady (Figures 2B,C). At first, from day 1 to day 40, the tank removed nitrogen well. But from day 41 to day 75, the nitrate in the outgoing water rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L. Ammonium and nitrite also built up at the end of phase I, which showed that the anammox bacteria were working less well. As a result, the share of nitrogen removed fell from 83% to 30%.

Figure 2

How much COD (A) and total nitrogen (B) the main-treatment anammox tank removed, and the amounts of different nitrogen compounds in the incoming and outgoing water (C).

In phase II, we added acetate as rbCOD, 24.2 mg COD/L. This raised the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen to 0.9, meaning 0.9 parts of carbon for every 1 part of nitrogen. On average, the tank removed 27.7 mg/L of COD, which shows that it used all of the rbCOD we fed in (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, the nitrate in the outgoing water dropped from 8.7 mg/L to 2.1 mg/L. After that, it stayed low, at 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L (Figure 2C). So the tank did remove nitrate. This suggested that denitrification was taking place in the tank. The ammonium and nitrite in the outgoing water also fell at the same time, which showed that the anammox bacteria had become active again. Overall, the tank removed nitrogen much better in phase II. On average, 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen was left in the outgoing water, and the share of nitrogen removed was 87.2% (Figure 2B).

3.2.

How the way nitrogen was changed changed after we added rbCOD

To see how nitrogen was being changed from one form to another, we followed the tank through a typical cycle. In phase I, before we added rbCOD, ammonium and nitrite were slowly used up, while nitrate built up a lot (Figure 3A). We compared how much nitrate was made with how much ammonium was used up. This ratio was 0.92. For the anammox reaction alone, the expected value is 0.26 (Strous et al., 1998). Our value was much higher, which showed that some other process was also making nitrate. When we traced how the nitrogen moved between forms, we found that nitrification was at work in the tank (Figure 3B). Nitrification is the work of two groups of bacteria: ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) turn ammonium into nitrite, and NOB turn nitrite into nitrate. Nitrification made 79% of the nitrate in the tank, and this is why the tank did not remove enough nitrogen.

Figure 3

How the amounts of different nitrogen compounds changed (A: phase I, C: phase II), and how nitrogen moved between forms (B: phase I, D: phase II), in a typical cycle of the main-treatment anammox tank.

In phase II, after we added rbCOD, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell at the same time in a typical cycle (Figure 3C). This shows that denitrification was removing not only the nitrate that came in with the wastewater but also the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself made. Tracing the nitrogen also showed that partial denitrification (bacteria turning nitrate into nitrite) was making extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria (Figure 3D). This boosted the anammox activity inside the tank. Even so, anammox was still the main way nitrogen was removed, accounting for 93% of it (Figure 3D). Denitrification removed even more nitrogen, so little total nitrogen was left in the outgoing water.

3.3.

What batch tests showed about partial denitrification/anammox in the anammox tank

To look more closely at partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) in the tank, we ran batch tests. In these tests, we took sludge out of the tank and grew the microbes in closed containers, so we could control exactly what we added. In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate, to study denitrification. We tried different ratios of carbon to nitrate-nitrogen (COD/NO3−-N). At every ratio, nitrite built up (Figures 4A–D). The largest share of nitrate that was turned into nitrite was 50.0%, at a carbon-to-nitrate ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the main-treatment anammox tank could supply extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria.

Figure 4

How the amounts of different nitrogen compounds changed in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we also added ammonium to the nitrate and acetate. In the first hour, a lot of nitrate was removed, but nitrite still built up at every carbon-to-nitrate ratio. This shows that partial denitrification was happening (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all fell at the same time. Because the batch tests had no oxygen, the ammonium was removed by anammox. The nitrite that the anammox bacteria needed came from partial denitrification. Together, these results prove that PD/A can take place in the main-treatment anammox tank.

3.4.

How the microbes in the main-treatment anammox tank changed

We used DNA sequencing to see how a small amount of rbCOD affected the microbes in the main-treatment anammox tank (Figure 5). In phase I, without rbCOD, anammox bacteria made up 2.08% of the microbial community at the start and 1.73% at the end. Most of them belonged to a group called Candidatus Kuenenia. Over the same time, AOB (Nitrosomonas) rose from 0.29% to 0.40% of the community, and NOB (Nitrospira) rose from 0.14% to 0.56%. These rises match what we saw in the tank: nitrate built up and nitrogen removal got worse.

In phase II, after we added rbCOD, anammox bacteria recovered to 2.48% of the community, while AOB fell to 0.05% and NOB to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding the right amount of rbCOD helps anammox bacteria thrive and holds back the nitrifying bacteria.

The denitrifying bacteria also changed after we added rbCOD. In phase I, the most common denitrifying bacteria were Denitratisoma, which can carry out complete denitrification, turning nitrate all the way into nitrogen gas (NO3− → N2). Its share of the community fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II. Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter, which earlier studies have identified as microbes that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020), became much more common in phase II. Thauera rose from 0.18% to 2.15% of the community, and Candidatus Competibacter rose from 0.15% to 1.35%. These results gave further evidence that PD/A was happening in the tank.

Figure 5

How the mix of microbes in the main-treatment anammox tank changed.

3.5.

How granules formed in the main-treatment anammox tank

The sludge we started the main-treatment anammox tank with already contained some granules. Granules are clumps of bacteria larger than 200 μm across (a micrometre, μm, is a thousandth of a millimetre). They made up 17.4% of the sludge, and the sludge particles were 130.8 μm across on average (Figure 6). The size of the sludge stayed steady in phase I. In phase II, it grew a lot, to 195.6 μm on average. Granules eventually made up 52.5% of all the sludge in the tank, which shows that adding rbCOD in phase II helped the sludge form granules. Granules can help anammox bacteria thrive, because these bacteria grow more easily in large clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

Figure 6

How the sizes of the sludge particles in the main-treatment anammox tank changed.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

4.1.

Why adding rbCOD helped the tank remove more nitrogen

In this study, adding rbCOD quickly brought the main-treatment anammox tank back from a state where a lot of nitrate had built up (Figure 2). The tank removed nitrogen well even with only a small amount of rbCOD. There may be several reasons why the tank removed more nitrogen once we added this food.

First, nitrification was held back more strongly, so less nitrate was made inside the tank. Nitrification is the work of bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate. In phase I, we ran the tank without rbCOD. Nitrification was fairly active, so more nitrate was made and the tank removed nitrogen less well (Figures 2, 3). Other researchers have shown the same thing (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020).

The dissolved oxygen in the tank was 0.06–0.08 mg/L. This oxygen came from the incoming wastewater and from air blown in at the top of the tank while the machine mixed the water (Figure 3A). Some kinds of nitrifying bacteria can live on very little oxygen. These include comammox bacteria, which can turn ammonium straight into nitrate, and NOB in the group Nitrospira (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have been doing much of the nitrification in the tank, because the share of Nitrospira rose a lot (Figure 5).

In phase II, after we added rbCOD, the dissolved oxygen in the tank fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L. This was possibly because of the activity of aerobic heterotrophic bacteria, which are bacteria that use oxygen to break down organic matter (Figure 3C). So the tank had even less oxygen in phase II than in phase I, and this held back nitrification. As a result, both the ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which turn ammonium into nitrite, and the NOB became less common in phase II (Figure 5).

Second, the tank carried out partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A). This removed two kinds of nitrate at the same time: the nitrate that came in with the wastewater, and the nitrate that the anammox reaction itself made. Our batch tests, in which we ran the sludge in closed containers, showed that nitrite can build up while nitrate is being turned into nitrite (Figures 4A–D). Anammox bacteria can then use this nitrite and remove it, with ammonium as their electron donor, the substance that supplies the electrons they need for the reaction. We saw this in our cycle analysis (Figure 3D) and in the batch tests (Figures 4E–H). In this way, the nitrate in the tank was cleaned up while using only a little organic matter, and the tank removed nitrogen very efficiently.

In addition, although the rbCOD came in with the wastewater at the start, nitrate was being made (by anammox) and used up (by denitrification) the whole time through the cycle (Figure 3). So we expected endogenous denitrification to happen, meaning denitrification by bacteria that live on their own stored food instead of on food from the wastewater. In this study, the bacteria Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter were the ones doing the partial denitrification in phase II (Figure 5). Both can rebuild rbCOD into their own stored food, such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). So the rbCOD that came in with the wastewater may have been turned into stored food at the start, and this stored food may have kept partial denitrification going through the whole cycle.

Third, anammox became more active and grew more, which made the process work better and more steadily. In this study, the direct effect of rbCOD (acetate) on anammox activity may be small. Small amounts of acetate do not hold back anammox activity (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox species, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can get energy from short-chain fatty acids (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this may not have mattered much in our study, because the anammox bacteria in the tank were mostly of the group Candidatus Kuenenia throughout the experiment.

So rbCOD mainly helped anammox in indirect ways. For example, when bacteria use oxygen to break down rbCOD, they use up the dissolved oxygen in the main body of the water. This reduces the harm that oxygen does to anammox activity (Strous et al., 1999). Also, when bacteria use rbCOD without oxygen to carry out partial denitrification, they make extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria, which made anammox more active (Figure 3). Furthermore, rbCOD helped the sludge in the tank release more extracellular polymers, sticky substances that bacteria make outside their cells, and helped the sludge form granules (Figure 6). Other researchers have shown the same (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). This helped the tank hold on to its slow-growing anammox bacteria and let them build up (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). As a result, the share of anammox bacteria rose from 1.73% to 2.48% after we added small amounts of rbCOD (Figure 5). At the same time, anammox stayed the main way nitrogen was removed (Figure 3).

4.2.

Using this approach and what to study next

In this study, we used an effective and practical way to solve the problem of nitrate build-up caused by unwanted NOB in main-treatment anammox tanks. Other ways of reducing nitrate have been reported. These include bubbling nitrogen gas through the incoming wastewater to remove its oxygen, building the tank tall and narrow so that less of its surface touches the air, and covering the anammox tank (Díaz et al., 2020). However, these measures may not be cheap or practical in some cases. This is especially true when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because they need big changes to how the tank is built.

That is why we chose to add a small amount of rbCOD. This can reduce nitrate build-up with only a small change: part of the raw city wastewater can be sent to the anammox tank, or a little extra organic carbon can be added (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). The rbCOD can also come from sludge fermentation liquid, the liquid left over when sludge is broken down, if the treatment plant has it (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). Finally, the way we ran the main-treatment anammox process can also be used in continuous flow reactors, where wastewater flows through the tank all the time. However, extra steps may be needed to help the anammox bacteria stay in the tank. These include filling the tank with suitable carriers, which are materials that give bacteria a place to grow, and using a cyclone, a spinning device that keeps the heavier granules while letting other sludge leave (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).

Even when NOB are not making too much nitrate, running a main-treatment anammox tank with a small amount of rbCOD is still helpful, because it can remove all of the nitrogen (Zhuang et al., 2022). Other researchers have reported that both partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) and partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) help remove nitrogen (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen without any added food, while PD/A removed the nitrate made by the anammox reaction.

Table 2 shows a theoretical equation for this process for Case III, and compares it with two other anammox-based processes that aim to remove all the nitrogen (Cases I and II). In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen without added food, but 11% of the ammonium ends up as nitrate. Cleaning up this nitrate by denitrification still uses organic carbon. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 mg COD for every mg of nitrogen removed.

In Case II, the nitrite that anammox needs is made by first turning all of the ammonium into nitrate (complete nitrification) and then turning some of that nitrate into nitrite (partial denitrification). This approach needs more oxygen and organic carbon than the way PN makes nitrite. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 mg of oxygen and 0.73 mg COD for every mg of nitrogen removed.

Case III has theoretical advantages over Cases I and II. First, most of the nitrite is made by PN, so we expect it to use less oxygen and organic carbon than Case II. Second, the nitrate is cleaned up by PD/A, which uses less organic carbon than Case I. In addition, the PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it also needs less oxygen than Case I. Overall, of the three cases, Case III can remove 100% of the nitrogen while needing the least oxygen (1.76 mg O2 for every mg of nitrogen) and the least organic matter (0.14 mg COD for every mg of nitrogen).

Table 2
