| | Reaction | Oxygen needed (mg O2 per mg N) | Organic matter needed (mg COD per mg N) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Case I: PN/A + denitrification | Partial nitrification: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii) Denitrification: NO3− + 0.625CH3COO− + 0.625H+ → 0.5 N2 + HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.75H2O (iii) Total reaction by (i × 1.32 + ii)/2.32 + iii × 0.11: NH3 + 0.85O2 + 0.07CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.11HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.51H2O + 0.07H+ | 1.94 | 0.32 |
| Case II: Complete nitrification + PD/A | Complete nitrification: NH3 + 2O2 → NO3− + H2O + H+ (i) Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (ii) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (iii) Total reaction by ((ii × 1.32 + iii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 1.03O2 + 0.16CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.16HCO3− + 0.16CO2 + 1.65H2O + 0.03H+ | 2.35 | 0.73 |
| Case III: PN/A + PD/A | Partial nitrification: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii) Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (iii) Total reaction by ((iii × 0.26 + ii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 0.77O2 + 0.03CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.03HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.52H2O + 0.03H+ | 1.76 | 0.14 |

Even with these theoretical and practical advantages, several questions need to be answered before this way of controlling nitrate can be used. First, we need to study more closely how the nitrogen is removed. When we worked out how nitrogen changed form in the tank, we left out some of the other ways the microbes handle nitrogen, and this may have made our calculations less accurate. Future studies should untangle the complicated networks in which microbes recycle nitrogen. They can use advanced tools such as isotope labeling, which tracks specially marked atoms as they move between microbes, and metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, which read the DNA of all the microbes and the genes they are actively using (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020).

Second, the approach should be tested further with real city wastewater, even though other researchers have reported partial denitrification and PD/A using the complex organic matter in real city wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to see the long-term effects of adding organic matter, especially as the temperature changes with the seasons. Third, future studies should find the best range for the amount of rbCOD and for the ratio of rbCOD to total nitrogen, so that as little organic matter as possible is used in real use.

parts.title: Adding a little easy-to-eat food to a nitrogen-removing tank helps it run steadily and remove more nitrogen
parts.abstract:
Abstract

We ran a tank of bacteria that removes nitrogen from wastewater using a process called anammox. Anammox bacteria turn ammonium and nitrite into nitrogen gas, so the nitrogen leaves the water. We tested the tank with wastewater that contained only small amounts of ammonium and nitrite (25–35 mg/L). In the first part of the study (phase I), we gave the tank no extra food. In the second part (phase II), we added a small amount of "readily biodegradable" food, meaning food that bacteria can break down easily. We measured this food as chemical oxygen demand (rbCOD), a standard way of measuring how much food is in the water.

In phase I, the tank removed nitrogen well at first. But after running for a long time (75 days), nitrate built up in the water leaving the tank. Nitrate is a form of nitrogen that is not removed, so the share of nitrogen the tank removed fell to 30%. When we checked which bacteria lived in the tank, we found that anammox bacteria made up 2.15% of the bacteria at the start and 1.78% at the end. Meanwhile, nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, rose from 0.14% to 0.56%.

In phase II, we added the food as acetate, a simple food that bacteria can use. We gave the tank 0.9 times as much carbon as nitrogen (a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 0.9). Within 2 days, the nitrate in the water leaving the tank dropped. The tank then removed nitrogen much better, with an average of 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen in the water leaving it. Even with the extra food, anammox was still the main way the tank removed nitrogen. We confirmed this with high-throughput sequencing, a method that reads the DNA of all the bacteria in a sample. It showed that anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the bacteria, which further supports their leading role.

We think the tank removed nitrogen better for three reasons. First, the NOB were held back more strongly. Second, a small amount of denitrification (bacteria using food to turn nitrate into nitrogen gas) cleaned up the nitrate at the same time as anammox did. Third, the sludge formed more granules, small clumps of bacteria. Overall, adding small amounts of easily broken-down food is a workable way to make anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream of wastewater run steadily and remove nitrogen well.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, mainstream, nitrogen removal, readily biodegradable organics
parts.introduction_first:
Over the past ten years, many researchers have become interested in a way of removing nitrogen from city wastewater that uses no added food. It is called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A). In the first step, called partial nitritation, bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite. In the second step, called anammox, anammox bacteria turn the nitrite and the ammonium into nitrogen gas. Because the bacteria make their own food from carbon dioxide, the plant does not need to burn fuel to run it. This can make a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) "energy-neutral", meaning it uses no more energy than it produces (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017).

People have built PN/A plants in two different ways, depending on how many tanks they use. A single-stage plant does both steps in one tank. A two-stage plant does them in two separate tanks. In the two-stage plant, the first tank carries out partial nitritation and the second carries out anammox. This lets each tank favour different bacteria, so each one can grow well (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). For this reason, a two-stage PN/A plant usually removes nitrogen faster than a single-stage one (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

In this study, we set up an anammox tank that treats the main nitrogen stream of wastewater. We used a sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a tank that is filled, mixed, settled and drained in repeated cycles. When we ran the tank with no extra food, nitrate built up in the water leaving it. This happened because NOB were active, and it lowered how much nitrogen the tank removed. When we ran the tank with a small amount of easily broken-down food, the nitrate no longer built up, and the tank removed nitrogen very well.

With this small amount of food, anammox stayed the main way the tank removed nitrogen. Partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A), in which bacteria use food to turn nitrate into nitrite and then anammox bacteria turn the nitrite and ammonium into nitrogen gas, removed the nitrate that anammox produced. The NOB were also held back well, because the tank had less oxygen than before. In addition, the sludge formed more granules, which helped the slow-growing anammox bacteria grow. Overall, adding small amounts of easily broken-down food is a workable way to make anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream of wastewater run steadily and remove nitrogen well.
parts.introduction_rest:
So far, it has been hard to use PN/A on the main nitrogen stream of wastewater, the large amount of nitrogen that comes straight from the city's sewers. One big worry is that too much nitrate ends up in the water leaving the plant. This pushes the total nitrogen above the limit that the rules allow for water being released (Zhuang et al., 2022).

In a two-stage plant, nitrate can be made in both tanks. In the first tank, which carries out partial nitritation, NOB turn nitrite into nitrate. In the second tank, which carries out anammox, nitrate is made by anammox bacteria and by NOB that are not wanted there. Recent studies show that the nitrate made in the first tank can be kept low. Researchers have developed several ways to hold back the NOB. One is to turn the air supply on and off. Another is to keep the sludge in the tank for only a very short time, so that bacteria that grow fast cannot build up. A third is to take some sludge out of the tank and treat it with chemicals that stop the NOB (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021).

The second tank, however, has become a major source of nitrate. Studies have reported that NOB can make too much nitrate in anammox tanks of several designs. These include sequencing batch reactors (SBRs), completely stirred tank reactors, where the water is mixed all the time, and expanded granular sludge blanket reactors, where the sludge settles into a thick layer (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most of the methods developed to hold back NOB in the first tank do not work in the second tank, because they may also slow down the anammox bacteria. So we need to find ways to stop nitrate from building up in anammox tanks.

In early studies, easily broken-down food was seen as a problem for anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream. The idea was that this food should be removed before the water reaches the tank. Otherwise, heterotrophs, bacteria that feed on food from other living things, could grow too much and outcompete the anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015). Recent studies, though, have shown that anammox bacteria can keep working when a suitable amount of this food is present. In fact, the share of nitrogen the tank removes can rise above 90% when the tank is given a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 0.5–1.5 (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

However, most of these studies treated wastewater with a lot of nitrogen, 100–300 mg of nitrogen per litre. At such high levels, free ammonia or free nitrous acid, two forms of nitrogen that can be harmful, can hold back the growth of NOB (Ge et al., 2015). So the extra nitrate these studies produced was small enough to ignore. We still do not know whether adding easily broken-down food can solve the problem of too much nitrate made by NOB in anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream.

There is another option. Partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) in anammox tanks means that some bacteria use food to turn nitrate into nitrite, and then anammox bacteria turn the nitrite and ammonium into nitrogen gas. This way, less food is needed to remove nitrogen, and the food has less of the harmful effect on anammox bacteria (Du et al., 2019). But in most PD/A studies, the water flowing into the tank contained mostly ammonium and nitrate (Du et al., 2019). In anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream, the incoming nitrite and nitrate are mostly in the form of nitrite. Nitrate is then made slowly as anammox goes on. Very few studies have reported how PD/A works in these tanks when easily broken-down food is also present, and this needs more research (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up and ran an anammox tank that treats the main nitrogen stream of wastewater. We ran it in two phases, once with easily broken-down food and once without. We compared the two phases in how well they removed nitrogen, how steadily they ran, which bacteria lived in them, and what the sludge looked like. From these results, we looked at how a small amount of easily broken-down food affects an anammox tank that treats the main nitrogen stream. We also judged whether this small amount could help the tank remove more nitrogen.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we set up the experiment

We treated the main nitrogen stream of wastewater in a 10-litre sequencing batch reactor (SBR), a tank that is filled, mixed, settled and drained in repeated cycles (Figure 1). To start it, we added sludge, the thick, muddy material full of bacteria, from a small lab-scale anammox tank that treated wastewater with a lot of nitrogen. After we added this sludge, the tank held 4.9 g of sludge per litre.

We ran the tank three times a day. Each cycle had five steps (Figure 1B). First, we fed in 50% of the tank's volume of wastewater for 10 minutes. Next, we mixed the tank for 360 minutes with no oxygen. Then we let the sludge settle for 30 minutes, drained out 10 minutes, and left the tank idle for 70 minutes. The tank ran at room temperature, between 24 and 26°C. Apart from letting some sludge wash out with the water leaving the tank and taking samples, we did not throw away any sludge while the tank was running. Because we kept the sludge, the sludge stayed in the tank for a long time. We estimated that the sludge age (the average time sludge stays in the tank) was longer than 30 days.

Figure 1

The anammox tank that treats the main nitrogen stream: (A) a diagram of the tank, and (B) the pattern of its daily cycles.

Depending on what was in the incoming wastewater, the tank ran in two phases (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the tank 5 litres of water leaving a partial nitritation (PN) tank. This PN tank treated made-up city wastewater, and we describe it in the Supplementary material. The water we fed in had a low amount of food, measured as chemical oxygen demand (COD), of 25.1 ± 8.8 mg/L. Because the wastewater had already been treated by bacteria, most of this food was probably hard-to-break-down organic compounds.

In phase II (days 76–135), we changed the feed. We took 0.5 litres of the raw made-up city wastewater and mixed it with 4.5 litres of water leaving the PN tank in a middle tank. We then fed this mixture into the anammox tank. This brought easily broken-down food into the system in the form of acetate, at 24.2 mg COD/L. Apart from the different food in the incoming water, the tank's daily cycles and conditions were exactly the same in phases I and II.

Table 1

Main features of the water fed into the anammox tank. NH4+-N is ammonium nitrogen, NO2−-N is nitrite nitrogen, NO3−-N is nitrate nitrogen, TN is total nitrogen, and COD is chemical oxygen demand. The number after ± shows how much the values varied.

| | NH4+-N (mg/L) | NO2−-N (mg/L) | NO3−-N (mg/L) | TN (mg/L) | COD (mg/L)

| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8

| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2

2.2.

Small tests outside the tank to check whether partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) could work

We ran two small tests outside the tank to see whether PD/A could work in the tank. PD/A is partial denitrification/anammox: bacteria use food to turn nitrate into nitrite, and anammox bacteria then turn the nitrite and ammonium into nitrogen gas.

For each test, we washed sludge from the tank three times with very pure water. We then put it into four separate cone-shaped flasks, each holding 0.5 litres. We added food and nitrogen to the flasks and kept them in shaking incubators at 25°C, shaking at 200 turns per minute. Throughout the tests, we bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks to keep them free of oxygen.

In Batch Test I, we wanted to find out whether nitrite could build up while denitrification was happening. So we added only nitrate (as sodium nitrate, NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. The nitrate started at the same level in every flask, 15 mg/L, and we added different amounts of acetate. This gave four flasks starting ratios of food to nitrate (COD/NO3−-N) of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0.

In Batch Test II, we wanted to find out whether denitrification could be combined with anammox. Besides nitrate (NaNO3) and acetate, we also added ammonium (as ammonium chloride, NH4Cl) to the feed. Ammonium started at 10 mg/L and nitrate at 15 mg/L. Again, we added different amounts of acetate to the four flasks, giving starting ratios of food to nitrate (COD/NO3−-N) of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0.

2.3.

How we measured things

We measured chemical oxygen demand (COD), ammonium nitrogen (NH4+-N), nitrite nitrogen (NO2−-N), nitrate nitrogen (NO3−-N), total nitrogen (TN), mixed liquor suspended solids, mixed liquor volatile suspended solids and sludge volume index using standard methods (APHA, 2005). The mixed liquor suspended solids are the amount of solid material in the mixed sludge water. The mixed liquor volatile suspended solids are the part of that material that burns away, which is mostly organic matter. The sludge volume index shows how much sludge settles into a given volume of water.

We tracked the temperature, pH (how acidic or alkaline the water is) and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the tank continuously with a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany). We measured the sizes of the sludge particles with a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom).

2.4.

Working out how nitrogen changed in typical cycles

We worked out how nitrogen changed in the tank from the changes in the amounts of different nitrogen compounds in typical cycles. Our calculations covered only the main ways nitrogen changed. We used different calculations for the two phases of the tank.

In phase I, almost no easily broken-down food entered the tank. So we left out denitrification in our calculations. We calculated how much nitrogen anammox bacteria, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and NOB changed using Equations 1–3. AOB are bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite, and NOB are bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate.

(1) TNanammox = ΔN = (NH4+−Ninitial + NO2−−Ninitial + NO3−−Ninitial) − (NH4+−Nfinal + NO2−−Nfinal + NO3−−Nfinal)

(2) NH4+−NAOB = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal − TNanammox/2.04

(3) NO3−−NNOB = NO3−−Nfinal − NO3−−Ninitial − TNanammox × 0.26/2.04

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in mg N/L. NH4+−NAOB is the ammonium used up by AOB, and NO3−−NNOB is the nitrate made by NOB, both in mg N/L. ΔN is the difference between the total inorganic nitrogen in the tank water at the start and at the end of the cycle, in mg N/L. NH4+−Ninitial, NO2−−Ninitial and NO3−−Ninitial are the amounts of ammonium, nitrite and nitrate in the tank water at the start of the cycle, and NH4+−Nfinal, NO2−−Nfinal and NO3−−Nfinal are the same amounts at the end of the cycle. All are in mg N/L.

In phase II, the tank had less oxygen than in phase I. The tank removed nitrate overall (Section 3.2). So we left out nitrification, the step that turns ammonium into nitrite, in our calculations. Instead, we calculated how much nitrogen anammox changed, how much denitratation (NO3− → NO2−) changed, and how much denitritation (NO2− → N2) changed, using Equations 4–6.

(4) TNanammox = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal × 2.04

(5) NO3−−Ndenitratation = NO3−−Ninitial + TNanammox × 0.26/2.04 − NO3−−Nfinal

(6) TNdenitritation = ΔN − TNanammox

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by the anammox pathway, in mg N/L. NO3−−Ndenitratation is the nitrate turned into nitrite by denitratation, and TNdenitritation is the total nitrogen removed by denitritation, both in mg N/L.

2.5.

Reading the DNA of the bacteria (high-throughput sequencing)

We collected sludge from the tank on day 1, day 75 and day 134. We freeze-dried the samples (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States) and stored them at −20°C. We pulled out the DNA with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the maker's instructions. We checked how pure the DNA was with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands).

To find out which bacteria were present, we focused on one gene, the 16S rRNA gene. All bacteria have this gene, but it differs slightly between kinds, so it works like a name tag. We copied one part of it, called the V3–V4 region, many times over using PCR, a method that makes many copies of a chosen piece of DNA. To do this, we used two short starter pieces of DNA, called primers: 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). The copied DNA was then read on an Illumina MiSeq machine (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China).

From these data, we worked out which bacteria were in the tank, as described in our earlier report (Yang et al., 2017). We have placed the raw DNA readings in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA), a public database, under Accession Number PRJNA942604.
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

How well the tank removed nitrogen with and without easily broken-down food

In phase I, we gave the tank almost no easily broken-down food. We could see this because the tank removed only a tiny amount of chemical oxygen demand (COD), a measure of how much food is in the water. The COD removed in the tank was 3.8 ± 2.1 mg/L (Figure 2A). The "±" shows how much the measurements varied.

The tank's nitrogen removal was unstable (Figures 2B,C). It removed nitrogen well at first, from days 1 to 40. But from day 41 to day 75, the nitrate in the water leaving the tank rose from 2.6 to 8.7 mg/L. At the end of phase I, ammonium and nitrite also built up in the tank. This showed that the anammox bacteria were becoming less active. As a result, the share of nitrogen the tank removed fell from 83% to 30%.

Figure 2

How much COD (A) and total nitrogen (B) the tank removed, and the amounts of each form of nitrogen in the water going into and coming out of the tank (C).

In phase II, we added 24.2 mg of acetate per litre of COD to the tank. This raised the amount of easily broken-down food to 0.9 times the amount of nitrogen. On average, the tank removed 27.7 mg/L of COD, which means it used up all of the food we fed it (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, the nitrate in the water leaving the tank dropped from 8.7 mg/L to 2.1 mg/L. It then stayed low, at 1.1 ± 0.9 mg/L, for the rest of the run (Figure 2C). So the tank did remove the nitrate. This suggested that denitrification had started in the tank. At the same time, the ammonium and nitrite in the water leaving the tank also went down, which showed that the anammox bacteria had become active again.

Overall, the tank removed nitrogen much better in phase II. The water leaving it held on average 3.4 mg/L of total nitrogen, and the tank removed 87.2% of the nitrogen on average (Figure 2B).

3.2.

How the way nitrogen was changed changed after we added easily broken-down food

We followed the tank over several cycles, and this showed that the way nitrogen was changed inside the tank had changed. In a typical phase I cycle, before we added the food, ammonium and nitrite were slowly used up, while nitrate built up a lot (Figure 3A).

To see why, we compared how much nitrate was made with how much ammonium was removed. We call this ratio ΔNO3−-N/ΔNH4+-N. In phase I it was 0.92. That is much higher than the 0.26 that the anammox reaction alone would produce (Strous et al., 1998). So something else was making nitrate. We also tracked how nitrogen moved between forms, which we call the nitrogen mass flow. It suggested that nitrification was happening in the tank (Figure 3B). Nitrification is the work of nitrifying bacteria, which turn ammonium into nitrite and then turn some of the nitrite into nitrate. Nitrification made 79% of the nitrate, and this was why the tank could not remove enough nitrogen.

Figure 3

Changes in the amounts of each form of nitrogen (A: phase I, C: phase II) and in the ways nitrogen was changed (B: phase I, D: phase II) in typical cycles of the tank.

In phase II, after we added the food, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all went down at the same time in a typical cycle (Figure 3C). This shows that denitrification removed not only the nitrate that came in with the wastewater but also the nitrate that anammox made. The nitrogen mass flow also showed that partial denitrification (PD) was happening (Figure 3D). In PD, bacteria turn nitrate into nitrite, and this gave the anammox bacteria extra nitrite to work with. As a result, the anammox bacteria in the tank became more active.

According to Figure 3D, anammox was still the main way the tank removed nitrogen, making up 93% of the nitrogen removal. Denitrification then helped the tank remove even more nitrogen, so the water leaving it held little total nitrogen.

3.3.

Testing partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) in separate bottles

To show more clearly how PD/A could work in the tank, we ran batch tests. In these tests, we took sludge out of the tank and put it in separate bottles, so we could control what went into each bottle.

In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the bottles, to study denitrification. At every carbon/nitrogen ratio we tried, nitrite built up (Figures 4A–D). The highest share of nitrate turned into nitrite was 50.0%, which happened at a carbon/nitrogen ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that denitrification in the tank could supply extra nitrite for anammox.

Figure 4

Changes in the amounts of each form of nitrogen in Batch Test I (A–D) and Batch Test II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we also added ammonium to the bottles, along with nitrate and acetate. In the first hour, nitrate was used up a lot, while nitrite built up at every carbon/nitrogen ratio. This showed that PD was happening (Figures 4E–H). After that, ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all went down at the same time.

The bottles had no oxygen at all. So the ammonium was removed by anammox, and the nitrite for anammox came from PD. This proves that PD/A can work in the tank.

3.4.

How the bacteria in the tank changed

We used high-throughput sequencing to find out how a small amount of easily broken-down food affected the bacteria in the tank (Figure 5). In phase I, without the food, anammox bacteria (mostly a group called Candidatus Kuenenia) made up 2.08% of the bacteria. They fell to 1.73%. Meanwhile, two other groups of bacteria grew a lot. Ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB), which turn ammonium into nitrite, rose from 0.29% to 0.40%. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), which turn nitrite into nitrate, rose from 0.14% to 0.56%. These changes match what we saw in the tank: nitrate built up, and the tank removed less nitrogen.

In phase II, after we added the food, the anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the bacteria again. The AOB fell to 0.05% and the NOB to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding the food in the right amount helps anammox bacteria grow and holds back the nitrifying bacteria.

The bacteria that carry out denitrification also changed after we added the food. In phase I, the main denitrifying bacteria were Denitratisoma, which can carry out complete denitrification, turning nitrate all the way into nitrogen gas (NO3− → N2). Their share of the bacteria fell from 3.91% in phase I to 2.00% in phase II.

Two other groups, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter, are known to carry out PD (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020). Both became much more common in phase II. Thauera rose from 0.18% to 2.15% of the bacteria, and Candidatus Competibacter rose from 0.15% to 1.35%. These results give further evidence that PD/A was happening in the tank.

Figure 5

Changes in the mix of bacteria in the tank.

3.5.

How the sludge formed granules

The sludge we started with already contained some granules, small clumps of bacteria. Granules larger than 200 μm made up 17.4% of the sludge, and the granules were 130.8 μm across on average (Figure 6). A micrometre (μm) is one-thousandth of a millimetre.

In phase I, the size of the sludge stayed the same. In phase II, it grew a lot, to 195.6 μm. Granules eventually made up 52.5% of all the bacteria in the tank. This shows that the sludge formed more granules after we added the food in phase II. Granules can help anammox bacteria grow, because these bacteria are more likely to grow in large clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

Figure 6

Changes in the sizes of the sludge in the tank.
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

4.1.

Why did adding easily broken-down food help the tank remove more nitrogen?

In this study, adding easily broken-down food quickly brought the anammox tank that treats the main nitrogen stream back to normal, after nitrate had built up (Figure 2). The tank removed nitrogen well even with only a small amount of this food. There may be several reasons why the food helped.

First, the food held back nitrification more strongly, so less nitrate was made inside the tank. Nitrification is the process in which bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate. In phase I, we gave the tank no extra food. Nitrification was fairly active, so more nitrate was made and the tank removed less nitrogen (Figures 2, 3). Other researchers have shown the same thing (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020).

The tank had a little oxygen in it, 0.06–0.08 mg/L. This oxygen came from the incoming wastewater and from the air at the top of the tank, and it was carried into the tank by the mechanical mixing (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying bacteria need very little oxygen to work. These include complete ammonia oxidizers (comammox), which can turn ammonium all the way into nitrate by themselves, and NOB in the group called Nitrospira (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have helped nitrification in the tank, because the number of Nitrospira bacteria rose a lot (Figure 5).

In phase II, after we added the food, the oxygen in the tank fell to 0.02–0.04 mg/L. This was probably because bacteria that feed on food and need oxygen were now active (Figure 3C). So the tank had less oxygen in phase II than in phase I, and this held back nitrification. As a result, both ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB, the bacteria that turn ammonium into nitrite) and NOB became less common in phase II (Figure 5).

Second, the tank carried out partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A). This removed the nitrate that came in with the wastewater and also the nitrate that anammox made. In batch tests, where we ran small amounts of water in containers, we found that nitrite can build up while bacteria turn nitrate into nitrogen gas (Figures 4A–D). Anammox bacteria can also use this nitrite and remove it, using ammonium as their food. We showed this with a cycle analysis, which tracks the nitrogen compounds through each cycle of the tank (Figure 3D), and with batch tests (Figures 4E–H). In this way, the nitrate in the tank was cleaned up while only a little food was used, and the tank removed nitrogen very well.

We also added the food with the incoming wastewater at the start, but nitrate was still made (by anammox) and removed (by denitrification) throughout the whole cycle (Figure 3). So we expected the bacteria to use up their own stored food for denitrification. In phase II, the bacteria that carried out partial denitrification were Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter (Figure 5). Both can turn their stored food, such as glycogen and polyhydroxyalkanoates, back into easily broken-down food (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). So the food in the incoming wastewater may have been turned into stored food at the start and then supported partial denitrification for the whole cycle.

Third, the food helped anammox bacteria work and grow, which made the process run better and more steadily. In this study, the food we added (acetate) may have had only a small direct effect on anammox. Low amounts of acetate do not stop anammox (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox bacteria, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can get energy from short-chain fatty acids, which are simple acids (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this may not have mattered much in our study, because anammox bacteria from the group Candidatus Kuenenia made up most of the anammox bacteria in the tank throughout the experiment.

So the food mainly helped anammox in indirect ways. For example, when bacteria use the food with oxygen, they use up the oxygen in the main body of the water. This reduces the oxygen that can hold back anammox (Strous et al., 1999). Also, when bacteria used the food without oxygen to carry out partial denitrification, they made extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria, which helped anammox work (Figure 3).

The food also helped the sludge in the tank form more granules (Figure 6), as other researchers have shown (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). Granules help keep the slow-growing anammox bacteria in the tank and make them more common (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). As a result, anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the bacteria after we added a small amount of food, up from 1.73% (Figure 5). At the same time, anammox stayed the main way the tank removed nitrogen (Figure 3).

4.2.

Using this approach and what to study next

In this study, we used a workable way to solve the problem of nitrate building up in anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream. The nitrate builds up because NOB are active when they are not wanted. Other ways to reduce nitrate have been reported. These include bubbling nitrogen gas through the incoming wastewater to remove its oxygen, making the tank taller than it is wide so that less of its surface touches the air, and covering the anammox tank (Díaz et al., 2020). However, these measures may not be cheap or practical in some cases, especially when upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because they need big changes to how the tank is built.

That is why we chose to add a small amount of easily broken-down food. This can reduce nitrate build-up with only a small change: either sending part of the untreated city wastewater to the anammox tank, or adding a small amount of food from outside (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). If a treatment plant already has liquid made by fermenting sludge, it can also supply the food in that way (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021).

Finally, our approach for anammox tanks that treat the main nitrogen stream also works for tanks that receive a steady flow of water. However, extra steps may be needed to keep the anammox bacteria in the tank. These include filling the tank with suitable carriers, which are materials the bacteria can grow on, and using a cyclone, a spinning device that keeps the granules in the tank (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).

Even when NOB are not making too much nitrate, running an anammox tank with a small amount of easily broken-down food is still useful, because it can remove all the nitrogen (Zhuang et al., 2022). Both partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) and partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) helped remove nitrogen, as other researchers have reported (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen by making the bacteria produce their own food, while PD/A removed the nitrate that anammox made.

We worked out the amounts of oxygen and food needed for three cases, shown in Table 2. Case III is our approach, and we compared it with two other anammox-based ways of removing all the nitrogen, Cases I and II.

In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen by making the bacteria produce their own food, but 11% of the ammonium ends up as nitrate. Cleaning up this nitrate by denitrification still uses food. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 mg COD of food for each mg of nitrogen removed.

In Case II, the nitrite for anammox is made by first turning all the ammonium into nitrate (complete nitrification) and then turning nitrate into nitrite by partial denitrification. This needs more oxygen and more food than making nitrite by partial nitritation alone. Case II uses 2.35 mg of oxygen and 0.73 mg COD of food for each mg of nitrogen removed.

Case III has advantages over Cases I and II. First, most of the nitrite is made by partial nitritation, so we expect it to use less oxygen and food than Case II. Second, the nitrate is cleaned up by PD/A, which uses less food than Case I. In addition, the PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it can also use less oxygen than Case I. Overall, Case III removes 100% of the nitrogen and needs the least oxygen (1.76 mg O2 for each mg of nitrogen) and the least food (0.14 mg COD for each mg of nitrogen) of the three cases.

Table 2

| | Reaction | Oxygen needed (mg O2 for each mg of nitrogen) | Food needed (mg COD for each mg of nitrogen) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Case I: PN/A + denitrification | Partial nitritation: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii) Denitrification: NO3− + 0.625CH3COO− + 0.625H+ → 0.5 N2 + HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.75H2O (iii) Total reaction by (i × 1.32 + ii)/2.32 + iii × 0.11: NH3 + 0.85O2 + 0.07CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.11HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.51H2O + 0.07H+ | 1.94 | 0.32 |
| Case II: Complete nitrification + PD/A | Complete nitrification: NH3 + 2O2 → NO3− + H2O + H+ (i) Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (ii) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (iii) Total reaction by ((ii × 1.32 + iii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 1.03O2 + 0.16CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.16HCO3− + 0.16CO2 + 1.65H2O + 0.03H+ | 2.35 | 0.73 |
| Case III: PN/A + PD/A | Partial nitritation: NH3 + 1.5O2 → NO2− + H2O + H+ (i) Anammox: NH3 + 1.32NO2− + H+ → 1.02 N2 + 0.26NO3− + 2H2O (ii) Partial denitrification: NO3− + 0.25CH3COO− → NO2− + 0.25HCO3− + 0.25CO2 + 0.25H2O (iii) Total reaction by ((iii × 0.26 + ii) + i × 1.06)/2.06: NH3 + 0.77O2 + 0.03CH3COO− → 0.5 N2 + 0.03HCO3− + 0.03CO2 + 1.52H2O + 0.03H+ | 1.76 | 0.14 |

Even though this approach has advantages in theory and in practice, several questions need to be answered before it is used.

First, how the tank removes nitrogen needs more study. When we worked out how nitrogen changed in the tank, we left out some of the other ways the bacteria process nitrogen. This might have made our calculations less accurate. In future studies, the complicated networks of bacteria that recycle nitrogen should be worked out using advanced methods. These include isotope labeling, which tracks a special form of an element to follow where it goes, and metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, which read all the DNA in a sample and all the genes the bacteria are actually using (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020).

Second, the approach should be tested further with real city wastewater. Other researchers have reported partial denitrification and PD/A using the complicated food found in real city wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to see what happens over time when food is added, especially as the temperature changes with the seasons.

Third, future studies should find the best amount of easily broken-down food and the best food-to-nitrogen ratio, so that as little food as possible is used in real plants.

parts.title: Removing nitrogen from wastewater with an anammox reactor, a nitrogen-removing bacterium, while adding a small amount of easily broken-down food for microbes
parts.abstract:
Abstract

In this study, we ran an anammox reactor to clean wastewater that contained only a little nitrogen. The wastewater held 25–35 milligrams of ammonium (NH4+) and nitrite (NO2−) in each liter. Anammox is a way for bacteria to turn ammonium and nitrite into harmless nitrogen gas without using oxygen. We ran the reactor in two phases. In phase I, we added no food for microbes that can break down nitrogen compounds. In phase II, we added a small amount of this food, which we call rbCOD.

In phase I, the reactor removed nitrogen well at the start. But nitrate, the form of nitrogen that anammox bacteria turn nitrite into, built up in the water leaving the reactor after 75 days of running. As a result, the reactor removed only 30% of the nitrogen. When we looked at the microbes, anammox bacteria made up 2.15% of the community in phase I but only 1.78% in phase II. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB), the bacteria that turn nitrite into nitrate, made up 0.14% in phase I but 0.56% in phase II.

In phase II, we added acetate, a simple carbon-rich food, to the reactor. We added it at a ratio of 0.9, meaning 0.9 times as much acetate as nitrate. Within 2 days, the nitrate in the water leaving the reactor dropped. The reactor then removed nitrogen very well, with an average of 3.4 milligrams of nitrogen per liter in the water leaving it. Even with this added food, anammox was still the main way the reactor lost nitrogen.

We also read the DNA of the microbes in the reactor, a method called high-throughput sequencing. It showed that anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the community, which further supports the idea that anammox was the main way the reactor removed nitrogen. We put the improvement in nitrogen removal down to three things. First, the food held back the NOB more strongly. Second, the reactor cleaned up nitrate by partly turning it into nitrite and then into nitrogen gas, a process called partial denitrification. Third, the sludge, the thick layer of microbes on the reactor walls, formed larger clumps. Overall, adding a small amount of this easily broken-down food is a workable way to remove nitrogen reliably and efficiently in anammox reactors that treat ordinary city wastewater.

Keywords: anammox, partial denitrification, mainstream (treatment of ordinary city wastewater), nitrogen removal, easily broken-down food for microbes
parts.introduction_first:
Over the past ten years, many researchers have become very interested in removing nitrogen from city wastewater without using oxygen. One approach is called partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A). In this approach, bacteria first turn ammonium into nitrite, and then anammox bacteria turn the nitrite into nitrogen gas. This approach can make a wastewater treatment plant that uses no extra energy (a wastewater treatment plant, or WWTP) (Kartal et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2017).

Different versions of this approach have been developed, depending on how many steps they use. Some use a single step, and others use two steps. The two-step version splits the work into two separate reactors. This helps each step focus on the right microbes, so that each one can grow and multiply (Isanta et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020). As a result, the two-step version usually removes more nitrogen than the single-step version (Liu et al., 2018).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

In this study, we set up an anammox treatment system that treats ordinary city wastewater, using a sequencing batch reactor (SBR). In this type of reactor, the wastewater is fed in batches, and the microbes work in a repeating cycle. When we ran the reactor without any food for microbes that can break down nitrogen compounds, a lot of nitrate built up in the water leaving the reactor. This happened because the NOB were doing something we did not want, and it lowered how much nitrogen the reactor removed.

Adding a small amount of this food brought the anammox reactor back from the nitrate buildup and made it remove nitrogen very efficiently. With the small amount of food, anammox was still the main way the reactor removed nitrogen. However, the reactor also removed nitrate that the anammox reaction itself made. The NOB were held back well because the reactor had no oxygen. The sludge also formed larger clumps, which helped anammox bacteria that grow slowly multiply. Overall, adding a small amount of this easily broken-down food is a workable way to remove nitrogen reliably and efficiently in anammox reactors that treat ordinary city wastewater.
parts.introduction_rest:
So far, it has been hard to run ordinary city wastewater treatment plants that use the two-step version of partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) on a full scale. One of the biggest worries is that the water leaving the plant can still contain a lot of nitrate. That means the total nitrogen in the water leaving the plant goes over the legal limit (Zhuang et al., 2022).

In the two-step version, nitrate can be made in two separate reactors. In the first reactor, the nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) turn nitrite into nitrate. In the second reactor, an anammox reactor, anammox bacteria turn nitrite into nitrogen gas. The NOB in the second reactor can also do something we did not want, and this nitrate is called undesired NOB.

Recent studies have found ways to keep nitrate from building up in the first reactor. One is to pump air into the reactor only at certain times. Another is to use a very short sludge retention time (SRT), which is the average time the sludge stays in the reactor. A third is to treat the sludge that is left over in the second reactor with chemicals that block the NOB (Gilbert et al., 2014; Regmi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014, 2021). The second reactor, the anammox reactor, has become a major source of nitrate.

In different kinds of anammox reactors, too much nitrate has been reported when the undesired NOB were doing something we did not want. This happened in sequencing batch reactors (SBR), in completely stirred tank reactors, and in expanded granular sludge blanket reactors, which are tanks where the sludge is packed into small grains (Sánchez Guillén et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020). Most of the ways of blocking the NOB in the first reactor do not work in the second reactor, because they may hold back the anammox bacteria. That is why we need to find ways to reduce the nitrate that builds up in an anammox reactor.

In the early studies, researchers treated the nitrate in the water leaving the anammox reactor as a problem. They measured it as rbCOD, the easily broken-down food for microbes. They thought this food should be removed by treating the wastewater first. The reason is that it can make heterotrophs, the microbes that feed on other material, grow too much. These microbes can then outcompete the anammox bacteria (Xu et al., 2015).

However, recent studies have reported that anammox bacteria can still be kept working. In particular, the reactor can remove more than 90% of the nitrogen when it is run with a suitable amount of this food. This happens when the ratio of nitrate to ammonium (the C/N ratio) is between 0.5 and 1.5 (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2021; Silveira et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021a; He et al., 2023).

But most of these studies used wastewater with a lot of nitrogen, 100–300 milligrams of nitrogen per liter. That nitrogen can hold back the NOB, because it can be present as free ammonia or free nitrous acid, which are forms of nitrogen that are easy for microbes to use (Ge et al., 2015). As a result, the reactor makes almost no extra nitrate. We still need to find out whether adding this easily broken-down food can fix the extra nitrate that anammox reactors make because of the NOB.

There is another option. An anammox reactor can also carry out partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A). In this approach, the anammox bacteria turn nitrite into nitrate, and the microbes turn that nitrate into nitrogen gas. This can lower the amount of organic nitrogen the reactor needs to remove, and it can reduce the harm that organic material does to the anammox bacteria (Du et al., 2019). However, in most studies of this approach, the nitrogen in the incoming wastewater is mostly ammonium and nitrate (Du et al., 2019).

In ordinary city wastewater treatment plants, nitrite is the main form of nitrate and nitrite in the incoming water. The anammox reaction then slowly turns nitrite into nitrate. Very few studies have looked at how PD/A works in these plants when the food for microbes is present, and this needs more research (Chen et al., 2020; Zhuang et al., 2022).

In this study, we set up and ran an ordinary city wastewater treatment plant that uses an anammox reactor, with and without the easily broken-down food for microbes. We compared how well the reactor removed nitrogen, how steady the process was, which microbes were present, and the shape of the sludge in the two phases. From these results, we tested how a small amount of this food affects the treatment process, and we judged whether it could improve nitrogen removal.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we set up the reactor

We ran the main treatment of ordinary city wastewater in a sequencing batch reactor (SBR) that held 10 liters (Figure 1). We filled it with sludge collected from a lab-scale anammox reactor that treated wastewater containing a lot of nitrogen. At the start, the reactor held 4.9 grams of microbes in each liter of water.

The reactor ran for three cycles a day. Each cycle had 10 minutes of feeding, when we added food. During this time, we replaced half of the water in the reactor (a volume exchange ratio of 50%). Next came 360 minutes of mixing without oxygen, then 30 minutes of settling so the sludge could sink, then 10 minutes of draining off the water, and finally 70 minutes of idling (Figure 1B). The reactor ran at room temperature, 24–26°C. We did not throw away sludge during the run, except for the sludge we washed out of the water leaving the reactor and the sludge we took samples from. We estimated that the sludge stayed in the reactor for more than 30 days on average. This is called the sludge retention time (SRT).

Figure 1

(A) Diagram of the main anammox reactor and (B) how we ran it.

Depending on what the incoming wastewater contained, the reactor ran in two phases (Figure 1A and Table 1). In phase I (days 1–75), we fed the reactor the 5-liter batch of water that came out of a partial nitritation (PN) reactor. This reactor had treated a man-made version of city wastewater. We describe it in the Supplementary material. The incoming wastewater had a low chemical oxygen demand (COD), 25.1 ± 8.8 milligrams per liter. COD is a measure of how much organic material is in the water, and the number after the ± sign shows how much the readings varied. Most of this organic material would probably be tough, hard-to-break-down compounds, because the wastewater had already been treated by microbes.

In phase II (days 76–135), we took out part of the raw city wastewater (0.5 liters) and sent it straight through. We mixed it with the PN wastewater (4.5 liters) in the middle tank. This mixed water then went into the anammox reactor. As a result, the reactor received a small amount of easily broken-down food for microbes, which we call rbCOD. It was added as acetate, at 24.2 milligrams of COD per liter. Apart from the different amounts of organic material in the incoming wastewater, the two phases were run in exactly the same way, with the same conditions.

Table 1

The main features of the incoming wastewater in the main anammox reactor.

| | NH4+-N (mg/L) | NO2−-N (mg/L) | NO3−-N (mg/L) | TN (mg/L) | COD (mg/L) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase I | 14.3 ± 2.5 | 14.1 ± 2.4 | 1.2 ± 0.8 | 29.4 ± 2.8 | 25.1 ± 8.8 |
| Phase II | 12.5 ± 1.8 | 12.3 ± 1.4 | 2.0 ± 0.6 | 26.8 ± 2.0 | 45.2 ± 11.2 |

2.2.

Small tests in flasks to see how well the food worked

We ran two small batch tests to see how well the food worked in the reactor. In a batch test, we put a set amount of microbes and food into a closed container and watch what happens. We first washed the sludge from the reactor three times with deionized water, which is very pure water with its dissolved minerals removed. Then we moved it into four separate 0.5-liter cone-shaped flasks. We added the food and the nitrogen compounds, and kept the flasks in shaking incubators (200 turns per minute) at 25°C. During the tests, we bubbled nitrogen gas through the flasks all the time to keep them free of oxygen.

In the first test, we wanted to know whether nitrite could build up while the microbes were turning nitrite into nitrogen gas. So we added only nitrate (as sodium nitrate, NaNO3) and acetate to the flasks. The starting amount of nitrate was the same in all four flasks, 15 milligrams per liter. We added different amounts of acetate, giving starting COD/NO3−-N ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 in the four flasks. The COD/NO3−-N ratio compares the amount of organic material with the amount of nitrate. A value of 1 means the two are in equal amounts.

In the second test, we wanted to see whether the anammox process could be combined with the microbes' work. Besides nitrate and acetate, the incoming water also contained ammonium (as ammonium chloride, NH4Cl). The starting amounts of ammonium and nitrate were 10 and 15 milligrams per liter, respectively. We added different amounts of acetate to the four flasks, giving starting COD/NO3−-N ratios of 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0.

2.3.

How we measured things

We measured several things using standard methods (APHA, 2005). These were COD, ammonium (NH4+-N), nitrite (NO2−-N), nitrate (NO3−-N), total nitrogen (TN), the amount of solid material floating in the mixed liquid, the amount of that floating material that turns into gas when heated, and the sludge volume index, which shows how much sludge the reactor holds. We also used a WTW Multi 3,620 instrument (WTW, Bavaria, Germany) to measure the temperature, the pH (how acidic or alkaline the water is) and the dissolved oxygen (DO) in the reactor. Finally, we used a laser particle size analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 2000, Malvern, United Kingdom) to find out how big the sludge clumps were.

2.4.

Working out how nitrogen was removed in typical cycles

We worked out how nitrogen was removed in the reactor from how the amounts of the different nitrogen compounds changed over typical cycles. Our calculation covered only the main ways nitrogen was removed. We used different methods in the two phases.

In phase I, we added almost no food for microbes, so we left out the ways the microbes turned nitrite into nitrogen gas. We worked out how much nitrogen anammox bacteria, ammonium-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and NOB removed using Eqs. 1–3.

(1) TNanammox = ΔN = (NH4+−Ninitial + NO2−−Ninitial + NO3−−Ninitial) − (NH4+−Nfinal + NO2−−Nfinal + NO3−−Nfinal)

(2) NH4+−NAOB = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal − TNanammox/2.04

(3) NO3−−NNOB = NO3−−Nfinal − NO3−−Ninitial − TNanammox × 0.26/2.04

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by anammox bacteria, in milligrams of nitrogen per liter. NH4+−NAOB is the ammonium used up by AOB, in the same units. NO3−−NNOB is the nitrate made by NOB, in the same units. ΔN is the difference between the total inorganic nitrogen at the start and at the end of the cycle, in milligrams of nitrogen per liter. NH4+−Ninitial, NO2−−Ninitial and NO3−−Ninitial are the starting amounts of ammonium, nitrite and nitrate, in milligrams of nitrogen per liter. NH4+−Nfinal, NO2−−Nfinal and NO3−−Nfinal are the amounts at the end of the cycle, also in milligrams of nitrogen per liter.

In phase II, the reactor ran with less oxygen than in phase I. Overall, it removed nitrate well (Section 3.2). So we left out the ways the microbes turned ammonium into nitrite. We worked out how much nitrogen anammox bacteria, nitrate reduction (turning nitrate into nitrite) and nitrite reduction (turning nitrite into nitrogen gas) removed using Eqs. 4–6.

(4) TNanammox = NH4+−Ninitial − NH4+−Nfinal × 2.04

(5) NO3−−Ndenitratation = NO3−−Ninitial + TNanammox × 0.26/2.04 − NO3−−Nfinal

(6) TNdenitritation = ΔN − TNanammox

Here, TNanammox is the total nitrogen removed by the anammox process, in milligrams of nitrogen per liter. NO3−−Ndenitratation is the nitrate removed by nitrate reduction, in the same units. TNdenitritation is the total nitrogen removed by nitrite reduction, in the same units.

2.5.

Reading the DNA of the microbes

We collected sludge from the reactor on days 1, 75 and 134 and freeze-dried it (BT2KXL, Virtis, United States), which removes the water from the sludge. We then stored it at −20°C. We pulled the DNA out of the sludge with the Fast DNA Kit (MPBiomedicals, CA, United States), following the maker's instructions. We checked how pure the DNA was with a Nanodrop Spectrophotometer (ND-1000, Isogen Life Science, Netherlands).

To find out which microbes were present, we read a gene called the 16S rRNA gene. All bacteria carry it, but it differs from one kind of bacterium to another, so it works like a name tag. We copied one part of this gene, the V3–V4 region, many times over using PCR (polymerase chain reaction). PCR needs short starter pieces of DNA, called primers. We used the primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACG GGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTAC HVGGGTWTCT AAT-3′). The copied DNA was then read on an Illumina MiSeq machine (Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China).

From these DNA readings, we identified the microbes as described in our earlier report (Yang et al., 2017). The raw DNA readings are stored in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database (Accession Number: PRJNA942604).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

How much nitrogen the reactor removed, with and without the food

In phase I, we ran the main anammox reactor with almost no food for microbes that can break down nitrogen compounds. We measured this food with a standard test called COD (chemical oxygen demand). COD tells us how much oxygen would be needed to break down the nitrogen compounds in the water. A low COD means there is little food. The reactor removed only 3.8 milligrams of COD per liter, give or take 2.1 (Figure 2A). The COD removal was not statistically significant. This means our measurements could not show a real drop, though it does not prove there was none.

The reactor's nitrogen removal was not steady, as Figures 2B and 2C show. It worked well at the start, from day 1 to day 40. But from day 41 to day 75, the nitrate in the water leaving the reactor rose from 2.6 to 8.7 milligrams per liter. Ammonium and nitrite also built up at the end of phase I. This shows that the anammox bacteria in the reactor were working less. As a result, the reactor removed only 30% of the nitrogen, down from 83% in phase I.

Figure 2

How much COD (A) and total nitrogen (B) the main anammox reactor removed, and how much of each nitrogen compound was in the water going in and coming out (C).

In phase II, we added 24.2 milligrams of COD per liter of acetate to the main anammox reactor. This raised the amount of food for microbes that can break down nitrogen compounds to 0.9 times the amount of nitrate. On average, the reactor removed 27.7 milligrams of COD per liter. This shows that the food was used up completely (Figure 2A). Within 2 days, the nitrate in the water leaving the reactor fell from 8.7 to 2.1 milligrams per liter. After that, it stayed low, at 1.1 milligrams per liter give or take 0.9. Overall, the reactor removed nitrate. This suggested that the nitrate in the reactor was being cleaned up. At the same time, the ammonium and nitrite in the water leaving the reactor went down at the same time, which shows that the anammox bacteria were working again. In phase II, the reactor removed nitrogen very well. On average, the water leaving it held 3.4 milligrams of total nitrogen per liter, and it removed 87.2% of the nitrogen (Figure 2B).

3.2.

How the nitrogen compounds changed after we added the food

We tracked the nitrogen compounds in the reactor over the repeating cycle to see how the main anammox reactor changed its nitrogen pathway. In a typical phase I cycle, before we added the food, ammonium and nitrite were slowly removed, while nitrate built up a lot (Figure 3A). We compared the nitrate made with the ammonium removed. We call this ratio ΔNO3−-N/ΔNH4+-N. It was 0.92. That is much higher than the 0.26 that an anammox reaction alone would give (Strous et al., 1998). This extra value points to a second way the nitrate was being made. The amount of nitrogen flowing in and out suggested that nitrification, the step where bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite, broke down some of the ammonium into nitrite and broke down part of the nitrite into nitrate in the anammox reactor (Figure 3B). Nitrification made up 79% of the nitrate made. That was not enough to remove all of the nitrogen from the main anammox reactor.

Figure 3

How the nitrogen compounds changed (A: phase I, C: phase II) and the nitrogen pathways (B: phase I, D: phase II) in typical cycles of the main anammox reactor.

After we added the food in phase II, the ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all went down at the same time in a typical cycle (Figure 3C). This shows that the reactor removed nitrate in two ways at once: the nitrate in the water going in, and the nitrate made by the anammox reaction itself. The amount of nitrogen flowing in and out also showed that the reactor was partly turning nitrate into nitrite, a process called partial denitrification (PD). This extra nitrite gave the anammox bacteria more material to work with (Figure 3D). As a result, the anammox bacteria in the reactor were working more actively. Figure 3D shows that anammox was still the main way the reactor removed nitrogen, making up 93% of the nitrogen removed. The partial denitrification then made the reactor remove even more nitrogen, leaving only a small amount of total nitrogen in the water leaving the reactor.

3.3.

Testing the food in small containers: how much partial denitrification the reactor could do

To see how much partial denitrification the main anammox reactor could do, we ran batch tests. In a batch test, we add a small amount of wastewater to a container, run it, and then measure what is left. We also ran them with the food added.

In Batch Test I, we added only nitrate and acetate to the feed, to see how much denitrification could happen. As Figures 4A–D show, nitrite built up at every ratio of food to nitrate. The highest nitrate-to-nitrite ratio, 50.0%, came with a food-to-nitrate ratio of 2.0. These results suggest that the denitrification in the main anammox reactor could supply extra nitrite for the anammox bacteria.

Figure 4

How the nitrogen compounds changed in Batch Tests I (A–D) and II (E–H).

In Batch Test II, we also added ammonium to the feed, together with nitrate and acetate. In the first hour, a lot of nitrate was removed. Nitrite, however, built up at every food-to-nitrate ratio, which shows that partial denitrification was happening (Figures 4E–H). After that, the ammonium, nitrite and nitrate all went down at the same time. Under these conditions, with no oxygen, the anammox bacteria removed the ammonium. The nitrite they needed for anammox was made by partial denitrification. So we have shown that the reactor could do partial denitrification together with anammox.

3.4.

How the microbes changed in the main anammox reactor

We used high-throughput sequencing, which reads the DNA of many microbes at once, to see how a small amount of food for microbes that can break down nitrogen compounds affected the community of microbes in the main anammox reactor (Figure 5). In phase I, without the food, anammox bacteria made up 2.08% of the community. Most of them were Candidatus Kuenenia. With the food, their share fell to 1.73%. Meanwhile, the share of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) rose from 0.14% to 0.56%, and the share of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria that can break down nitrate (AOB) rose from 0.29% to 0.40%. These trends fit with the nitrate building up and the reactor removing nitrogen less well as the reactor ran.

After we added the food in phase II, the anammox bacteria made up 2.48% of the community again. The NOB fell to 0.05%, and the AOB fell to 0.23%. These results suggest that adding the food properly helped anammox bacteria grow and helped hold back the nitrifying bacteria.

We also saw a change in the denitrifying bacteria after we added the food. In phase I, the most common denitrifying bacteria were Denitratisoma, which can carry out complete denitrification, turning nitrate all the way into nitrogen gas (N2). Their share fell from 3.91% to 2.00% in phase II. Two other groups, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter, have been identified as the microbes that carry out partial denitrification (Du et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2020). Both became much more common in phase II, with their shares rising from 0.18% to 2.15% and from 0.15% to 1.35%. These results give further evidence that the reactor was doing partial denitrification together with anammox.

Figure 5

How the mix of microbes in the main anammox reactor changed.

3.5.

How the sludge formed clumps in the main anammox reactor

The sludge we added to the main anammox reactor was made of sludge grains larger than 200 micrometers (μm), which is 0.2 millimeters. That is 17.4% of the sludge's total weight. On average, the grains were 130.8 micrometers across (Figure 6). The sludge size stayed steady in phase I and grew a lot, to 195.6 micrometers, in phase II. In the end, the sludge grains made up 52.5% of the reactor's total weight of microbes. This shows that the sludge clumps formed after we added the food in phase II. Sludge clumps can help anammox bacteria grow, because these bacteria are more likely to grow in large clumps (Vlaeminck et al., 2010; Laureni et al., 2019).

Discussion

4.1.

Why adding the easily broken-down food helped the reactor remove nitrogen

In this study, adding the easily broken-down food for microbes quickly brought the main anammox reactor back from the nitrate buildup (Figure 2). The reactor removed nitrogen very well even with only a little of this food. There may be several reasons why adding the food helped the reactor remove nitrogen.

First, the food held back nitrification, the process in which bacteria turn ammonium into nitrite and then into nitrate. With less food, the reactor made less nitrate in its own water. In phase I, we ran the reactor without any food. At that time, nitrification was fairly active, so the reactor made more nitrate and removed less nitrogen (Figures 2, 3). Other researchers have shown the same thing (Díaz et al., 2020; Li W. et al., 2020).

The oxygen in the reactor, 0.06–0.08 milligrams per liter, came from the incoming wastewater and from the air at the top of the reactor while the reactor was being mixed (Figure 3A). Some nitrifying bacteria can use oxygen very readily. These include the complete ammonia oxidizer (comammox), a type of nitrifying bacterium, and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) from the group Nitrospira (Liu and Wang, 2013; Akaboci et al., 2018; Roots et al., 2019). They may have helped nitrification in the reactor because the number of Nitrospira rose a lot (Figure 5).

In phase II, however, the oxygen in the reactor dropped to 0.02–0.04 milligrams per liter. This may be because of the activity of bacteria that use oxygen to feed on organic matter (Figure 3C). As a result, the reactor had much less oxygen than in phase I, and this held back nitrification. So both the number of ammonium-to-nitrite bacteria (AOB) and the number of NOB went down in phase II (Figure 5).

Second, the reactor reached a balance between the food and the nitrate. We call this balance PD/A. It removed nitrate from the incoming wastewater and nitrate made by the anammox reaction at the same time. Batch tests, where we run the reactor in a closed container, have shown that nitrite can build up while nitrate is being turned into nitrogen gas (Figures 4A–D). The cycle analysis, which tracks which microbes use which chemicals, showed that anammox bacteria can use this nitrite and remove it (Figure 3D). The batch test showed the same thing (Figures 4E–H). In this way, the nitrate in the reactor was cleaned up with only a little organic matter being used up. This made the reactor remove nitrogen very efficiently.

The food was added to the incoming wastewater at the start. Even so, nitrate was made by the anammox reaction and then turned into nitrogen gas by the nitrate-removing bacteria, and this went on without a break through the whole cycle (Figure 3). We therefore expected the bacteria to carry out denitrification themselves. In this study, two kinds of bacteria, Thauera and Candidatus Competibacter, did the cleaning-up of nitrate in phase II (Figure 5). Both can use the food as their own source of carbon, such as glycogen (stored sugar) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (Lopez-Vazquez et al., 2009; Andreolli et al., 2022). So the food in the incoming wastewater may have been passed on to these bacteria at the start and kept them going through the whole cycle.

Third, the food helped anammox bacteria grow and work, which made the process work better and more stable. In this study, the direct effect of the food (acetate) on anammox activity may be limited. A small amount of acetate does not hold back anammox activity (Huang et al., 2014). Some anammox bacteria, such as Candidatus Anammoxoglobus propionicus and Candidatus Brocadia fulgida, can use short-chain fatty acids to get their energy (Kartal et al., 2007, 2008). However, this route may play little part in our study, because throughout the experiment the anammox bacteria in the reactor were mostly from the group Candidatus Kuenenia. So the food mainly helped anammox indirectly.

For example, when the food is broken down with oxygen, it uses up oxygen in the water. This lowers the oxygen that would otherwise hold back anammox activity (Strous et al., 1999). In addition, the anammox bacteria that use the food without oxygen gave the anammox bacteria extra nitrite, which helped anammox activity (Figure 3). The food also helped the sludge in the main anammox reactor form larger clumps (Figure 6), as other researchers have shown (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2021a). This helped hold back and encourage anammox bacteria that grow slowly (Zhu et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2021b). As a result, the share of anammox bacteria rose from 1.73% to 2.48% after we added a small amount of the food (Figure 5). At the same time, anammox stayed the main way the reactor removed nitrogen (Figure 3).

4.2.

How to use this approach, and what to study next

In this study, we used an effective and practical way to solve the nitrate buildup caused by the NOB doing something we did not want in the main anammox reactors. Other researchers have reported ways to lower the amount of nitrate produced. These include flushing the incoming wastewater with nitrogen gas to remove its oxygen, making the reactor walls shorter by building a tall wall for each meter of width, and covering the anammox reactor with protective covers (Díaz et al., 2020). However, these measures may not be cheap or work well in some cases. This is especially true for upgrading existing wastewater treatment plants, because the reactor design has to be changed a great deal.

So we used a different approach: adding a small amount of the easily broken-down food. This can reduce nitrate buildup, with only a small change, by sending part of the incoming city wastewater into the anammox reactor or by adding a small amount of organic carbon from outside (Le et al., 2019; Fofana et al., 2022). The food can also be supplied as liquid from sludge fermentation, if the treatment plant has it (Cao et al., 2013; Basset et al., 2016; Ali et al., 2021). Finally, our approach for treating ordinary city wastewater can also be used in reactors that treat wastewater continuously, where the water flows through the system all the time. However, extra measures may be needed to keep more anammox bacteria in the reactor. These include filling the reactor with proper carriers and using a cyclone, a device that spins the sludge, to keep only the clumps (Wett et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).

Even when the NOB do not make too much nitrate, running the main anammox reactor with a small amount of the food is useful, because it can remove all the nitrogen (Zhuang et al., 2022). Other researchers have reported that both partial nitritation/anammox (PN/A) and partial denitrification/anammox (PD/A) help remove nitrogen (Li J. et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022). In our study, PN/A removed most of the nitrogen by itself, while PD/A removed the nitrate made by the anammox reaction.

We worked out a theoretical equation for this process in Table 2 for Case III. We compared it with the other anammox processes that aim to remove all the nitrogen (Cases I and II). In Case I, PN/A removes nitrogen by itself, but 11% of the ammonium is eventually turned into nitrate. The nitrate then has to be cleaned up by denitrification, which still uses organic carbon. Overall, Case I needs 0.32 milligrams of organic carbon for every milligram of nitrogen.

In Case II, the nitrite made by anammox comes from complete nitrification of ammonium followed by the cleaning-up of nitrate by PD/A. This approach needs more oxygen and organic carbon than the PN route. Overall, Case II uses 2.35 milligrams of oxygen and 0.73 milligrams of organic carbon for every milligram of nitrogen.

Case III has theoretical advantages over Cases I and II. First, nitrite is made mainly by PN, so we expect it to save oxygen and organic carbon compared with Case II. Second, the cleaning-up of nitrate by PD/A uses less organic carbon than in Case I. In addition, the PD/A in Case III can remove some ammonium without using oxygen, so it also saves oxygen compared with Case I. Overall, Case III can remove all the nitrogen while needing the least oxygen (1.76 milligrams of oxygen per milligram of nitrogen) and the least organic matter (0.14 milligrams of organic carbon per milligram of nitrogen) of the three cases.

Even with these theoretical and practical advantages, several questions still need to be answered before we can use our nitrate control approach. First, we need to learn more about how the reactor removes nitrogen. When we calculated how nitrogen changed in the reactor, we left out some of the other ways microbes recycle nitrogen, and this might affect how accurate our calculations are. Future studies should work out the complex networks of microbes that recycle nitrogen, using advanced methods such as isotope labeling (tagging nitrogen with slightly different forms of nitrogen so we can trace where it goes), metagenomics and metatranscriptomics (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020).

Second, we need to check whether this nitrate control approach works with real city wastewater. Other researchers have reported using PD and PD/A with complex organic carbon in real city wastewater (Shi et al., 2019; Du et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2020). Longer experiments are also needed to see how adding organic matter affects the reactor over a long time, especially as temperatures change with the seasons.

Third, future studies should find the best range of the amount of food and the best ratio of food to nitrogen (the rbCOD/TN ratio). This would keep the use of organic matter as low as possible in real use.
